According to the World Health Organization, harmful use of alcohol is a leading cause of poor health and premature death globally [ 1 ]. On a global basis, deaths attributable to alcohol intake include deaths due to chronic diseases such as cancer (4.8%) and cardiovascular disease (3.2%) [ 2 ]. Observational studies have also suggested a lower risk of ischaemic heart disease [ 3 , 4 ], ischaemic stroke [ 5 ] and death from these [ 6–8 ] with low levels of alcohol intake in the absence of heavy episodic drinking, compared with abstention. The validity of these findings is not universally accepted [ 9 ], as these studies classify individuals who have given up drinking due to poor health (‘sick quitters’) within the reference population of non-drinkers [ 10 , 11 ]. In addition, cohort studies assessing the association between alcohol intake and mortality have predominantly measured intake close to study enrolment [ 12 ], usually during middle age, or have used a summary measure of cumulative lifetime intake [ 13 , 14 ], although intake is likely to vary over the life course [ 15 , 16 ]. As a consequence, these studies fail to capture adverse mortality effects from more complex patterns of alcohol intake over time.

In the present study, we aimed to minimize limitations of published work by identifying long-term drinking trajectories over the life course using retrospectively collected intake data at various age periods before enrolment in a cohort study, and we examined associations with all-cause, cardiovascular disease-specific, and cancer-specific mortality.
### Participants

The Melbourne Collaborative Cohort Study (MCCS) is a prospective study of 41 513 people (58.9% women; 99.2% aged 40–69 years) recruited during 1990–94 in Melbourne, Australia [ 17 ]. The Cancer Council Victoria Human Research Ethics Committee approved the study protocol. We excluded participants aged <40 or ≥70 years ( n = 325) at recruitment, with missing lifetime alcohol intake data ( n = 399) or reporting alcohol intake for fewer than three decades of life ( n = 2), with extreme values of total energy intake (<1st percentile and >99th percentile) ( n = 807) or with missing data on any of the covariates modelled ( n = 392), leaving 39 588 (95.4% of the total cohort; 23 527 women and 16 061 men) for analysis ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ).

### Collection of data

Information on demographics and potential risk factors, including lifestyle behaviours, was collected using structured questionnaires at study entry in 1990–94. A 121-item food frequency questionnaire was used to collect dietary information [ 18 ], and height and weight were measured.

### Assessment of alcohol intake

Participants were asked at baseline if they had ever drunk at least 12 alcoholic drinks in a year. Those who answered yes (‘non-lifetime abstainers’) were then asked about their usual frequency of consumption and usual quantity consumed per drinking occasion for beer, wine, and spirits separately during 10-year age periods commencing at age 20 years, up to the decade of their age at baseline attendance. We calculated the usual intake within each age period in grams per day for each beverage type by multiplying intake frequency by quantity and standard amount of alcohol per container using data from Australian food composition tables [ 19 ]. The alcohol intake for each age period in grams per day was calculated as the sum of intake from the three beverage types. The alcohol intake for the age decade encompassing baseline was considered the intake at baseline age. The average lifetime alcohol intake in grams per day was derived by dividing the total lifetime intake by the total number of days within the age intervals up to study enrolment [ 20 ].

### Cohort follow-up and ascertainment of deaths

Deaths were identified from the Victorian Cancer Registry and the Victorian Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages up to 30 June 2021. Information on cause of death was obtained up to 31 October 2018 (99% complete). The cause of death was classified as cardiovascular [410–414 and 430–438 for the 9th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9); I20–I25 and I60–I69 for the 10th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10)], cancer (140–239 for ICD-9 and C00–C97 for ICD-10), or due to other causes (including 1% missing cause of death).

### Alcohol intake trajectories

Clusters of individuals following similar long-term sex-specific alcohol intake trajectories from age 20 years to baseline were identified using a semiparametric group-based trajectory model. This model is an application of finite mixture modelling, which assumes the study sample is composed of a mixture of groups following homogenous courses [ 21 ]. Sex-specific longitudinal alcohol intake data were fitted as a mixture of several latent trajectories in a censored normal model, allowing for the lower (zero g/day) and upper intake (capped at 100 g/day; <2% of men and <0.2% of women had intakes of >100 g/day at each age decade) limits, with a polynomial function for age [ 21 , 22 ]. A two-step modelling process was used where we first selected the optimal number of trajectories and then determined the optimal shape of these trajectories using the Bayesian information criterion and an approximation of the log Bayes factor [ 21 , 23 ]. Approximately 30% of MCCS participants had never drunk alcohol or had very low intakes (<0.5 g/day) over the observation period, so in the first step, we included a zero-order (or constant) trajectory and selected five more groups as quadratic functions of age. Next, we determined the preferred order of the polynomial (i.e. constant, linear, quadratic, or cubic) for each trajectory. Participants were assigned to the group for which their posterior predicted probability calculated from the final model was highest. The adequacy of the fit of the final model was evaluated using recommended diagnostic measures: average posterior probability of assignment for each group of 0.7 or higher; odds of correct classification of 5.0 or higher; the proportion of the sample assigned to a certain group close to the proportion estimated from the model; and a reasonably narrow confidence interval (CI) around each trajectory. Alcohol intakes reported by each participant for each 10-year age period preceding their age decade at baseline attendance were considered intakes at the start of those age decades, and intake reported for the decade of age at baseline attendance was used as their intake at baseline age.

### Statistical analyses

We used Cox regression [ 24 ] to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% CIs for associations with all-cause mortality and disease-specific mortality, with age as the time metric. Follow-up began at baseline attendance and ended at the earlier of the date of death or the end of follow-up (30 June 2021 for all-cause mortality and 31 October 2018 for disease-specific deaths). To estimate HRs for cardiovascular disease-specific and cancer-specific mortality, Cox regression models were fit using a data duplication competing risks method [ 25 ], which also included competing deaths due to other causes. We fit interaction terms to test for differences in associations by smoking status (never vs current/former), a potential effect modifier. We compared findings for alcohol intake trajectories with the HRs obtained for lifetime and baseline alcohol intake (women: abstention; >0–19; 20–39; and ≥40 g/day; men: abstention; >0–19; 20–39; 40–59; 60–79; and ≥80 g/day).

A causal diagram and existing evidence guided the inclusion of confounding variables [ 26 ] (all measured at baseline, at the last alcohol assessment) in multivariable models. Alcohol intake was modelled as sex-specific trajectories in models adjusted for education, socioeconomic status, household size, smoking status, fruit intake, vegetable intake, physical activity [ 27 ], body mass index (BMI), energy from food, saturated fat intake, and stratified by birth cohort and country of birth. Excess body fatness might be a consequence rather than a cause of alcohol consumption. Therefore, we fitted models with and without adjustment for BMI. We considered the model with adjustment for BMI to be the primary analysis.

Sensitivity analyses were performed excluding the first 2 years of follow-up to account for potential reverse causation and with models adjusted for Mediterranean diet score [ 28 ] instead of fruit, vegetable, and saturated fat intake. Each model was examined for outliers and influential points. Nested models were compared using the likelihood ratio test [ 29 ]. Tests based on Schoenfeld residuals were used to examine the proportional hazards assumption [ 30 ]. Cox models assessing overall mortality were stratified on smoking status and household size (men only) as there was evidence of non-proportional hazards for these variables. All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 16.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX).
There were 7664 deaths in women during 595 456 person-years of follow-up (mean 25.3 person-years) and 7132 deaths in men during 377 314 person-years of follow-up (mean 23.5 person-years). There were 1117 (14.6%) deaths due to cardiovascular disease and 2251 (29.4%) due to cancer in women and 1283 (18.0%) cardiovascular deaths and 2340 (32.8%) cancer deaths in men.

We identified six trajectories (TR) of lifetime alcohol intake for men and three for women ( Fig. 1 ). Lifetime abstention (classified as TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’) was selected as the reference category and included 39% of the women (99.7% of whom had never consumed alcohol over their lifetime and maximum mean <1.0 g/day at each data point for the other 0.3%) and 14% of the men (99.5% of whom had never consumed alcohol over their lifetime and maximum mean <1.0 g/day at each data point for the other 0.5%). Most men (72%; TR2 ‘stable light’, TR3 ‘stable moderate’) and women (54%; TR2 ‘stable light’) had relatively stable alcohol intake over their lifetime; 6%–7% of men and women tended to increase their alcohol intake across the lifespan (men: classified as TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ who reported a mean intake of 36–55 g/day at age 20–39 years but increased their alcohol intake markedly over time, consuming over 60 g/day from age 40–49 years before reducing their intake by age 60–69 years; women: classified as TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ who tended to consume around 22 g/day at age 20–29 years but gradually increased their alcohol intake over time to consume close to 40 g/day at age 50–59 years). The heavy drinkers among men at age 20–39 years (mean intake ≥60 g/day) tended to either cut down their intake from age 40–49 years and had lower mean intakes compared with TR2 ‘stable light’ drinkers by age 60–69 years (5.4%; TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’) or continued to drink heavily until age 60–69 years before cutting down their intake, but still remained heavy drinkers at age 60–69 years (2.1%; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’).

Out of the men with intake data for age 60–69 years, 55% classified as TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ had quit drinking by age 60 years compared with 13% classified as TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’. The drinking trajectories remained relatively consistent across participants aged 40–49, 50–59, and 60–69 years at study enrolment ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Sex-specific model adequacy diagnostics are presented in Supplementary Table S1 and characteristics of participants by alcohol intake trajectories in Table 1 .

### Alcohol intake trajectories and all-cause mortality

For both women and men, stable intake trajectories were associated with lower overall mortality (women: TR2 ‘stable light’ HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.87–0.96; men: TR2 ‘stable light’ HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.82–0.94 and TR3 ‘stable moderate’ HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.81–0.96), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’ ( Table 2 ). For men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, heavy intake trajectories were associated with higher overall mortality (TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ HR 1.18; 95% CI 1.05–1.32; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ HR 1.21; 95% CI 1.04–1.40) ( Table 2 ). HRs for TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ for women and TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ for men were not suggestive of associations with all-cause mortality. The strength of these associations did not vary appreciably according to smoking status ( P interaction > .5) except for the weakening of associations for TR3 ‘stable moderate’ and TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ for never smoking men ( Supplementary Table S2 ).

### Alcohol intake trajectories and disease-specific mortality

An association between stable intake, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, and lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality was limited to TR2 ‘stable light’ for men (HR 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.97). Only weak inverse associations were observed for TR2 ‘stable light’ for women and TR3 ‘stable moderate’ for men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, and lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.79–1.02 and HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.70–1.01, respectively) ( Table 3 ).

For women, 19% higher cancer-specific mortality for TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.00–1.43), and for men, 34%–37% higher cancer-specific mortality for TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ (HR 1.34; 95% CI 1.10–1.64) and TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ (HR 1.37; 95% CI 1.06–1.77), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, were observed; the 95% CIs included the null for cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (for these groups for men) ( Table 3 ).

For men, TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ demonstrated lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.61–1.01) and higher cancer-specific mortality (HR 1.16; 95% CI 0.97–1.39), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, although the strength of the association was weak ( Table 3 ).

### Lifetime and baseline alcohol intake and mortality

The associations between usual lifetime and baseline alcohol intake and overall and disease-specific mortality are shown in Table 4 . Positive associations were limited to all-cause mortality for the heaviest-drinking men for lifetime and baseline intake and to cancer-specific mortality for the heaviest-drinking women and men for lifetime intake.

### Sensitivity analyses

The sex-specific results from the analysis excluding the first 2 years of follow-up, without adjusting for BMI or adjusting for Mediterranean diet score were not materially different from the main results ( Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ). Models including alcohol-intake trajectories showed overall better model fit in comparison to models using lifetime or baseline intake ( Supplementary Table S6 ).
discussion:
Compared with lifetime abstention, stable light and moderate drinking were associated with ∼10% lower all-cause mortality for women and men, largely attributable to lower cardiovascular disease mortality. Heavy drinking during early adulthood for men, irrespective of intake after age 40 years, was associated with ∼20% higher all-cause mortality and 35% higher cancer-specific mortality, while increasing alcohol intake with advancing age for women was associated with ∼20% higher cancer-specific mortality.

Strengths of our study include the detailed assessment of alcohol intake over the life course and the long follow-up. There are several limitations. Alcohol intake was self-reported, which is prone to measurement error. For example, studies using data from surveys asking about frequency and amount of consumption of different alcoholic beverages in the last year have typically found coverage rates (comparing self-reported drinking and data from production, sales, trade, and tax records in a population) of <50% [ 31 ]. Intake at baseline may have influenced their recall of past alcohol intake, while misclassification due to participants having to summarize their frequency and quantity of alcoholic beverage intake for 10-year age intervals into single ‘usual’ values is also possible. According to Rehm et al. [ 32 ] measuring intake both at a point in time (e.g. at baseline) and over a period of time (e.g. during lifetime) helps limit problems related to intake measurement. We previously established the accuracy of recalled alcohol intake data in the MCCS by comparing matching temporal changes in intake over time for study participants with Australian per capita trends. However, it is still possible that drinking trajectories in the MCCS may not fully represent recent drinking rates in Australia, particularly for women [ 33 ].

Cancer is the second-leading cause of death due to alcohol use in Australia. Globally, 740 000 new cancer cases [ 34 ] and 400 000 cancer deaths each year are attributed to drinking [ 35 ]. In the present study, heavy drinking during different age periods in women and men was related to higher cancer-specific mortality. Acetaldehyde, the toxic metabolite of ethanol in alcoholic beverages, is a carcinogen [ 36 ] causally linked to cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus (squamous-cell carcinoma), liver, colorectum, and female breast [ 37 ]. Several of these cancers remain among the most lethal cancers, with median survival <1 year [ 38 , 39 ]. Two key findings in our study merit further examination in future research: (i) men who drank heavily in their 20s and 30s were at higher risk of death by middle age even when most had quit by then; and (ii) women with markedly lower intake compared with men were at higher risk of cancer-specific mortality in their middle age. These findings emphasise the potential relevance of age and sex when formulating national drinking guidelines. The current Australian guidelines on reducing health risks from drinking alcohol advocate that healthy men and women should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any 1 day [ 40 ]. In comparison, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend limiting intake to two drinks or less in a day for men and one drink or less in a day for women, on days when alcohol is consumed, and avoiding binge drinking.

In the present study, in line with published data [ 14 , 41 ], we identified a relatively small mortality benefit for stable light and stable moderate drinking due to lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality, particularly for men. In a comparatively smaller study employing group-based trajectory modelling, four long-term drinking patterns were identified in 5298 Chinese women and men [ 42 ]. The authors found 24% lower risk for long-term light drinking (median intake ∼2.5 g/day) (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.61–0.95) and 39% lower risk for moderate drinking (median intake ∼20 g/day) (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.46–0.81) with all-cause mortality ( n = 568 total deaths); no evidence of increased mortality for heavy drinking (median intake ∼59 g/day) was observed (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.63–1.43) [ 42 ]. While the authors acknowledge the limited availability of data on confounders, mediators of the alcohol–mortality association may also have been included in the models [ 42 ]. Our analysis is also not immune from other biases seen in observational studies that potentially overestimate the size of any health benefits arising from light to moderate drinking [ 43 ], although the use of drinking trajectories limits the contamination of the reference abstainer category by former heavy drinkers. The World Health Organization’s latest expert summary states that no safe amount of alcohol consumption can be established [ 11 ]. Any longevity benefit of light to moderate drinking at an individual level is complex and intertwined with distinct life circumstances and personal medical histories [ 9 ]. While there is no consensus on the health benefits of light to moderate drinking [ 11 ], it is widely recognized that people who do not consume alcohol should remain non-drinkers [ 40 ], as even low intakes have been shown to be associated with increased cancer risk [ 44–46 ].

In summary, we highlight the importance of avoiding higher levels of alcohol intake at any age to reduce all-cause and cancer-specific mortality. Prospective studies with similar data should aim to replicate these analyses.

inputs:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD), which affects more than 500 million people worldwide, poses a heavy burden on the health system [ 1 ]. High levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and unhealthy lifestyle factors have been listed as top-ranked contributors to this global cardiovascular pandemic and related high mortality and disease burden [ 1 , 2 ]. High lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] levels have also been found to be associated with an increased risk of CVD and proposed as another emerging risk factor for CVD onset [ 3 ].

Both Lp(a) and LDL-C are lipoproteins involved in cholesterol transport in the blood and have been linked to CVD, thus they may interact with each other, and treatments targeting the two markers may exhibit synergistic effects. For example, earlier prospective studies identified that the associations of Lp(a) with the risk of CVDs may be more marked among individuals with elevated LDL cholesterol [ 4 , 5 ], and treating elevated LDL-C in those with elevated Lp(a) has been shown to attenuate the increased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) [ 6 ]. In addition, body weight, blood pressure, and certain lifestyle factors may interact with Lp(a) through their effects on lipid metabolism and cardiovascular health. Briefly, body weight plays a crucial role, as obesity is always linked to higher LDL-C and potentially elevated Lp(a) [ 7 ]. Although elevated blood pressure itself may not increase Lp(a), both conditions can coexist and interact to amplify cardiovascular risk [ 8 ]. Smoking and alcohol consumption can impact lipid profiles by affecting liver function and increasing oxidative stress, respectively [ 9 ]. While regular physical activity enhances lipid clearance from the bloodstream, thereby potentially lowering both LDL-C and Lp(a) [ 10 ].

Lipid-lowering therapies and lifestyle modifications have been recommended to lower the risk of CVD [ 11 , 12 ]. Lp(a) is a novel causal risk factor for CVD [ 13 ] and has been identified as a potential target for lowering CVD risk, although no directed therapies have been approved in the United States or Europe [ 14 ]. Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide targeting apolipoprotein(a), shows promise as a therapy for Lp(a) lowering [ 15 ]. However, its effects on cardiovascular outcomes are unknown and are being investigated in the Lp(a) HORIZON trial (Phase 3) [ 16 ]. Besides, the interactions across Lp(a) lowering, LDL-C lowering, and lifestyle improvements in modifying CVD risk remain unexplored, yet understanding this interplay is crucial for improving our understanding of the etiological basis of CVD and optimizing prevention and treatment strategies, particularly for high-risk patients.

The Mendelian randomization (MR) paradigm is an epidemiological approach based on observational genetic data with the merit of reinforcing causal inference by minimizing the risk of confounding and reverse causation [ 17 ]. Several previous MR studies have established causal associations of Lp(a)-lowering and LDL-C-lowering therapies with CVD risk by using genetic variants as instruments to mimic the therapeutic effects [ 13 , 18–20 ]. The factorial MR analysis, designed to mimic a randomized controlled trial, has been developed to examine the interactions of two interventions [ 21 , 22 ]. Here, we conducted a factorial MR study to assess the effects of genetically predicted low-level Lp(a) on a broad range of CVD outcomes as well as to explore its interactions with genetically predicted low-level LDL-C and interventions on body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and lifestyles.
### Study design

We first explored the associations of genetically proxied Lp(a) lowering and LDL-C lowering with the levels of blood lipids and lipoproteins to examine the validity of selected instruments. Then, we estimated the associations of genetically predicted low-level Lp(a) with major CVDs, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality. Finally, we conducted factorial MR to investigate the joint effects of genetically predicted Lp(a) lowering and LDL-C lowering or lifestyle improvements in the risk of CVDs and mortality ( Fig. 1 ).

### Study population

The UK Biobank study is a population-based prospective cohort study, which recruited over 500 000 adults aged between 40 and 69 years in 2006–2010 [ 23 ]. To minimize the influence of diverse population structure, we excluded participants with high heterozygosity, or with high missing rate, sex mismatch, or putative aneuploidy in sex chromosome, or non-White ancestry, or with high relatedness. After filtering ineligible samples, the current study was based on 385 917 UK Biobank participants.

### Outcome ascertainment

Major cardiovascular outcomes included CAD, peripheral artery disease (PAD), stroke and its subtypes [i.e. ischemic stroke (IS), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)], atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and venous thromboembolism (VTE). Two additional composites [i.e. three- and four-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)] [ 24 , 25 ] and cardiovascular and all-cause mortality were also considered. Detailed definitions of these studied outcomes are shown in Supplementary Table S1 . We included both prevalent and incident cases, with participants followed up until 31 December 2021.

### Genetic instruments

LPA gene region was ultra-finely mapped among 48 333 individuals from the CHD Exome+ consortium using a customized version of the Illumina Exome Beadchip array [ 13 ]. We selected the variants associated with Lp(a) levels at the genome-wide levels of significant ( P < 5 × 10 −8 ) and generated a list of 43 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which was demonstrated to be strong and validated genetic instruments (IVs) for Lp(a) [ 13 ]. Then, a weighted genetic score that reflected genetically predicted levels of Lp(a) was calculated using individual-level data in the UK Biobank weighted by each variant’s association with the change in Lp(a) levels in milligrams per deciliter.

We used summary data of European populations from a genome-wide meta-analysis of LDL-C levels in the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium [ 26 ] to generate genetic instruments to proxy LDL-C lowering via HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), NPC1-like intracellular cholesterol transporter 1 (NPC1L1), proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin Type 9 (PCSK9), and low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). For each target, we constructed a genetic score by including all variants within 100 kb on either side of each gene that were associated with LDL-C levels at P < 5.0 × 10 −8 and that were in weak linkage disequilibrium ( r 2 < 0.2) to increase the proportion of variance explained by the instruments. In total, 26 SNPs for HMGCR, 6 SNPs for NPC1L1, 42 SNPs for PSCK9, and 52 SNPs for LDLR were obtained, respectively [ 19 , 21 , 27 ]. We also established a genetic score to proxy overall LDL-C levels (not specific to any lipid-lowering drug target) that included 237 independent SNPs ( r 2 < 0.001) associated with LDL-C levels at genome-wide significance level ( P < 5.0 × 10 −8 ), serving as a positive control [ 28 ]. Detailed information on the genetic instruments is presented in the Supplementary Tables S2–S4 .

BMI, SBP, and lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol drinking, and physical activity) were also included in this study. For each factor, we selected associated genetic instruments at the genome-wide significance ( P < 5.0 × 10 −8 ) from external large-scale genome-wide association studies [ 29–32 ], and clumped them using a linkage disequilibrium threshold of r 2 < 0.001 according to the European reference panel of the 1000 Genomes project. As a result, 62 SNPs for BMI, 455 SNPs for SBP, 248 SNPs for smoking initiation, 98 SNPs for alcohol consumption per week, and 16 SNPs for moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity during leisure time were included. Details regarding the related studies and the instruments are presented in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 .

### Statistical analysis

We divided the population into higher-level and lower-level groups based on the median values of genetic scores and applied a multivariable linear regression model to estimate the associations between genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C and the measurements of seven blood lipids and lipoproteins, with adjustment of age, sex, assessment center, and the first 10 principal components (PCs). Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was conducted to estimate the multivariable-adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for CVD and mortality outcomes. The models were also adjusted for age, sex, assessment center, and the first 10 PCs. In factorial MR analysis, the population was naturally randomly allocated into four subgroups based on the median values of genetic scores. We then estimated the change of blood lipids and the risk of CVD and mortality between the groups and the reference group using the multivariable linear and Cox proportional hazard regression, respectively, with adjustment for age, sex, assessment center, and the first 10 PCs. Given that taking dichotomized gene scores is generally inefficient for detecting statistical interactions, we thus examined the interaction of the two arms using continuous genetic scores and their product in the interaction regression model [ 33 ]. The tests were two-sided and performed using R software version 4.2.1.
In this study, we used the UK Biobank genetic data of 488 366 participants. Genetic quality control was done centrally by UK Biobank, and a total of 385 917 unrelated European individuals were finally included, containing 177 690 (46.0%) men and 208 227 (54.0%) women. The mean age of the population was 56.7 ± 8.0 years, and the mean levels of Lp(a) were 17.6 ± 19.7 mg/dl. More details regarding socio-demographic information, lifestyle factors, and blood lipid concentrations are presented in Table 1 .

### Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels in relation to measured blood lipids

Genetic prediction of all studied targets was associated with decreased levels of measured LDL-C [HMGCR: effect size, −2.50 mg/dl; 95% confidence interval (CI): −2.72, −2.29; NPC1L1: effect size, −1.06 mg/dl; 95% CI: −1.28, −0.84; PCSK9: effect size, −2.70 mg/dl; 95% CI: −2.91, −2.48; LDLR: effect size, −3.86 mg/dl; 95% CI: −4.10, −3.67; LPA: effect size, −1.42 mg/dl; 95% CI: −1.64, −1.20], whereas only genetic variants in the LPA gene region were associated with reduced levels of measured Lp(a) (effect size, −19.68 mg/dl; 95% CI: −19.80, −19.56) ( Fig. 2 ). Of note, genetic variants in the LPA gene region were associated with increased levels of triglycerides (effect size, 3.25 mg/dl; 95% CI: 2.68, 3.82) ( Fig. 2 ). In factorial MR, the levels of LDL-C and apoB were further reduced in individuals with genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ).

### Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) levels and cardiovascular risk and mortality

Genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) were significantly associated with a reduced risk of CVD, CAD, PAD, stroke, IS, AF, HF, three- and four-point MACE, cardiovascular, and all-cause mortality. Per 50-mg/dl decrease in genetically predicted Lp(a) levels, the HR ranged from 0.73 (95% CI: 0.73, 0.73) for PAD to 0.95 (95% CI: 0.92, 0.99) for VTE ( Fig. 3 ). We did not observe an association between genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and the risk of SAH (HR, 0.98; 95% CI: 0.89, 1.07) and ICH (HR, 1.02; 95% CI: 0.94, 1.12) ( Fig. 3 ).

### Joint associations of genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol lowering with cardiovascular risk and mortality

Compared to the reference group, the risk of CVD, CAD, PAD, three-point MACE, four-point MACE, and cardiovascular mortality was lower in the group with genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C ( Fig. 4 ). The HR of overall CVD was 0.92 (95% CI: 0.90, 0.93) for genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C via HMGCR target, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.89, 0.92) for genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C via NPC1L1 target, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.88, 0.91) for genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C via PCSK9 target, and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.87, 0.90) for genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDL-C via LDLR target, compared to the reference group. Interactions were not observed except for PAD outcome when combining lower levels of Lp(a) with LDL-C via LDLR target (HR, 0.71; 95% CI: 0.65, 0.76; P interaction = .006) ( Fig. 4 ). This represents a sub-additive interaction, as the estimate for Lp(a) and LDL-C lowering is less than the combination of estimates for Lp(a) and LDL-C lowering. The results for stroke and its subtypes, AF, HF, VTE, and all-cause mortality are shown in Supplementary Figs S2–S6 . However, we did not observe any interactions between the two arms in the analyses of these outcomes ( P interaction > .05).

### Joint associations of genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) lowering and interventions on body mass index, systolic blood pressure, and lifestyles with cardiovascular risk and mortality

Compared to the reference group, the risk of CVD, CAD, PAD, three-point MACE, four-point MACE, and cardiovascular mortality was reduced in the group with genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and lifestyle improvements ( Fig. 5 ). For CVD outcome, we observed a HR of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.86, 0.89) for genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and lower BMI, 0.81 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.82) for genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and lower SBP, 0.85 (95% CI: 0.83, 0.86) for genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and lower smoking intensity, 0.90 (95% CI: 0.89, 0.92) for genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and lower drinking intensity, and 0.90 (95% CI: 0.88, 0.91) for genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels and higher physical activity intensity ( Fig. 5 ). The similar pattern of the associations was identified for stroke and its subtypes, AF, HF, VTE, and overall mortality that lower risk was observed among the group with genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and lifestyle improvements ( Supplementary Figs S7–S11 ). Again, no interactions were identified between the two arms in the analyses of these outcomes ( P interaction > .05).
discussion:
This study found that genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) were associated with a reduced risk of various CVDs, particularly PAD. The factorial MR analysis observed no clear evidence for interactions between Lp(a) lowering and LDL-C lowering or lifestyle improvements in CVD risk reduction, except for the PAD outcome when combining low-level Lp(a) with low-level LDL-C.

The causal potential of the association between Lp(a) and the risk of CVDs has been explored in previous cohort and MR studies and clinical trials [ 3 , 13 , 34–39 ]. Our findings are in line with these studies in support of a positive association between Lp(a) levels and the risk of CVDs, in particular atherosclerotic outcomes, and therefore potentially beneficial effects on CVD risk reduction after Lp(a)-lowering treatment. As far as we know, there is no approved treatment targeting Lp(a). Apolipoprotein(a) antisense oligonucleotide (pelacarsen) has been found to be a promising target for Lp(a) lowering [ 15 ], and whether it can generate clinical benefits on cardiovascular endpoints is unknown and under investigation in a Phase 3 clinical trial [ 16 ]. In addition, whether this approach should be recommended in a general population, like for the primary prevention [ 3 ], or merely among patients at a high risk [ 40 ] needs to be assessed by comprehensively considering the cost-effectiveness and safety of the treatment.

Polypill strategy, including lipid-lowering pills, antihypertensive drugs, aspirin, etc., has been found to lower incidence of cardiovascular events compared to the usual care [ 41 , 42 ]. For example, the PolyIran study, a two-group, pragmatic, cluster-randomized trial, aimed to assess the effectiveness and safety of a four-component polypill for primary and secondary prevention of CVD. This study found that using the polypill could effectively prevent major cardiovascular events, achieve high medication adherence, and result in a low frequency of adverse events [ 42 ]. In addition, some MR studies explored the potential effects of polypill inhibiting PCSK9 and HMGCR [ 21 ], PCSK9 and CETP [ 22 ], and HMGCR and NPC1L1 [ 27 ] on the risk of developing CVDs, and consistently revealed joint effects of genetically predicted LDL-C-lowering treatments with different targets on CVD risk reduction [ 21 , 22 , 27 ]. Our study examined the interactions of Lp(a) lowering with LDL-C lowering via four targets in CVD and generated similar findings that Lp(a) lowering might have generally synergistic effects on CVD risk when combined with LDL-C lowering. Even though effect sizes were incomparable between LDL-C-lowering targets due to varying instrument strengths for each LDL-C-lowering target, the study supported a potentially better combination of genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) and LDLR in lowering the levels of apoB, which may drive the associations between non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and CVD [ 43 , 44 ].

Although the evidence for lifestyle interventions in reducing CVD risk is compelling [ 45 ], it remains unclear if the combination of medications and lifestyle modifications exhibits a synergistic effect in reducing cardiovascular risk. A cohort study among 41 225 participants found that the initiation of preventive antihypertensive or statin therapy could lead to both favorable and unfavorable lifestyle changes [ 46 ], indicating that there may exist interaction effects. Given the limited research on the interactions between Lp(a) and lifestyle factors, our study conducted factorial MR and identified suggestive joint effects of genetically predicted lower levels of Lp(a) in reducing CVD risk when combined with healthy lifestyle factors, particularly lower smoking intensity. Although BMI and SBP are not lifestyle factors, they represent anthropometric and physiological changes that can be greatly influenced by lifestyle, and this study also identified potential interaction effects between Lp(a) reduction and blood pressure lowering or weight loss in modifying CVD risk. These findings imply the importance of advising lifestyle modifications in lowering CVD risk even among individuals receiving Lp(a)-lowering therapy.

This study had several strengths. We used genetic variants to proxy the effect of Lp(a)-lowering therapies, which can diminish the biases caused by confounding and reverse causality since genetic variants are usually not associated with confounders and unmodifiable by the onset of disease. In addition, we included a wide range of CVD endpoints and mortality to reveal a comprehensive cardiovascular effect of Lp(a)-lowering therapies individually or when combined with other treatments. Horizontal pleiotropy (the genetic variants used as the instrumental variable influence the outcome not merely via the exposure) may be minimized for drug targets given that all used genetic instruments were selected from corresponding gene regions for studied therapeutic targets.

Limitations of this study need to be discussed. First, the genetically proxied effects of lowering Lp(a) or LDL-C by targeting HMGCR , NPC1L1 , PCSK9 , and LDLR genes could only reflect the target pathways, which therefore might confine the comparability of our findings to results of trials since off-target pathways were not considered in the analysis. Second, the genetically predicted effects are small and lifelong, in contrast to the larger effects of shorter duration observed by pharmaceutically inhibiting a target. Third, our analysis included only participants of European ancestry, which confines the generalizability of our findings to the populations with different ethnic backgrounds. Last, some other lifestyle factors, like diet, were not included in the analysis due to no robust genetic instruments for these traits.
In summary, our study suggests that lowering Lp(a) levels may reduce the risk of various CVDs, as well as cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Lp(a) lowering may have a sub-additive effect on reducing the risk of PAD when combined with LDL-C lowering. Further clinical studies are warranted to validate our findings among CVD patients.
target: High levels of lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD); however, the effects of Lp(a)-lowering therapy in combination with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)-lowering treatment or lifestyle improvements on CVD risk remain unexplored.We conducted a factorial Mendelian randomization study among 385 917 participants in the UK Biobank. Separate genetic scores were constructed to proxy the effects of Lp(a) lowering, LDL-C lowering through different targets [HMG-CoA reductase, NPC1-like intracellular cholesterol transporter 1, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin Type 9, and low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR)], as well as improvements in body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and lifestyle factors (cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, and physical activity).Genetically predicted lower Lp(a) levels were associated with a decreased risk of CVD and CVD-specific mortality. Per 50-mg/dl, the hazard ratio ranged from 0.73 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.73, 0.73] for peripheral artery disease (PAD) to 0.95 (95% CI: 0.92, 0.99) for venous thromboembolism. In factorial analyses exploring combined exposure to low-level Lp(a) and low-level LDL-C, there was no consistent evidence for departure from an additive model for any outcome ( P interaction > .05), with the exception of the analysis using the LDLR score and PAD ( P interaction = .006). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the leading cause of respiratory mortality globally, leading to over 3 million deaths per year. 1 Smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD and, historically, has been largely focused on as part of the control of COPD. 2 However, there is a growing realization that a large proportion of COPD cannot be explained by smoking, and that there may be important secondary risk factors. 3

There is mounting concern about the possible impact of pulmonary tuberculosis on long-term lung health. 4–7 Several studies have reported persistence of airway obstruction as well as chronic or recurrent symptoms after individuals recover from tuberculosis. 6 , 8 Tuberculosis may result in significant lung impairment; however, whether residual lung damage due to tuberculosis results in clinically significant outcomes has not been well studied. Although tuberculosis has been mentioned in some COPD guidelines, there is limited evidence of an association. 2 Few studies have assessed the relationship between prior tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD. Most of these studies have assessed tuberculosis diagnoses retrospectively or through self-report, and have been located in settings with a low burden of COPD, limiting generalizability. 9–14 Furthermore, whether an association between tuberculosis and subsequent development of COPD is independent of smoking status, a risk factor for both diseases, is not well elucidated. 2

China is going through large-scale health transitions. 15 , 16 An estimated 100 million people in China are estimated to have COPD, accounting for approximately 25% of total cases worldwide. 17 , 18 Tobacco use and an aging population are considered leading risk factors for this increasing COPD burden; however, risk factors for COPD beyond these, in China and more broadly, are not well understood. 2 , 3 , 13

To attempt to improve our understanding of the risk of COPD after developing tuberculosis, we used the Chinese Electronic Health Records Research in Yinzhou (CHERRY) study, a large, ambispective, population-based, observational cohort of participants in a setting with a high burden of COPD. 19 We assessed the association between tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD, adjusted for a range of potential confounders. We then evaluated whether important secondary characteristics, such as smoking status, modified this relationship.
### Study design and data source

We performed a longitudinal cohort study using the CHERRY, a population-based electronic health database established in 2006 and containing 98% of permanent adult residents in Yinzhou ( Supplementary Figure S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). 19 This database has been used extensively in our previous epidemiological studies. 20–22 The CHERRY is based on the Yinzhou Health Information System (YHIS) that contains comprehensive information, such as health check information, inpatient and outpatient electronic medical records, chronic disease surveillance system and death certificates. These databases are inherently linked to each other by a unique and encoded individual identifier. 19 In Yinzhou district in Ningbo, 96% of permanent residents are covered by the health insurance system. Residents of all ages are covered by the system; however only adults above 18 years of age on 1 January 2009 are included in the CHERRY Study. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.

### Identification of study cohort

In order to bypass the integration and preliminary test period of the system and to allow for full coverage of the regional population, we recruited residents who had registered in the CHERRY during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. Exclusion criteria included age <35 years, participants with a previous history of COPD or with a previous history of cancer and participants with missing values of covariates. We excluded younger participants because the vast majority of COPD occurs >35 years of age. The cohort was dynamic and therefore participants could enter at different time points if they had the exposure at baseline or during follow-up.

### Identification of tuberculosis and COPD

The exposure of interest was tuberculosis, from the health insurance database. In China, tuberculosis care is provided by the national government special funds and has a wide and comprehensive coverage rate. Tuberculosis events were recorded based on the Chinese National Disease Reporting system which includes all diagnosed tuberculosis cases at the city, provincial and national levels. 23–26 The definition of pulmonary tuberculosis disease and all tuberculosis was based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Due to the dynamic nature of the cohort, persons could contribute to the unexposed and, if they were diagnosed with tuberculosis during follow-up, also to the exposed ( Supplementary Table S2 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

We identified participants with the outcome as those diagnosed with COPD, defined by ICD-10 codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) during the study period (1 January 2009 to 30 September 2021). 27 The diagnostic date of COPD was defined as the endpoint date for persons developing COPD.

### Measurement of covariates

Demographic characteristics were collected as part of the baseline survey and included lifestyle factors, socioeconomic status, comorbidities and use of medications. Demographic characteristics included age, sex and marital status. Lifestyle factors were recorded at baseline, including smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and body mass index (BMI). We dichotomized weight into a group that was either overweight or obese (≥24 kg/m 2 and over) or normal and underweight (<24 kg/m 2 ). 28 , 29 Smoking intensity was defined as the average number of cigarettes smoked per day. Current alcohol drinking was defined as drinking at least 100 grams of any alcohol per week during the past year. Education level was measured at the baseline visit and included illiterate, primary school, middle school and high school and above. Important factors related to COPD were also considered, including diabetes, hypertension, asthma, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, arrhythmia, ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, heart failure, depression, anxiety, osteoporosis and the use of COPD medications ( Supplementary Tables S1 and S3 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

### Statistical analysis

We used Cox proportional hazards survival time regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of tuberculosis or pulmonary tuberculosis with risk of subsequent COPD. For COPD incidence, time-to-event data were constructed at first date of study recruitment and/or the date of tuberculosis diagnosis. Participants could have entered the study as unexposed (no history of tuberculosis) and then become exposed over follow-up upon developing tuberculosis. In the analysis, once COPD occurs, participants could no longer contribute to follow-up, regardless of their exposure status. We excluded 126 new cases of tuberculosis after a COPD diagnosis. Follow-up was censored at death or end of follow-up. The time to event in exposed and unexposed groups was defined as the time interval between the date participants were registered in the YHIS (or the time of TB diagnosis if diagnosed during follow-up) to the date of the earliest of COPD outcome (defined in the outcome measurement), death or the end of the study period (30 September 2021). Incidence rates for COPD were compared using two-sample Poisson tests. We defined three distinct regression models. In the first model, we adjusted for age and sex. Model 2 further adjusted for marital status, education level, smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for comorbidities and use of medications. Models 2 and 3 are the primary multivariable models in our analysis. One provides all potential confounding variables into the model (Model 3), and the other (Model 2) provides a simpler model (with less variables) which is less likely to be over-adjusted. In each of these models, we treated age as a continuous variable. We used Schoenfeld residuals to test for proportional hazard assumption ( P > 0.05).

We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD. Smoking status was categorized into current smokers if they smoked ≥1 cigarette per day for >1 year, former smokers if they had quit smoking for >1 year and never smokers for all others. Smoking intensity was divided into never smoking, <10, 10–20, ≥21 cigarettes per day. 30 , 31 Number of pack-years, representing cumulative dose, was calculated as (cigarettes per day/20) × smoking duration in years, and categorized into never smokers, <13, 13–24, ≥25 pack-years. 30 , 31 We combined former and current smokers when calculating smoking intensity and cumulative dose.

We also performed subgroup analyses to assess whether the associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD varied by age (35–49, 50–64 and ≥65 years), sex, smoking intensity, alcohol drinking, BMI (<24 or ≥24 kg/m 2 ), physical activity (<1 or ≥1 time/week) and education level. To evaluate whether an interaction was present, we used multivariable regression models with a multiplicative interaction term between each characteristic of interest and pulmonary tuberculosis. Then, we determined statistical significance for the interaction based on the maximum likelihood χ 2 from a nested model with and without the interaction term. 32

We calculated the population attributable fraction (PAF) of pulmonary TB and COPD using standard formulas 33 .

We conducted several sensitivity analyses. First, we excluded participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) as possible pre-symptoms of COPD. 34 Second, we further excluded incident COPD cases that occurred within the first year of follow-up or within 1 year of diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis and tuberculosis, to minimize reverse causation. Third, we used multiple imputation via chained equations (MICE) to impute missing values of covariates. Fourth, we altered the end of follow-up to 31 December 2019, in order to exclude the potential influence of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on outdoor physical activity, hospital visits and air pollution 22 . Fifth, we also excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline. Finally, we calculated E-value to assess the potential effect of unmeasured confounders. 35

All statistical tests were two-sided; 95% confidence intervals were considered to assess statistical significance.
We recruited 477 046 residents who had registered in the CHERRY study during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. We excluded 244 831 participants aged <35 years, 1552 participants with a previous history of COPD, 1008 participants with a previous history of cancer and 30 773 participants with missing values of covariates. Finally, we included a total of 198 882 participants in this study aged >35 years ( Figure 1 ). Median age of the study population was 46.5 [interquartile range (IQR), 40.5–56.2] ( Table 1 ); 51% of subjects were men.

Overall, a total of 1414 participants was identified with pulmonary tuberculosis, of whom 1413 were incident cases. The median follow-up time was 9.9 years (IQR, 8.8–11.1) and a total of 16 449 cases developed COPD during the study period ( Supplementary Table S4 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Median follow-up times between enrolment and incident tuberculosis diagnosis, as well as tuberculosis and COPD diagnosis, were 3.1 (IQR, 0.8–6.2) and 3.1 (IQR, 0.9–6.2), respectively. In the full cohort, the cumulative incidence of COPD was 8.3%, among individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis this was 23.6% ( Figure 2 ). When using a secondary exposure classification of all tuberculosis, cumulative incidence of COPD was 16.5%. The association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD was present in all multivariable models. Hazards ratios, derived from multivariable models measuring the association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD, ranged from 2.63 (95% CI, 2.36–2.93) in Model 1 to 1.77 (1.59–1.97) in Model 3 ( Table 2 ). For the association between all tuberculosis and COPD, the HR ranged from 1.71 (1.51–1.94) in Model 1 (adjustment for age and sex) to 1.18 (1.04–1.34) in Model 3 (adjustment for all demographic and clinical variables). When using differing classifications of smoking ( Supplementary Table S5 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) in model adjustments or a three-category variable for tuberculosis ( Supplementary Table S6 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online), results were similar. Using estimates of Model 2 and Model 3, the PAF for COPD due to pulmonary TB was 1.1% (0.9–1.3) and 0.5% (0.4–0.7), respectively.

When we further stratified our results to assess for interaction ( Figure 3 ), the relationship between pulmonary tuberculosis and increased risk of COPD was present across most but not all subgroups. An increased hazard of COPD was seen among persons aged 50–64 (aHR, 1.83; 1.56–2.15) and 65 years and above (aHR, 1.80; 1.50–2.16), but a weaker association was seen in those 35–49 years old (aHR, 1.40; 1.08–1.82). Associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD were observed among participants with poor education [less than high school: aHR, 1.90 (1.69–2.13); P interaction <0.001). We did not find evidence that smoking intensity, sex, alcohol use or physical activity were effect modifiers ( P interaction >0.05) ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). When we restricted our analysis to all tuberculosis; only smoking intensity did not modify the association.

Sensitivity analyses did not meaningfully change our findings ( Table 3 ). When excluding participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses, the aHRs were 1.91 (1.68–2.18) and 1.31 (1.13–1.52) for pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis exposure classifications, respectively. We also further excluded incident COPD cases occurring within the first year of follow-up, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.69 (1.51–1.90) and 1.18 (1.04–1.35), respectively. When using MICE to impute missing values of covariates, the corresponding aHRs were 1.76 (1.59–1.95) and 1.15 (1.02–1.30), respectively. Upon restricting follow-up duration to 31 December 2019, the corresponding aHRs were 2.04 (1.79–2.33) and 1.27 (1.09–1.49), respectively. In further sensitivity analyses, we excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.86 (1.66–2.08) and 1.24 (1.09–1.41), respectively. E-values were 2.94 and 1.64 for the associations of pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis with risk of COPD, respectively.
The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.
discussion:
In this large, population-based cohort study, we found that persons who developed tuberculosis were at severely elevated risk of subsequently developing COPD. This relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent COPD was present even after accounting for smoking intensity (i.e., smoking did not confound, modify or interact with the relationship) and remained after several sensitivity analyses and after adjusting for a large selection of potentially relevant lifestyle, demographic and clinical confounders. This finding supports and extends prior work demonstrating lung impairment after a tuberculosis episode, 6 , 36 , 37 showing subsequent severe clinical chronic lung disease as a result. This work provides empirical evidence that tuberculosis is an important and underrecognized risk factor for COPD. The relationship was larger when considering pulmonary tuberculosis rather than all tuberculosis, supporting the hypothesis that pulmonary activity and damage during disease may be one mechanism of subsequent elevated COPD risk. We further found that certain subgroups of participants (participants who were older and with lower education, BMI and physical activity) were at highest risk of developing COPD after tuberculosis, which may suggest that targeted follow-up after recovery from tuberculosis may be a pragmatic and meaningful intervention to prevent severe lung disease.

Although lung damage due to smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD, there has been a growing push to recognize other routes or groups of patients that do not smoke who are also at high-risk. 2 , 3 Alternative risk factors may represent contributions to future COPD cases and may provide more amenable intervention strategies. The World Health Organization currently does not recognize tuberculosis as a risk factor for COPD. Our findings suggest that tuberculosis patients have increased risk of COPD, after controlling for the smoking variable, and that a proportion of COPD is attributable to tuberculosis. The results highlight the push for tuberculosis to be included. 9 There is growing realization in the tuberculosis field that post-disease sequalae and morbidity are immense. 4 , 6 , 7 , 38 Recent estimates suggest that there are approximately 155 million survivors of tuberculosis globally 39 ; our results indicate this population must be prioritized or, at a minimum, followed to prevent further lung damage. 38 , 40

Importantly, we found subgroups of participants that were at highest risk of developing COPD after a tuberculosis episode, including persons with low education, low BMI and not as physically active. Prior studies have either not identified important subgroups of persons with prior tuberculosis that are at particularly high risk of COPD, or shown heterogeneous results. 9 , 41 Groups at high-risk of COPD in our study may be an overlapping population, representing populations with low socioeconomic status (i.e., persons with low socioeconomic status may have low BMI, education level, etc.), suggesting that post-tuberculosis lung damage leading to COPD may be concentrated in the most at-need populations. Pathways explaining how these secondary variables accentuate the relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent tuberculosis cannot be ascertained with our data; however we hypothesize that low BMI may represent a severe form or more advanced stage of tuberculosis. 42

Our study has several strengths, including the large sample size with a wealth of demographic and clinical information on included participants. Second, distinct from most other databases of this kind, important individual-level, lifestyle risk factor information was available, including extent of physical activity, smoking intensity and alcohol use, among others. Our results are subject to less recall biases, as participants were administered surveys at multiple time points and were followed over time through a comprehensive health insurance system that detected diagnoses rather than self-reported prior tuberculosis. The CHERRY study, like large health insurance system datasets in many European countries, covers almost the entire district population (>99% of area inhabitants), thereby minimizing chances of missed tuberculosis diagnosis. 19 Last, tuberculosis diagnoses were assessed and confirmed through ICD-10 coding rather than through retrospective diagnosis or recall through self-report, as seen in prior studies. 12–14 This allows for direct confirmation of tuberculosis diagnosis and reduces potential exposure misclassification.

There are limitations to our analysis. First, despite the strengths of the comprehensive health system that the CHERRY study provides, tuberculosis cases that are never diagnosed and subsequently resolve are not covered, leading to underdiagnosis of tuberculosis. 43 Second, we did not measure household socioeconomic status or smoke exposures (e.g., use of biomass fuels), potential confounders that may impact on both tuberculosis and COPD. Third, although we stratify our analysis by whether the tuberculosis episode was pulmonary, the type, severity and drug-resistance profile of tuberculosis was not recorded. Future studies should further refine specific features of tuberculosis that are more likely to lead to COPD. Fourth, residual or unmeasured confounding is possible. For example, we did not measure characteristics at the time of tuberculosis diagnosis. Despite this, the high observed E-values suggest that any unmeasured characteristics would need to be heavily influential to affect our findings. Last, an underlying lung damage or susceptibility prior to the development of both COPD and tuberculosis, not available within our cohort, may be the cause of both diseases.
In conclusion, in our study of almost 200 000 participants within a population-based cohort study of an entire district area in eastern China, we found a markedly higher risk of COPD among persons with a tuberculosis episode. Importantly, this relationship remained after accounting for participant smoking status and intensity and was more pronounced among people with pulmonary tuberculosis. These results suggest that a prior tuberculosis episode should be considered an important risk factor for COPD and that prevention of tuberculosis may have indirect, downstream individual- and population-level health benefits.

Household-based studies are often used to identify risk factors for tuberculosis (TB) infection transmission and evaluate the efficacy of TB preventive therapies. Typically, these studies define the earliest diagnosed TB patient within a household as the index patient and subsequently monitor their household contacts (HHCs) for incident TB disease. This design assumes that HHCs who develop TB disease are likely to have been infected by their respective index patients. However, this assumption may be challenged, as some HHCs likely acquire TB infections from community sources, introducing the non-differential misclassification of TB outcomes [ 1–5 ].

In principle, such non-differential misclassification biases study results toward the null, underestimating the true magnitude of the associations. Nevertheless, when unexpected or strong associations emerge, questions regarding the robustness and validity of the findings frequently arise. These concerns become particularly important in high-TB-burden settings, in which higher levels of community-based TB exposure may increase the potential for misclassification, thus weakening the conclusions derived from household-based studies [ 6 , 7 ].

To better understand the impact of community-acquired TB infections on household-based transmission studies, it is necessary to quantify the proportion of genetically linked index–HHC pairs, as these are likely the result of within-household transmission. In this study, we address this question in two ways. First, we assess the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs that are genetically linked by using data from a longitudinal household study that we previously conducted in Lima, Peru. We then incorporate the findings from this study into a systematic review of other studies that have applied molecular genotyping methods to index–HHC patient pairs. By synthesizing evidence across diverse epidemiological contexts and combining it with our primary data, we aim to rigorously evaluate the robustness and validity of household-based study designs across settings with different TB burdens. By clarifying the extent to which household transmission can be distinguished from community-acquired infection, this work also informs the design and interpretation of contact investigations, preventive therapy trials, and vaccine studies across settings with different TB burdens.
### Study setting and design

We conducted a prospective cohort study in 20 districts of Lima, Peru (population ∼3.3 million). The study design and methodology have been described previously [ 5 ]. Between September 2009 and August 2012, we enrolled incident pulmonary TB patients aged ≥16 years from 106 health centers and confirmed diagnoses by using sputum smear and culture. At enrolment, we collected sociodemographic and clinical data by using a structured questionnaire. Within 2 weeks of an index diagnosis, we invited HHCs to participate; consenting HHCs underwent TB symptom screening and, if positive, were referred for further evaluation. HHCs without TB at baseline were followed for 1 year, with visits at 2, 6, and 12 months. We classified HHCs diagnosed within 14 days as co-prevalent patients and those diagnosed between 14 and 455 days as secondary TB patients. Sputum samples were obtained whenever possible at enrolment or follow-up.

### Genotyping, whole-genome sequencing, and genetic distance analysis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) isolates from culture-positive index and HHC patients were genotyped by using 24-locus mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit–variable number tandem repeat (MIRU–VNTR) typing and sequenced by using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on the Illumina HiSeq platform. The read lengths ranged from 100 to 150 base pairs, with a minimum coverage of 20-fold. Raw WGS reads were mapped to the Mtb H37Rv reference genome by using the BWA-MEM algorithm [ 8 ]. We identified variants, including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), by using an alignment-based approach [ 9 , 10 ]. Isolates with <95% genome mapping coverage were excluded. We considered nucleotide calls missing if the valid depth of coverage was <10% of the mean coverage of the isolate, the mean read-mapping quality was <10, or the alternative allele frequency was <85%. Variants within the PE/PPE gene family and previously identified high-error regions were excluded [ 11 , 12 ]. Index–HHC pairs in which at least one isolate showed evidence of mixed infection were excluded from the analysis [ 13 ].

### Assessment of within-household transmission for index–HHC patient pairs

As a proxy for within-household transmission, we estimated the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs who were genetically linked by using MIRU–VNTR genotyping and WGS genetic distance analysis. A genetically linked transmission event was defined using MIRU typing as an index–HHC pair with ≥23 matched loci out of 24. In the WGS analysis, a genetically linked transmission event was defined as a genetic distance of ≤12 SNPs between Mtb isolates from the index–HHC pair [ 14 ]. We reported the overall proportion of genetically linked pairs, then stratified by co-prevalent versus secondary HHCs. Because many household studies focus on child contacts, who are more likely than adults to be infected by the index patient, we also reported matching proportions for pairs with a child contact [ 15 ]. Finally, we evaluated the associations between index and HHC characteristics and within-household transmission among index–secondary patient pairs by using a modified Poisson generalized estimating equation to account for correlation between pairs from the same households.
Among 12 676 HHCs exposed to a microbiologically confirmed index patient, 692 (5%) developed TB, of whom 246 (36%) were confirmed by using culture.

### MIRU genotyping matching

Among the 246 culture-confirmed HHC patients, 192 (78%) were successfully genotyped by using MIRU–VNTR, with data available for 168 index–HHC pairs. Twenty-three (14%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 145 pairs. Of these, 81 [56%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 47%–64%] were genetically linked. Twenty-six of 51 (51%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 55 of 94 (59%) index–secondary pairs were genetically linked. The HHC patients of 28 pairs were children. Of these, 4/5 (80%) co-prevalent and 15/23 (65%) secondary pairs were linked.

### WGS matching

Of 190 index–HHC pairs with WGS data, 15 (5%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 175 pairs from 152 households. Overall, 109 pairs (62%) were genetically linked. Transmission was observed in 34 of 66 (52%, 95% CI: 39%–64%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 74 of 109 (68%, 95% CI: 58%–77%) index–secondary pairs, with most secondary pairs (72/74) differing by up to five SNPs. When restricting to the 33 pairs with a child HHC, we noted 5/8 (63%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 19/25 (76%) index–secondary pairs ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Secondary pairs with female contacts were more often linked than those with male contacts (79% vs 54%, P = .008), while the Mtb lineage was not associated with genetic linkage ( P = .342).
### Search strategy and study selection

We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for papers that reported Mtb genotyping results for TB patients within the same household. We searched for papers published between 1 January 2006 and 20 June 2025, reflecting the time period following the widespread adoption of standardized 12-locus MIRU–VNTR [ 16 ]. Supplementary Table 2 describes the search strategy for each database.

### Screening

We performed an initial title and abstract review, excluding papers that did not discuss the household contacts of TB patients. For qualifying studies, we searched the full-text files for keywords related to Mtb molecular typing. Publications containing one or more keywords underwent full-text evaluation by two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. We excluded publications if they (i) did not involve original research on TB patients, (ii) did not include information on household membership, (iii) did not apply a qualifying genotyping method [spoligotyping, restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs), MIRU–VNTR, WGS] to Mtb samples, (iv) did not report Mtb genotype matching for household index–contact pairs, (v) enrolled fewer than five households, or (vi) obtained genotyping results for fewer than five index–contact pairs. We examined the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews for additional studies. A validation sample of 227 records was independently reviewed by a fourth reviewer, confirming the accuracy of the screening process.

### Data extraction

For qualifying studies, two reviewers extracted the following data: location and dates of patient enrolment, study design, eligibility criteria for index patients and contacts, procedure for identifying HHCs, definitions of household contacts, genotyping method(s), and the genotyping matching proportions for household patient pairs. We initially intended to extract individual patient data to assess the risk factors for genotype matching but this was unavailable in most studies. Instead, we extracted results based on the most stringent definition of matching of each study; when individual results were available, we calculated the proportion of identical genotypes. We reported the combined matching proportions for co-prevalent and secondary HHCs, and, when possible, separately for secondary HHCs as defined by the study authors. If the site-specific TB incidence was not reported in the publication, then we used WHO national estimates from the first year of enrolment or from 2000, whichever was later [ 17 ]. We also extracted individual-level metadata on age and gender when available.

### Quality assessment

We assessed the study quality by study design rigor and statistical robustness. Design rigor was scored (0–8) by using an eight-question framework on patient enrolment, household definitions, HHC follow-up, and genotyping completeness ( Supplementary Table 3 ). Statistical robustness was evaluated by the width of the Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs, with intervals of <40% considered robust.

### Modeling the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs

We modeled the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs by using a binomial generalized additive model with a logit link and spline term, with smoothness selected by using restricted maximum likelihood. For each incidence value, we estimated the fitted proportion and 95% CI on the probability scale.
The study selection process is shown in Fig. 1 . Out of 5910 unique citations identified from the search, we completed a full-text review of 231 publications. Two reviewed studies from Brazil were follow-up publications from an earlier and larger genotyping study, so we reported data from the larger study [ 18 ]. Ultimately, 22 articles met all inclusion criteria [ 18–39 ].

The 22 included studies, all published in English, evaluated within-household transmission between approximately 12 000 index patients and 2800 household contacts with TB, enrolled between 1995 and 2023 ( Table 1 ). These studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa (South Africa, Ghana, Uganda, the Gambia, Malawi), South America (Brazil, Argentina, Peru), Central and Western Europe (Poland, Spain, the UK), Southeast Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines), the USA, and China. Two studies [ 19 , 21 ] included co-prevalent household patients only, 5 studies [ 18 , 24 , 26 , 30 , 31 ] included secondary household patients only, and 15 studies [ 20 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 27–29 , 32–39 ] included both. Four studies focused their enrolment on patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis [ 27 , 29 , 30 , 32 ]. The included studies encompassed a wide range of TB-burden settings, with community incidence rates ranging from 6.7 to 845 TB patients per 100 000 person-years. The number of index–HHC pairs with genotyping data ranged from 6 to 344 per study, with a median of 17.5 pairs ( Table 2 ). Genotyping for one or more index–child HHC pairs was available for five studies and gender information for patient pairs was partially or completely available for eight studies ( Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 ).

### Quality assessment

Among the 22 studies from the systematic review, 10 studies (45%) [ 18–21 , 24–27 , 29 , 36 ] were scored as ≥5/8 for study design. The most common methodological gaps were the failure to report the proportion of eligible index patients who agreed to participate ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 2), the lack of active follow-up to detect incident TB among HHCs ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 7), and the prolonged interval allowed between the index patient’s diagnosis and the subsequent diagnosis of HHC TB patients ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 8).

Eleven (50%) reviewed studies reported matching proportions with a Clopper–Pearson exact 95% CI width of >40% [ 19–21 , 24 , 26–30 , 33 , 38 ]. Therefore, only 11 reviewed studies were considered statistically robust ( Fig. 2 ).

### Host factors and within-household transmission

Among the 11 reviewed studies that met our criteria for statistical robustness, three reported genetic linkage by age ( Supplementary Table 4 ). However, two of these studies [ 31 , 34 ] included three or fewer child contacts. In the third study [ 25 ], the matching proportion was 90% (26/29) in pairs with child contacts and 63% (20/32) in pairs with adult contacts. Three statistically robust studies reported gender information for comparison ( Supplementary Table 5 ). One study [ 37 ] reported 100% matching for all pair types and the two other studies [ 31 , 34 ] found matching proportions that were similar for female and male contacts, with slightly higher values in females (88% vs 81%, P = .656; 73% vs 70%, P = .999).
### All pairs (index–co-prevalent and index–secondary patient pairs)

Across 23 studies (22 from the review and our Lima study), the proportion of genetically matched index–HHC pairs ranged from 17% to 100%. Of six studies using multiple methods independently, five reported variability across the methods. No method universally yielded higher or lower proportions, though spoligotyping gave the highest proportions in three out of four studies. Eleven studies used MIRU–VNTR (with varying loci) and seven implemented WGS ( Table 2 ).

Among the 12 total studies with greater statistical robustness [ 18 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 31 , 32 , 34–37 , 39 ], 10 reported an overall matching proportion of ≥62% and two studies from the same cohort in Malawi reported proportions of 44% and 49%, respectively ( Fig. 2a ). The nine studies that reported a matching proportion of ≥62% were conducted in settings with a TB incidence of ≤276 patients per 100 000 person-years, while the studies from Malawi were conducted in an area with a TB burden of 386 patients per 100 000 person-years.

The spline regression model of all patient pairs suggests that, in study settings with an annual TB incidence of ≤250 per 100 000 population, at ≥61% (95% CI: 55%–67%) of household patients are genetically matched to their index patient, likely reflecting household TB infection transmission ( Fig. 2b ). However, estimates of the matching proportion in regions of exceptionally high TB incidence are limited by sparse data.

### Index–secondary patient pairs only

Eleven studies, including our study in Lima, reported a separate matching proportion for index–secondary patient pairs ( Fig. 3 ).
