discussion:
This is the first study to describe the birth prevalence and characteristics of isolated clubfoot in the NT. The overall birth prevalence was 2.80/1000, with a five times higher prevalence for Indigenous babies (5.99/1000) than for non-Indigenous babies (1.16/1000). Among babies with clubfoot, Indigenous babies were more likely to be male, live in remote areas, and have younger mothers who reported smoking or alcohol use during pregnancy. These findings—among the highest prevalence rates globally—warrant further investigation.

We have identified that the NT has the highest prevalence of clubfoot reported in Australia, particularly for Indigenous Australians. While interstate non-Indigenous rates are comparable, rates for Indigenous babies are five times higher than those for non-Indigenous babies in the NT (5.99 vs 1.16), three times higher than those in WA (3.46 vs 1.11), 1 and twice as high as those in SA (2.1 vs 1.0) 2 (calculations shown in Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ). Given that 73% of babies with clubfoot in the NT are Indigenous and the disproportionate rate of clubfoot prevalence, consultation with Indigenous people and communities regarding further research in the NT and throughout Australia is warranted.

We found that, in the NT, like WA, clubfoot was four times more common in Indigenous males than in Indigenous females. 1 Typically, clubfoot shows a 2:1 male-to-female ratio, suggesting a stronger-than-typical tendency in Indigenous males compared with non-Indigenous males. 7 While there could be genetic explanations for this, given the controversial history of genetic testing with Indigenous people, 27 an important next step in the NT will be to collaborate with Indigenous people to understand the importance of clubfoot itself before that of potential inheritance patterns, and for that to guide future research directions.

Some findings reflect the characteristics of the NT population overall and should be interpreted cautiously. Indigenous babies with clubfoot predominantly live in remote areas, reflecting the NT population distribution. 28 Consequently, access to care requires long-distance travel and separation from family, community, and culture. With 76 remote communities and ∼600 homelands in the NT, 29 , 30 remote clubfoot services warrant exploration with ACCHOs and government services. Additionally, Indigenous people, including expectant mothers, report higher smoking and alcohol rates compared with non-Indigenous counterparts, especially in remote areas. 5 , 31–33 Similarly, Indigenous mothers are younger throughout Australia, the NT, and in our study (mean age 27, 26, and 25 years, respectively) than non-Indigenous mothers (mean age 31, 31, and 30 years, respectively). 34 , 35 Although this study does not investigate the risk factors for clubfoot itself, it is noteworthy that maternal smoking and Indigenous maternity are recognized risk factors, whereas alcohol use and maternal age lack association. 13 , 36 The potential impact of these characteristics and other social determinants of health on clubfoot prevalence needs careful attention.

The high prevalence of clubfoot among First Nations groups has been previously reported. Studies reporting Māori 37 and Hawaiian 38 prevalence groups (8 and 7/1000, respectively) are frequently cited, but the primary evidence is equivocal, minimal, and dated. In other ethnically diverse groups, prevalence patterns are unclear. A US study that pooled birth defect registry (BDR) data from 10 states found a slightly lower prevalence for African American, Hispanic, and Asian people and no difference for Native American people compared with non-Hispanic White people. 39 In other North American studies, no differences or a lower prevalence was found between ethnic groups. 40–42 The prevalence for Black South Africans was 1.5–3.5/1000, varying between tribal groups and between urban and rural areas. 43–45 The paucity of contemporary, comparable, quality data suggests a need to explore clubfoot with ethnically diverse and Indigenous populations.

A comparison of clubfoot prevalence estimates nationally and globally is difficult due to differing methodologies and therefore requires caution. For example, prevalence estimates in WA and SA identified cases through a BDR and included stillbirths and late terminations, which we deemed unnecessary. 23 The SA study confirmed cases with medical record review, leading to the exclusion of 15% of the cases. 2 We have demonstrated that, without multiple sources and full record reviews, many true cases would have been missed and hundreds of false cases could have been included ( Supplementary Tables S2A and S2B ). A recent global estimate of clubfoot prevalence included 35 studies, although none was from Australia. 3 Only four included studies (India 46–48 , Nigeria 49 ) reported a prevalence that was comparable to or higher than that in the NT (2.79–4.23/1000). However, these were single-hospital BDR studies that were not exclusive to clubfoot, lacked detail regarding ascertainment, and did not report the differentiation of isolated from non-isolated cases, and thus could have been overestimates. We have shown that, without rigorous ascertainment processes, single-source BDR studies may report the prevalence of clubfoot inaccurately. In our study, with careful ascertainment processes, utilizing all conceivable sources to confirm cases, our confidence is high that the clubfoot prevalence has been accurately established for the NT.

### Limitations

Limitations have largely arisen from the challenges of retrospective medical record audits and from sourcing data that were not collected for our research purposes. 50 Non-specific diagnostic terminology and the use of umbrella rather than precise ICD-10-AM codes for clubfoot have reduced the confidence in these datasets, requiring verification through full medical audit. Correctly applied umbrella codes, while not incorrect, are imprecise. Consistent, accurate nomenclature (e.g. eliminating the ambiguous term ‘talipes’ from the paediatric lexicon) and use of the available specific codes for clubfoot could reduce the need for a record audit to obtain accurate data. Generalizing our prevalence findings requires caution given the unique cultural setting, small population, and small absolute number of cases ( n = 150) in the NT. Additionally, some cases classified as isolated clubfoot at birth may later have been diagnosed with comorbidities that would have then excluded them from our analysis. Social determinants are important confounders of health outcomes 5 , 51 (e.g. socioeconomic status) but were not available. More importantly, cultural determinants of health must be considered in the future, as Indigenous cultural practices and traditional lifestyles are common in the NT and are a protective force for families and communities. 6 , 52 , 53 The mismatch between Indigenous cultural values and the delivery of mainstream Australian healthcare must be acknowledged and addressed. 54–56

### Strengths

The principal strength of our study is its meticulous ascertainment process. We reviewed electronic records for every potential case and, despite the vast regional coverage, audited complete medical records across the NT to confirm cases and gather data. Combining coding, registry, and clinical data strengthened our findings compared with studies using only one source, and we have shown that code- or registry-based data alone may incorrectly inform prevalence estimates.

### Further research

Further systematic epidemiological studies would be invaluable for service mapping and addressing areas of need. Identifying modifiable factors associated with the risk of clubfoot among Indigenous people would be valuable, but, most importantly, research with Indigenous families who have experienced clubfoot will ensure that service providers can recognize and meet the needs of this population.

Establishing a high-quality clubfoot-specific registry across Australia with comprehensive demographic and clinical data would enhance data quality, linkage, evaluation, and interpretation. It would also facilitate high-quality Australia-wide clubfoot research, which is lacking. To achieve this, collaboration across clinical, coding, and data-management fields to standardize terminology, measures, and reporting processes is required. In the absence of such a registry, our ascertainment methodology could serve as a template for accurately determining clubfoot prevalence.

### Conclusion

Clubfoot prevalence in the NT, especially for Indigenous people, is disproportionately high compared with national and global data. Clinically, this highlights the need to align clubfoot services with the needs of recipients—in this case, developing and embedding culturally responsive care. The establishment of a national clubfoot registry and qualitative research to understand the implications of clubfoot for Indigenous people in the NT is recommended.

inputs:
Preterm birth (PTB)—delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation, with a global prevalence of 10.6%—is the leading cause of death in children who are <5 years old [ 1 ]. This condition is also a common reason for newborn hospital admissions due to severe complications and is associated with poor health in childhood and adulthood [ 2 ].

Tens of studies report associations of ambient temperature with PTB by using various epidemiological study designs, exposure measures, and exposure periods. Most of these studies have examined short-term exposures only. For example, several time series studies found that immediate exposure to high temperature on the day of birth or a few days before is associated with PTB [ 3–7 ]. Similarly, a handful of case-crossover studies observed that exposure to heat during the week before birth is related to PTB [ 8–11 ]. In addition, several cohort studies reported positive associations between high temperatures or heatwaves in the week before birth and PTB [ 12–18 ]. While this literature generally demonstrates positive associations for acute exposures, its main limitation is the lack of consideration of effects in earlier gestation weeks.

Other cohort studies have examined longer-term exposures, such as the last month before birth, the entire pregnancy average, and trimester-specific exposures [ 19–26 ]. Most of these studies fitted separate models for each exposure period. However, as temperatures in different periods during pregnancy are highly correlated, exposure in one period might confound the association between exposure in another period and PTB [ 27 ].

Distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) add different exposure periods (lags) to the model while addressing their collinearity by using a lag–response function [ 28 ]. To date, only three cohort studies have examined associations between temperature and PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis [ 29–31 ]. Adapting DLNMs to prenatal exposures creates a challenge due to varying gestational lengths. A study in France used two exposure periods in a DLNM: the last 30 days of pregnancy and 26 weeks after conception, to avoid this issue [ 29 ]. While innovative, this approach mixes the reference times of the exposure, as some exposures are defined by gestation week, while other exposures in the same model are determined by the birth date. Moreover, some of these exposure periods overlap for some of the pregnancies. This limits the interpretation of critical periods by gestation weeks. A study in Sweden defined exposure weeks backward from the week of birth, which leads to a similar limitation [ 30 ].

DLNMs can also estimate associations of cumulative exposures throughout pregnancy, calculated for scenarios of fixed exposure relative to another fixed reference exposure. However, such scenarios are unrealistic for most climates, in which temperatures vary throughout pregnancy due to seasonality.

Few studies also examined the effect modification by socioeconomic status (SES) [ 3 , 7 , 11 , 14 , 17 , 22 ], race [ 4 , 8 ], or body mass index (BMI) [ 8 , 32 ], with inconsistent results. The effect of ambient temperature on very early, early, or late PTB may also be different. Several studies stratified the associations by the timing of PTB and yielded incongruent results [ 5 , 6 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 18 , 23 , 24 ]. However, stratifying by gestational age groups may induce a collider bias [ 33 ] and an alternative methodological approach may be pursued.

In this study, we aimed to examine the critical temperature exposure periods for PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis in an innovative methodological approach. This enabled us to differentiate between PTB during various phases of pregnancy, estimate associations with realistic exposure scenarios throughout pregnancy, and examine vulnerable groups in Southern Israel by using a historical cohort of ∼130 000 births.
### Study design and study population

We employed a historical cohort design utilizing electronic health records of members of Clalit Health Services (henceforth: Clalit), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, who gave birth at Soroka University Medical Centre in Be’er Sheva. Soroka is the only tertiary-level hospital in Southern Israel and ∼70% of the population in that area are Clalit members [ 34 ]. We obtained data on all live births that occurred at Soroka between 1 January 2005 and 31 December 2019 ( n =
 157 478) and had 131 599 births available for analysis after exclusions (see Supplementary Figure S1 for a complete description of the exclusions).

### Outcome definition

Gestational age at delivery was estimated at the hospital by using the last menstrual period (LMP) date (when available) and ultrasonography. PTB was defined as a birth occurring before 37 completed gestation weeks and categorized into four groups: <28, 28–31, 32–33, and 34–36 completed weeks [ 1 , 35 ].

### Exposure assessment

We assessed ambient temperature with a spatiotemporal model—an ensemble of machine-learning models of random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and generalized additive models [ 36 ]. Its estimates are based on satellite measurements, observations from weather stations, and reanalysis of synoptic conditions. The model performs well with an overall root mean square error of 0.3°C, providing hourly temperature estimates for a grid of 1 km × 1 km for Israel for the study period [ 36 ].

The Clalit database provided coordinates for residential addresses when available. As noted above, we excluded all addresses outside the southern district ( n =
 3558; 2.4%), as they might have been outdated. For other addresses, the geocoding quality and exposure assignment are described in Supplementary Table S1 . Further details on the exposure assessment are found in the Supplementary Material .

### Covariates

We drew a directed acyclic graph (DAG) [ 37 ] showing our assumptions about the causal relationships among the study variables to determine the minimal set of variables to be conditioned to eliminate bias and confounding ( Fig. 1a ). According to the analysis of the DAG using DAGitty [ 38 ], the minimal set of variables to be adjusted for was: SES, ethnicity, locality, seasonality, and air pollution ( Fig. 1b ). As the confounding effects of air pollution and locality on other associations of temperature and pregnancy outcomes in the region seemed negligible in prior studies, we adjusted for these variables only in sensitivity analyses.

We examined effect modification by ethnicity (Arab/Jewish), infant sex, area-level SES, and pre-pregnancy BMI. Area-level SES was based on census-level small-statistical-area classification from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics [ 39 ]. We estimated pre-pregnancy BMI by the median of height measurements and the last weight measurement within 2 years prior to the pregnancy until the first month of the pregnancy.

### Statistical analyses

We fitted Cox proportional-hazards models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM [ 28 , 40 ]. We utilized gestation weeks as the time and birth as the event to estimate how the conditional associations between the mean weekly temperature and PTB varied throughout gestation. Further details about the model can be found in the Supplementary Material .

Formula 1 specifies the primary model equation for the hazard function λ i ( t ) ⁠ , where C i represents time-independent covariates, such as SES and ethnicity, Z i ( t ) represents time-dependent covariates (sine and cosine of the week of the year for each gestation week, adjusting for seasonality), and X i represents the time-dependent exposures (i.e. weekly temperature) added into the model in a cross-basis function s x ( X i , t ; β x ) ⁠ . λ 0 ( t ) is the baseline hazard function and β c ⁠ , β z ⁠ , and β x are the other Cox model parameters with respect to the time-independent covariates C i ⁠ , time-dependent covariates Z i ( t ) ⁠ , and the cross-basis functions, respectively [ 41 ]. The causal structure assumed for the time-dependent covariates and exposures is demonstrated by the schematic DAG in Supplementary Figure S2 . Robust standard errors were used to account for the dependency between pregnancies of the same mother [ 42 ].

To examine whether the association of exposure in a specific gestation week with PTB changes for different delivery weeks, we used an extension of the previous Cox model, which enables time-dependent coefficients differing by PTB groups based on gestational age at delivery (as defined above) without stratifying the model (see Supplementary Material for technical details) [ 40 ].

In addition, we used the primary model to examine the associations of exposure to minimum (instead of mean) temperature with the risk of PTB. We also added possible effect modifiers to the primary models as interaction terms, calculated P -values for interaction using likelihood ratio tests, and stratified models by these modifiers. In sensitivity analyses, we further adjusted our models for air pollution by using weekly PM 2.5 concentrations and locality. We also fitted a model without seasonality covariates. All analyses were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ 43 ], using the survival [ 42 ] and dlnm [ 28 ] packages.

### Risk estimation by temperature trajectories

To demonstrate the implications of our results for the risk of PTB by different realistic exposure trajectories throughout pregnancy, we estimated the survival probability by Week 37: S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ . For this estimation, we used 37 weeks of exposure and covariates of each pregnancy according to LMP date and residential address, regardless of the actual date of birth. We then estimated the cumulative PTB risk by using 1 – S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ , i.e. the probability of not completing 37 gestational weeks.

For the current dataset, the seasonal factor plays a major role in determining the exposure estimated by the spatiotemporal model: by using a univariate linear regression model, we found that 86% of the variability in weekly temperature can be explained by the LMP month. Therefore, we calculated the average estimated PTB risk by using the LMP month. Finally, we estimated the relative risks for each LMP month by dividing the average risk in each month by the risk of the lowest average risk (March). The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by bootstrapping using 500 samples with replacement. A formal description of this approach can be found in the Supplementary Material .
In our cohort of 131 599 deliveries in Southern Israel, the prevalence of PTB was 7%. More than half of the study population were Bedouin-Arab and nearly half of the mothers with available pre-pregnancy BMI data were overweight or obese ( Table 1 ). Supplementary Figure S3 illustrates the exposure distribution, Supplementary Figure S4 presents its spatial distribution, and Supplementary Figure S5 demonstrates the correlation structure among exposure weeks of gestation. The proportions of Arabs and mothers with lower SES were higher in the lower-temperature quintiles ( Supplementary Table S2 ) and Arabs comprised the majority in the first and second SES quartiles ( Supplementary Table S3 ).

Temperature exposures in gestation Weeks 1–28 were not associated with PTB. However, higher temperatures during the third trimester were associated with a higher risk of early delivery. For example, exposure to 31°C (99th percentile) in Week 29 presented an hazard ratio (HR) of 1.02 (95% CI: 1.00–1.03) with PTB compared with the minimum-risk temperature (16°C). Similarly, exposures to 31°C in Weeks 30–37 were associated with PTB, with increasing strength towards the end of the third trimester. The strongest association was for exposure during Week 37 (HR= 1.04, 95% CI: 1.01–1.07; Fig. 2 ). There were no major differences in associations by groups of PTB severity ( Supplementary Figures S6–S9 ).

We did not find any interaction with ethnicity and SES ( P for interaction = 0.18 and 0.84, respectively). Weekly associations were slightly stronger in female than male fetuses ( P for interaction < 0.001; Supplementary Figure S10 ). In addition, associations were somewhat different in women with pre-pregnancy underweight or overweight, but the pattern of difference was unclear ( P for interaction <0.001; Supplementary Figure S11 ). Cancelling the seasonality adjustment or adding adjustments for PM 2.5 and locality did not materially change the results ( Supplementary Figures S12–S14 ). Associations with minimum (instead of mean) daily temperature were also similar ( Supplementary Figure S15 ).

The average estimated risk of PTB across exposure trajectories defined by the LMP month displayed a clear seasonal pattern, with the lowest risk estimated for pregnancies with LMP between February and April and the highest risk for those with LMP during the autumn ( Fig. 3 , top). The average estimated risk by LMP month varied between 6.5% and 7.6% for pregnancies with LMP in March and October, respectively, translated into a relative risk of 1.17 with a 95% CI of 1.07–1.27 ( Fig. 3 , middle; Supplementary Table S4 ). Exposure trajectories for pregnancies starting in the autumn also included the highest temperatures during Weeks 33–37 of gestation ( Fig. 3 , bottom).
The Soroka Institutional Review Board approved the study (approval number: 0341-19), including the exemption from informed consent due to the sample size and de-identified nature of the records.
discussion:
In this cohort of >130 000 singleton live births in Southern Israel, we examined the critical periods of and vulnerable groups to the associations between temperature and PTB. Exposures to high temperatures during gestation Weeks 29–37 were associated with an increased risk of PTB, with stronger associations in females. Pregnancies starting in the autumn were exposed to the highest temperatures in Weeks 33–37 and had the highest estimated PTB risk.

Our findings align with most literature showing an association between heat and PTB. For example, cohort studies in Australia, the USA, Israel, and China found that heat in the week before birth was associated with PTB, with HRs ranging from 1.02 to 2.00 [ 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 ]. However, a few studies found no association with heat exposure in the last week of pregnancy [ 21 , 24 , 30 ] and a time-series study from China found a negative association [ 44 ]. While the associations that we found in the final weeks of the PTB risk period support the associations of acute exposures in these studies, our findings are not fully comparable due to different definitions of the exposure windows. Our exposures were defined by gestation week, while theirs were determined by the date of birth, which does not correspond to a specific gestation week. Fetuses go through different physiological stages in each gestation week and examining exposures by gestation weeks—instead of relative to birth date—enables the detection of critical periods and an understanding of biological mechanisms.

Some cohort studies investigating exposures throughout gestation found similar associations in later stages of pregnancy. For example, a cohort study in Australia fitted separate Cox models for temperature in each trimester and found positive associations for extreme heat and cold only in the third trimester [ 26 ]. However, some found associations in the earlier stages, such as a Korean cohort that demonstrated positive associations for heatwaves in the first and second trimesters [ 19 ]. Another study from China found the strongest associations for the average exposure in Weeks 8–14 [ 25 ]. While our results partly overlap with those of these studies, it is challenging to draw comparisons due to the different exposure windows. More importantly, these studies examined each exposure window in a separate model, raising concern that some associations were confounded by exposure in other gestation weeks.

Three studies used a Cox model with a DLNM. One study in China found that high temperatures in Weeks 4–8 and 22–27 were associated with increased PTB risk, while the same exposure during Weeks 10–20 was associated with decreased risk [ 31 ]. A similar study in France found positive associations for heat in Weeks 3–7 and 22–28 for minimum temperatures but not for mean temperatures [ 29 ]. A study in Sweden did not find clear associations, possibly explained by the different climates [ 30 ].

Several studies examined whether the associations vary according to the timing of the PTB by stratifying their analyses by gestational age categories, with contradictory findings [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 18 , 23 , 24 ]. Using a new statistical approach, we observed no major difference in associations, consistently with an American time-series study that examined the issue [ 6 ]. In addition, we did not observe any interaction with ethnicity or SES, despite the differences in living conditions between Jews and Arabs and among SES strata in Southern Israel.

Consistently with our findings, most studies reported stronger associations for female fetuses [ 5 , 10 , 16 ], whereas a case-crossover study in the USA found the opposite [ 11 ] and a few other studies did not detect any interaction [ 6 , 13 , 22 ]. Although male fetuses are at higher risk of PTB [ 45 ], heat-related PTB may be more prominent in female fetuses. The unclear interaction pattern with BMI could be due to a small sample size in subgroups or a selection bias, as BMI was missing for 63% of our population.

The weekly associations that we reported as HRs should not be interpreted as causal effects. Although HRs are standard association measures for Cox models, they suffer from an inherent collider bias due to the conditioning on survival in each follow-up step [ 46 , 47 ]. To partially overcome the limited interpretation of our results, we further estimated cumulative PTB risk for realistic exposure scenarios—a method that does not suffer from the limitations of HRs [ 46 ]. However, defining a causal estimand in this context is more challenging. It is beyond the scope of this work, as it involves the debatable possibility of intervening in temperature exposure.

Examining the time-varying temperature across pregnancy as seasonal exposure trajectories defined by LMP month and comparing the risk by these trajectories is a new methodological approach presented in this work. Although the distribution of higher temperatures at the end of the preterm risk period by the LMP month does not entirely align with the estimated PTB risk, the overlap for the months in autumn demonstrates the relationship between exposure and risk of PTB in our models. While the magnitude of the weekly associations is limited to HRs of 1.04, the cumulative associations throughout pregnancy, when comparing LMP months, are approximately 4-fold higher. Considering also the high incidence of PTB and the abundant exposure—predicted to increase with climate change—emphasizes the importance of our findings.

The main strength of our study was that we used state-of-the-art statistical methods and further developed them. First, we used Cox models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM and improved these models to fit prenatal exposures by addressing the issue of differing pregnancy lengths. Second, we applied a new approach to demonstrate the predictions of the model for realistic cumulative exposure trajectories. Third, we used time-dependent coefficients to determine whether the associations varied by follow-up time, avoiding exclusion or stratification by gestational age that may have led to collider bias [ 33 ]. Fourth, we introduced adjustment for seasonality as a time-varying covariate and found through a sensitivity analysis that seasonality was not an actual confounder in our study.

Our study had limitations as well. Exposure was based on residential addresses, creating some exposure error. However, this error was likely to be non-differential and therefore more likely to bias the associations to the null. We also lacked data on indoor temperatures, air-conditioner use, or other ways to change personal exposure. Instead, our exposure estimate was a proxy for personal exposure, creating another source of non-differential error [ 48 ]. However, proxy measurements have the methodological advantage of not being prone to confounding by personal behaviors [ 48 ]. Additionally, we only had data on live births, which are prone to live-birth bias [ 49 ].

In summary, our findings highlight the late weeks of the third trimester as the critical window concerning heat and PTB. Future research on biological mechanisms can focus on the possible effects of heat in the later stages of fetal development. In addition, this study underlines the need for future studies to consider the role of seasonality thoroughly.
target: Accumulating evidence suggests links between ambient temperature and preterm birth. We aimed to explore susceptible exposure weeks and groups concerning temperature and preterm birth in an innovative methodological approach.We conducted a historical cohort study of 131 599 singleton live births in Southern Israel in 2005–19. Weekly mean temperatures were assessed based on residential address and a spatiotemporal model. We fitted Cox models with time-dependent covariates and distributed lag non-linear models, adapting them for the challenges of examining prenatal exposures. We further extended the models with time-dependent coefficients to assess variations by preterm birth categories. Finally, we estimated associations of cumulative exposures by using predicted survival curves contrasting realistic exposure trajectories by month of the last menstrual period (LMP).Exposures to high temperatures in gestation Weeks 29–37 were associated with increased preterm birth risk. The highest hazard ratio was 1.04 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.01–1.07] in Week 37 for the 99th percentile (31°C) compared with the minimum-risk temperature (16°C). There was a strong seasonal pattern in the estimated risk, with pregnancies with LMP in autumn having a higher risk. The average estimated risk by LMP month varied between 6.5% and 7.6% for pregnancies with LMP in March and October, respectively, corresponding to a relative risk of 1.17 (95% CI: 1.07–1.27).The final weeks of the third trimester are the key window for heat exposure in Southern Israel, creating a distinguished estimated risk by LMP month, with the highest risk for pregnancies conceived in the autumn.

Congenital anomalies (CAs), also known as congenital malformations or birth defects, are structural or functional anomalies that occur in utero . They may be identifiable prenatally, at birth, during infancy, or later in life. Globally, an estimated 240 000 newborns die annually within 28 days of birth due to congenital disorders, and 170 000 additional related deaths occur up to 5 years of age [ 1 ].

In recent decades, deaths from communicable diseases in both high- and low-income countries have decreased [ 2 ]. Consequently, the relative contribution of CAs to under-five mortality is now among the 10 leading causes of death worldwide [ 3 , 4 ].

For many CAs, including rare structural anomalies, most deaths occur in the first weeks of life, and survival beyond 10 years, conditional on surviving this crucial window, is actually quite high, frequently over 90% [ 5 ]. Children with cardiovascular, renal, and gastrointestinal abnormalities require specialized care. However, there is little population-based research about the long-term survival of individuals with a broad range of CAs beyond the second decade of life [ 3 ]. Information about the long-term outcomes of individuals with CAs who reach adulthood is important for counselling affected individuals and their parents and for adequate planning of health and other services [ 3 ].

We aimed to investigate associations between CAs and premature adult mortality. We focused on individuals who survived to the age of 18 years, comparing all-cause adult mortality of individuals with and without CAs in the Jerusalem Perinatal Study (JPS), a birth cohort with over four decades of follow-up. Previous work from this cohort had demonstrated a relatively high rate of CAs and an association between consanguinity and CAs [ 6 , 7 ].
### Study design and study population

The population-based JPS cohort has been previously described [ 8 ]. It includes all 92 408 still- and live births to West Jerusalem mothers in 1964–76. Vital status was verified via linkage of unique national identity numbers to the Israeli Population Registry, updated through 31 December 2016. Data on demographic, perinatal, and parental characteristics were obtained at birth. We excluded stillbirths ( n = 949), offspring who could not be traced in the Population Registry ( n = 1409; henceforth “unverified”), and those who did not survive until 18 years of age ( n = 2429). The final study population consisted of 87 621 individuals ( Fig. 1 ).

### Study variables

The outcome variable was all-cause adult mortality, defined as deaths occurring at 18 years or older. Data on CAs and affected body systems were recorded postnatally using birth records, and updated during follow-up in the first months of life from hospitalization records, nurse examinations, and death certificates [ 6 ]. Prenatal ultrasound was not prevalent during this period. Starting in 1969 CAs were categorized in terms of severity according to the International Classification of Diseases (Seventh Edition), in use at the time [ 7 ]. Of 5538 individuals with missing CA status at birth, 5078 (92%) were defined as CA-free using data collected during postnatal follow-up ( Supplementary Methods ). However, the affected body system remained missing for 36% of infants with CAs.

We defined four exposures of interest: dichotomous CA status (none versus at least one), multiplicity (0 = none, 1 = single, and 2 = multiple anomalies), severity (0 = none, 1 = only mild/moderate anomaly, 2 = only severe anomaly, and 3 = moderate and severe anomalies combined). Finally, we assessed CAs in specific body systems, namely the cardiovascular, central nervous system (CNS), gastrointestinal, respiratory, genitourinary and musculoskeletal systems, ear or eye, other (unclassified), or “unknown” system. Risk of death was assessed separately by each system.

All multivariable models were adjusted for the following covariates: Offspring sex, birth weight in gram (<2500, 2500–4000, and >4000), mode of delivery (vaginal/caesarean section), maternal place of birth (Israel or abroad), maternal age at delivery (<20, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35+), maternal level of education at delivery (0–8, 9–12, and >12 years) and socioeconomic status recoded into three levels (low, medium, high) [ 8 ]. Participants with missing values for maternal age (0.7%), education (6.7%), and delivery mode (2.8%) were assigned a separate “missing” category and therefore retained in the multivariable analyses.

### Statistical analysis

We plotted crude survival probabilities from birth for the entire cohort by presence of CA and CAs in specific body systems ( n = 90 050), using the Kaplan–Meier approach and counting time from birth to death or end of follow-up (31 December 2016).

All subsequent analyses were based on the subsample of individuals who survived to 18 years of age ( n = 87 621). In multivariate models, time-to-event was defined from the 18th birthday to death or censored at the end of follow-up. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by fitting Cox proportional hazard models. We also present adjusted absolute risks (1 − survival probability) and risk differences for individuals with and without CAs.

Separate models were constructed using the following exposures: CA status, number of CAs, anomaly severity, compared to a reference category of no CAs. Additional models compared mortality risks by the presence of a CA in a specific body system to “No CAs” or CAs in other systems. The models were adjusted for covariates previously found to be related to CA or death [ 9 , 10 ] and those found to be associated with mortality in univariate Cox models (not shown).

We conducted several sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Materials ): first, we assessed the impact of excluding “unverified” individuals by predicting their absolute risks over time from the CA status-mortality model using their baseline characteristics. We next compared these with observed risks in verified individuals using the Kaplan–Meier approach. Next, to evaluate the potential bias due to missing CA data in a few specific birth hospitals, we excluded infants born in these hospitals and compared results with the main models.

Thirdly, we imputed missing values in maternal age, education, and delivery mode using the multiple imputations by chained equations with five imputation datasets (R package mice ) [ 11 ]. The missing-at-random assumption was tested and supported by strong associations between the probability of missingness in imputed variables and the observed predictors.

To verify that our findings were robust to the non-independence of sibling observations, we conducted analyses selecting a single random child per family . Finally, since our data on family background are limited, we performed a sibling fixed-effects analysis. This design compares the mortality of siblings with and without anomalies within the same family and thus controls for unmeasured shared factors, including genetic background and household environment, that might confound the observed association.

For all main Cox models, the proportional hazards assumption was examined using the test of scaled Schoenfeld’s residuals [ 12 ] (R package survival [ 13 ]). Subsequently, we stratified all the main models on offspring’s sex and maternal education, which were the only variables exhibiting time-dependency ( Supplementary Tables S16–S19h and Figs S5–S8h ). The analyses were performed in R software (version 4.2.2).
The final study population is shown in Fig. 1 . Of the 92 408 offspring in the JPS cohort, 91 459 (99%) were live births, of which 90 050 (97.5%) were verified in the Population Registry. Kaplan–Meier plots illustrate mortality over the life-course ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ) for this population; most infants with malformations in cardiovascular and CNSs died very soon after birth and well before reaching 18 years. Of the verified population, 87 621 (97.3%) individuals attained the age of 18 years (and are the focus of this report), of whom 5621 (6.4%) had some form of CA.

Follow-up time from the 18th birthday ranged from 0 to 35 years with a median of 27.5 years and totalled 2 428 002.5 person-years. Deaths occurred in 1454 individuals from age 18.0 to 52.6 years; of these, 143 (2.5%) were in individuals with and 1311 (1.6%) without CAs ( Fig. 1 ).

Individuals with anomalies who survived to age 18 years were more likely to be male, to have low or high birth weight, low socioeconomic status at birth, Israel-born mothers, and to be delivered by caesarean section compared to those without CAs. Maternal age and education level at the time of delivery were similar between the groups ( Table 1 ), as was paternal age (mean 32 years ±7 in both). Of 5228 mothers whose children had CAs, about 7% ( n = 365) had more than one affected child.

In a multivariable Cox model, having any CA was associated with a 53% increase in the risk of death (CI: 1.29–1.83, P < .001) after stratification by offspring sex and maternal education and adjusting for other covariates ( Table 2 ).

Similar increased risks were observed for participants with single malformations (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.27–1.81) compared to those with none ( Table 3 ). The presence of multiple anomalies was associated with an even higher mortality risk (HR = 1.99, CI: 0.99–3.99), although the CI crossed unity. The risk of adult mortality was doubled in persons with severe anomalies (HR = 2.21, CI: 1.75–2.77) and with combined moderate and severe CAs (HR = 2.19, CI: 1.09–4.40) compared with those without anomalies. There was, however, no association between having a moderate anomaly and adult mortality. Adjusted HRs were elevated for CAs in the cardiovascular (HR = 4.81, CI: 2.15–10.70), gastrointestinal (HR = 2.74, CI: 1.47–5.11), and genitourinary (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.07–2.14) systems and among individuals with a CA in an unknown system (HR = 1.42, CI: 1.09–1.86) compared to all the others.

The absolute risk of death varied over time, and after 30 years of follow-up was 2.4% (CI: 1.8%–3.0%) in those with CAs, but only 1.5% (CI: 1.2%–1.9%) in those without, resulting in a risk difference of 0.9 percentage points ( Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 and Table S4 ).

All analyses aimed to assess the robustness of our findings produced results consistent with the main models. Supplementary Fig. S4 shows that the predicted risks for unverified individuals were almost identical to those of the verified cohort members in both exposure groups, suggesting that their risk of death is similar. The imputation analysis confirmed that missingness in covariates was unlikely to affect our results ( Supplementary Tables S6–S8 ). Likewise, the analyses excluding offspring born in hospitals with 75% of the missing CA status also supported our main estimates ( Supplementary Tables S9 and S10 ). Additionally, selecting a single random child per family suggested that non-independence of observations did not bias the reported associations ( Supplementary Tables S11–S13 ).

Finally, the fixed-effect within-family models were also consistent with the main analysis: siblings with CA, with all other shared characteristics being equal, had a 1.6-fold higher risk of adult mortality (CI: 1.06–2.42, Supplementary Table S14 ), and system-specific assessments, where there were sufficient cases to assess these, were generally consistent with the original models ( Supplementary Table S15 ).
The study was approved by the institutional review board (Helsinki committee) at Hadassah University Hospital (HMO0200-09). Since anonymized retrospective data were used, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.
discussion:
In this population-based cohort, we found an increased risk of premature all-cause mortality among individuals with CAs who survived until adulthood. Moreover, participants with severe anomalies had an over two-fold higher risk. Having an anomaly in the cardiovascular system was associated with a striking almost five-fold increased risk, while anomalies in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary systems were associated with an almost three-fold and 1.5-fold increased risk of premature death in adulthood, respectively.

The association between the presence of any form of CA and all-cause mortality in adulthood has been rarely reported. A review of 55 studies showed that overall, long-term survival in children born with CAs was much lower than in reference populations, in agreement with our findings [ 3 ]. Nine of the included studies analysed long-term survival among those with any CAs, while 46 others focused on subtypes of anomalies. Most studies reported 1–5-year follow-ups, with the longest one being 25 years from birth [ 14 ], while in our study, the median follow-up was 46 years from birth, or 27.5 years after reaching adulthood.

We found a higher risk of premature adult mortality in those with combined severe and moderate CA as well as multiple CAs, although we had limited power to assess the latter. Similarly, a European cohort study noted that the presence of multiple structural anomalies is an important predictor of reduced survival [ 10 ].

Multiple studies have assessed mortality in individuals with cardiovascular CAs. A Swedish study with 19 years of mean follow-up in adulthood showed a 3.2-fold mortality risk among those with congenital heart disease [ 15 ], while a study based on United States census data reported that among those surviving past their first birthday, 76% of deaths occurred after age 18 years [ 16 ]. A Finnish nationwide cohort study reported increased long-term mortality in patients with atrial septal defects [ 17 ], while a single-centre study in Holland showed comparable mortality to the general population in individuals who underwent atrial septal defect repair, with surveillance up to 50 years [ 18 ]. Regarding ventricular septal defects, Eckerström et al . reported 1.5- and 2.5-fold increases in mortality in individuals with and without surgical repair, respectively, when compared with those without CAs, underscoring an increased risk of death in patients with CA despite treatment [ 19 ]. Our data did not allow us to distinguish the type of cardiac anomaly or its treatment.

Several conceptual frameworks can help explain our findings. Since most anomalies result from genetic or acquired insults to the developing foetus, our findings are congruent with the concept of long-term consequences of intrauterine events [ 20 ]. Muller and colleagues, reporting morbidity and mortality in patients with congenital heart diseases after correction or palliation, conjectured that the increased risks of adulthood death could be related to the accumulated lifetime comorbidities and risk factors in those affected by cardiovascular CAs [ 21 ]. Moreover, cardiovascular lifestyle risk factors such as obesity and decreased physical activity may be more prevalent among those with CAs and may increase with age, thereby, combined with the structural CAs, heightening the risk of premature death [ 22 , 23 ].

We found a strong association between gastrointestinal anomalies and adult mortality, not previously reported, to our knowledge. A follow-up of a cohort of patients with anorectal, urological, and gynaecological system anomalies found long-term functional disturbances [ 24 ]. Although these anomalies may be corrected surgically, affected individuals may remain vulnerable to continuous morbidity leading to premature mortality.

Similarly, we found a positive association between genitourinary anomalies and adult mortality. Urinary system abnormalities and childhood kidney diseases may cause chronic kidney disease with severe consequences for premature mortality and cardiovascular morbidity [ 25 ], including a five-fold risk of end-stage kidney disease in young adults [ 26 ]. However, we are unaware of reports of association between genitourinary anomalies and all-cause mortality after age 18.

This paucity of data may be due to a perception that genitourinary and gastrointestinal CAs are “less lethal” compared with the life-threatening/immediate consequences of cardiovascular anomalies [ 27–29 ]. The latter enjoy sustained attention throughout the lifespan, and affected individuals are usually closely followed up by specialized clinics [ 30 ]. Nevertheless, gastrointestinal and genitourinary anomalies can also be debilitating, and our findings support recommendations for more research and careful follow-up in the transition between paediatric, adolescent, and adult clinical care [ 31 ]. Indeed, recommendations for life-long follow-up for individuals with anogenital malformations have recently been made by the eUROGEN group [ 32 ].

A key strength of our study is its population-based design with rich data collection at baseline [ 8 ] and long follow-up, compared to most published studies. The multi-generational nature of the JPS provided robust data on the parents’ sociodemographic characteristics, while the sample size provided sufficient power to assess most of the exposures. Although we lacked data on familial genetic and behavioural factors (e.g. consanguinity, maternal smoking, or medications) on all cohort members (which might have influenced the risk and consequences of CA), the family-based design of the JPS allowed comparison of the mortality of siblings with and without anomalies, thus controlling for unmeasured shared family factors. Loss-to-follow-up is also uncommon in this cohort because the identification number given to all Israelis enables highly accurate data linkage to population-based registries, and emigration was rare.

The study has several limitations. First, 1409 participants lacked outcome data. However, sensitivity analysis demonstrated that excluding them was unlikely to bias the estimated CA-mortality associations. Second, the ascertainment of CAs took place prior to the widespread use of prenatal ultrasound, and CAs may have been missed. This would misclassify affected individuals as CA-free, biasing towards the null hypothesis. Data collection proceeded in stages; we used data collected later in life to correct and complete the data recorded at birth. Nevertheless, CA data were missing for 5078 individuals (5.8%), and, as has been done in previous JPS-based studies [ 6 , 7 ], we chose to classify them as CA-free, a decision that might also have contributed to bias towards the null hypothesis. Moreover, our findings remained robust in analyses that excluded infants born in hospitals with incomplete ascertainment of CAs. The affected body system was unfortunately unknown for 36% of 5621 newborns with CAs. An early study from our team estimated that all major CAs were fully recorded, though some minor ones may be missing [ 6 ]. The current study was underpowered to assess associations between CNS and respiratory malformations and adult mortality. Additionally, some covariate data were missing, but individuals with missing covariates were retained in the models, thus minimizing selection bias or diluted power. Imputation of missing values yielded similar effect sizes.

The JPS cohort represents the population of West Jerusalem during the study years, and includes Israel-born parents and immigrants from over 60 countries, representing various degrees of religious affiliation and practice [ 6 ], and a fairly high rate of consanguinity, itself associated with CAs [ 7 ]. Arab citizens of Israel are under-represented due to the geographic boundaries of the cohort, and they have patterns of CA and consanguinity patterns different from those of the Jewish population [ 33 ]. Finally, regarding generalizability to other geographic settings, the prevalence of CA in the JPS is comparable to that documented from Nordic countries with intensive reporting [ 34 ].

In conclusion, both the presence and severity of CAs increase the risk of premature adult death. Our findings that gastrointestinal and genitourinary CAs are associated with adult mortality add to the known association with cardiovascular anomalies and call for increased surveillance in these individuals. Given improvements in neonatal care, cardiac surgery, and chronic disease management over recent decades, it is expected that survival past childhood in individuals with CA will improve. Thus, focused long-term follow-up care, risk factor management in adulthood, and early detection of potentially fatal complications and prevention of chronic diseases among affected individuals will become more pertinent. Our findings call for more research into the mechanisms by which CAs may cause premature adult mortality, including exploring interactions with postnatal risk factors, such as exposure to diagnostic radiation and medications, obesity, and restricted physical activity.
target: While risks associated with congenital anomalies (CAs) in childhood are well documented, data on the long-term impact of CAs on adult mortality are lacking. We aimed to study mortality risks in adults born with CAs using the population-based Jerusalem Perinatal Study cohort.Individuals born in 1964–1976 who attained 18 years of age were followed up until 2016 or date of death (median 27.5 years). We categorized anomalies by presence/absence, severity, multiplicity, and body system affected. Of 87 621 who survived to age 18, 5621 (6.4%) had CAs. Mortality was increased in those bearing any (adjusted HR (HRadj) = 1.53, CI: 1.29–1.83), single (HRadj = 1.51, CI: 1.27–1.81), severe (HRadj = 2.21, CI: 1.75–2.77), and moderate and severe malformations combined (HRadj = 2.19, CI: 1.09–4.40), when compared to individuals without anomalies. Household food security (FS) is an important determinant of physical and emotional health [ 1 ]. FS is characterized by consistent access to ample nutritionally adequate and safe foods [ 2 ]. FS levels exist on a continuum and can be categorized as high, marginal, low, and very low FS [ 3 ]. Food insecurity (FI)—i.e. the absence of FS—which typically encompasses low and very low FS [ 3 ], is defined as having restricted or unreliable access to nutritious food in a manner that is socially accepted [ 2 ]. Marginal FS is characterized by some anxiety over the amount of food in the house [ 3 ].

FI impacts populations in low-, middle-, and high-income countries across the globe. In 2022, 29.6% of the world was food-insecure [ 4 ]. Low-income households [ 5 ], racial/ethnic minorities [ 6 ], and households with children [ 7 ] bear a disproportionate brunt of FI. Various factors may contribute to these disparities; neighborhood context (e.g. grocery infrastructure) [ 8 ], accessibility (transportation to and availability of quality foods) [ 9 ], and the affordability of foods [ 5 ] are key factors [ 10 ]. As the energy density of foods increases, their cost tends to decrease [ 11 ]. Thus, FI drives a reliance on low-cost, palatable, energy-dense foods to fulfill caloric requirements [ 12 ], propagating life-long diet-related consequences such as type 2 diabetes [ 13 ]—consequences linked with high weight [ 14 ], depression and other mental health problems [ 15 ], and other chronic diseases [ 16 ].

More recently, eating disorder (ED) behaviors have gained increased attention as a negative outcome of FI [ 17 ]. ED behaviors span a spectrum, including, but not limited to, disinhibited (e.g. binge eating) and compensatory (e.g. self-induced vomiting) behaviors to offset the effects of overeating or to control weight [ 18 ]. Though such behaviors are implicated in clinical EDs (e.g. bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder) [ 19 ], they can also occur among individuals without clinical EDs. ED behaviors have psychological and physical repercussions, such as an increased risk of developing full-blown EDs [ 19 ], poor dietary intake [ 20 ], and depressive symptoms [ 21 ].

In the past, research on the driving forces behind the development of ED health-risk behaviors have predominately revolved around body dissatisfaction and weight control [ 22 ]. While these motivations are still relevant, individuals experiencing FI may face additional pressures. Those who are affected by FI may engage in ED behaviors for reasons that do not fit into the mold of typical ED pathology that is traditionally targeted in preventative, diagnostic, and treatment practices [ 23 ]. A commonly discussed theory within the discourse on the association between FI and ED behaviors is the feast-or-famine cycle. This cycle refers to the fluctuating patterns of food availability and scarcity that breed variability in food intake [ 24 ]. Binge eating could be considered a consequence of FI, as suggested by the restraint theory in which limiting food intake can lead to uncontrolled eating under certain circumstances (e.g. an abundance of palatable foods); self-induced vomiting may then result from a feeling of uncomfortable fullness that accompanies overeating [ 25 ]. In the USA, for example, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program has been criticized for potentially exacerbating this problem, with the timing of monthly allocation encouraging a disproportionate use of benefits at the beginning of the month and funds running out towards the end of the month [ 18 ]. Outside of the USA, cyclical food availability may take form in other ways, such as periodic paycheck distribution. The same cycle may occur when pay is received on a monthly basis, leading to the overaccumulation of food at the time of receiving the paycheck, with both money and food dwindling as the month progresses.

While conceptualizing ED pathology in the context of FI has come a long way in recent years, the majority of research has been conducted within the USA, thereby limiting understanding of these associations within the confines of USA-based food-assistance policies and practices [ 18 ]. Furthermore, the role of sociodemographic and other relevant variables on the strength of association remains understudied. Therefore, the purpose of this investigation was to (i) use repeated cross-sectional data from Australia, Canada, Mexico, the UK, and the USA to evaluate the generalizability of associations between household FS levels and ED behaviors across countries and (ii) explore the extent to which sociodemographic and other relevant variables may moderate such associations. We hypothesized that lower levels of FS would be associated with greater prevalence of ED behaviors across the countries studied and that the strength of these associations may be magnified or attenuated by some of the potential moderators.
### Study design and participants

Repeated cross-sectional data from Australia, Canada, Mexico, the UK, and the USA were drawn from the International Food Policy Study [ 26 ]. The present study uses data from self-administered web-based surveys conducted in 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022. Adults between 18 and 100 years of age were recruited through the Nielson Consumer Insights Global Panel and their partner panels each survey year. Age and sex quotas were used to recruit participants with characteristics representative of each country’s population. E-mail invitations with unique survey access links were sent to a random sample of panelists within each country, age, and sex quota. After eligibility screening based on age, sex, and residence in a target country, potential respondents were provided with information about the study and an opportunity to consent. Respondents received incentives in accordance with their panel’s usual incentive structure. The study was reviewed and approved by the University of Waterloo Research Ethics Committee [ 27–31 ]. The analytic sample size for the present study was 104 881. Information on survey cooperation rates, explanations for participant exclusions, and post-stratification sample weight construction is included in the Supplementary material [ 27–31 ].

### Measures

Surveys were conducted in English in Australia and the UK, Spanish in Mexico, English and French in Canada, and English and Spanish in the USA. Spanish and French translations were reviewed by members of the International Food Policy Study research team who were fluent in each language [ 27–31 ].

The household FS level over the past year was assessed with the 18-item US Household Food Security Survey Module (HFSSM) [ 32 ]. Ten items assess FS status among adults in the household and, where applicable, the remaining eight items ask about the experiences of children in the household. Missing responses at the item level were filled in with affirmative responses if a participant provided (i) a valid affirmative response to at least one item that was more severe than the missing item and (ii) no negative response to any item that was less severe than the missing item; all other missing items were filled in as negative responses [ 33 ]. Consistently with the scoring guidelines for the HFSSM [ 34 ], a score of 0 (i.e. no affirmative responses) was classified as high FS, a score of 1–2 was classified as marginal FS, a score of 3–7 (for households with children) or 3–5 (for households without children) was classified as low FS, and a score of 8–18 (for households with children) or 6–10 (for households without children) was classified as very low FS.

Binge eating and self-induced vomiting for weight control were assessed by asking participants how often over the past 3 months they had “gone on eating binges” and “made yourself sick (vomited) to control your weight” [ 35 ]. Response options were “never,” “less than 1 time a month,” “1 to 3 times a month,” “once a week,” “2 to 6 times a week,” “once a day,” and “more than once a day.” For the main analyses, responses were collapsed to represent having ever (with any frequency) or never engaged in a given behavior over the past 3 months.

In addition to country and survey year, which were part of the study design, variables considered as covariates and/or potential moderators included the following, which were assessed via self-report: age, gender (derived from self-reported sex assigned at birth and gender identity), ethnicity (categorized into country-specific “majority” or “minority” groups in line with census questions asked in each country), educational attainment (categorized as “low,” “medium,” or “high” according to country-specific criteria of the highest level of formal education attained), perceived income adequacy (assessed with the question, “Thinking about your total monthly income, how difficult or easy is it for you to make ends meet?”), perceived social status (assessed by using the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status [ 36 ]), employment status, student status, status as a parent with a child aged <18 years living in the household (including step-children and adopted children), and perceived weight status (“Obese,” “Overweight,” “Underweight,” or “Just about right”).

### Statistical analysis

Analyses were conducted in Stata 16.1 and incorporated post-stratification sample weights to minimize nonresponse and selection bias. Descriptive statistics were calculated and associations between household FS level and ED behaviors were examined by using modified Poisson regression models (i.e. with robust standard errors) to calculate prevalence ratios [ 37 ]. Models were adjusted for country, survey year, age, gender, ethnicity, educational attainment, perceived income adequacy, perceived social status, employment status, student status, and parent status to account for potential confounding; these covariates were selected a priori. Perceived weight status was not included as a covariate because, as a consequence of FI [ 38 ], weight status may act as a mediator or collider on the pathway from FI to ED behaviors, in which case adjustment for it could have introduced overadjustment bias or selection bias, respectively. Variables with the highest item-level missingness were perceived social status (1.88%; n = 1974), binge eating (1.32%; n = 1386), and perceived weight status (1.18%; n = 1236). To minimize nonresponse bias due to item-level missingness, we conducted multiple imputation with 20 replications by using the fully conditional specification method, pooling regression results across replications. We assessed for interaction on the additive scale (i.e. corresponding to differences in absolute risk) between household FS level and each hypothesized potential moderating variable (country, survey year, age, gender, ethnicity, parent status, and perceived weight status) by using the identity link function with a Gaussian distribution and robust standard errors [ 39 ]. Interaction results were interpreted graphically by plotting adjusted prevalence estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) computed with marginal standardization, a Poisson distribution, the log link function, and robust standard errors via mimrgns.
Table 1 outlines sample characteristics of the analytic sample for the present study. Nearly half of the participants reported binge eating over the past 3 months, and nearly 1 in 10 reported self-induced vomiting to control weight over the past 3 months.

### Associations between household FS level and ED behaviors

Marginal, low, and very low FS were associated with greater prevalence of both types of ED behaviors examined. The household FS level exhibited associations that suggested dose–response relationships for both ED behaviors, such that increasing severity of FI corresponded to increasing prevalence of both behaviors. Compared with households with high FS, after adjusting for covariates, the prevalence of past-3-month binge eating was 1.34 (95% CI: 1.31–1.37) times the prevalence in households with marginal FS, 1.54 (95% CI: 1.50–1.57) times the prevalence in households with low FS, and 1.73 (95% CI: 1.69–1.77) times the prevalence in households with very low FS, and the prevalence of past-3-month self-induced vomiting to control weight was 2.40 (95% CI: 2.15–2.68) times the prevalence in households with marginal FS, 7.10 (95% CI: 6.49–7.77) times the prevalence in households with low FS, and 11.98 (95% CI: 10.99–13.05) times the prevalence in households with very low FS.

Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to examine associations between household FS level and frequencies of past-3-month binge eating and self-induced vomiting. These associations were similarly suggestive of dose–response relationships across all behavior frequencies examined (<1 time a month, 1–3 times a month, and at least weekly, relative to never over the past 3 months) for both binge eating and self-induced vomiting ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Moreover, the strength of these associations generally increased with increasing behavior frequencies, additionally suggesting dose–response relationships between FI and frequency of binge eating and self-induced vomiting.

### Differences in associations by potential moderating variables

Results of moderation analyses exploring potential differences in associations between household FS level and ED behaviors by various factors are illustrated in Figures 1–7 and described below.

Associations between household FS level and both ED behaviors were weaker in Mexico compared with Australia, Canada, the UK, and the USA ( Figure 1 ). Across all FS statuses, a higher prevalence of binge eating but lower prevalence of self-induced vomiting was observed in Mexico relative to other countries. In a post-hoc analysis to assess whether these patterns may have been driven by differences in survey language, a similar pattern by language within the USA was observed for binge eating, but not self-induced vomiting, with a weaker association between FS status and binge eating among participants who completed the survey in Spanish compared with those who completed it in English ( Supplementary Figure S1 ).

Examination of potential moderation by survey year did not reveal meaningful differences, though associations between household FS level and past-3-month self-induced vomiting were somewhat stronger in later survey years ( Figure 2 ).

Associations between household FS level and both ED behaviors were generally strongest in young adulthood and weaker in older adulthood ( Figure 3 ).

Among trans women, those with low FS were particularly likely to report both ED behaviors ( Figure 4 ). However, such differences should be interpreted cautiously given the wide CIs.

Associations between household FS level and both ED behaviors were stronger among participants representing a minority ethnicity in their country relative to those representing the majority ethnicity in their country ( Figure 5 ).

Associations between household FS level and both ED eating behaviors were generally stronger among parents than nonparents ( Figure 6 ).

The association between FS level and binge eating was weakest in those perceiving themselves to be “obese”—the group exhibiting the highest prevalence of binge eating across FS statuses. The association with self-induced vomiting was weakest for those perceiving themselves to be “just about right”—the group exhibiting the lowest prevalence of self-induced vomiting across FS statuses ( Figure 7 ).
The study was reviewed by and received ethics clearance through a University of Waterloo Research Ethics Committee (ORE #21460 for the 2018 survey and ORE #30829 for the 2019–2022 surveys).
discussion:
In this large study utilizing data from five waves of the International Food Policy Study across Australia, Canada, Mexico, the UK, and the USA, a greater severity of household FI was associated with an increased prevalence of binge eating and self-induced vomiting. Moderation analyses revealed differences in associations by country, age, gender, ethnicity, parental status, and perceived weight status. Notably, the strongest associations between household FS and ED behaviors were observed among younger adults, minority ethnic groups, and parents. Weaker associations were observed in participants from Mexico, who exhibited a higher prevalence of binge eating but lower prevalence of self-induced vomiting compared with other countries. Additionally, the link between household FS and binge eating was weakest among those who perceived themselves to be “obese,” whereas the association with self-induced vomiting was weakest among individuals who felt that their weight was “just about right.”

Consistently with previous research on FI and disordered eating, these findings support the prevailing claim that lower FS is associated with elevated prevalence of ED behaviors. Prior USA-based investigations suggest that a “feast-or-famine” cycle induced by public food-assistance programs that distribute benefits once a month may contribute to ED behaviors in the context of FI [ 18 ]. However, in the present study, increasing severity of FI was associated most strongly with engagement in ED behaviors at least weekly, suggesting that these behaviors may occur throughout the full month even if they may have initially developed as a response to cyclical fluctuations in food availability. Of note, the stronger association observed between FI and self-induced vomiting suggests that compensatory behaviors to control weight may occur independently of binge eating in the food-insecure context, or at least independently of eating episodes perceived to be binge eating. The strength of the association between FI and self-induced vomiting to control weight can perhaps be contextualized by considering the pervasiveness of the thin ideal in Western cultures, the challenge of affording healthful foods coupled with weight-stigmatizing public health messaging [ 40 ], and the established link between internalized weight stigma and ED pathology, including in food-insecure populations [ 41 ]. Such a context may illustrate why, across countries, Mexico—likely the least influenced by Western culture among the countries studied—exhibited the lowest prevalence of self-induced vomiting and the weakest associations between FI and ED behaviors. However, it remains important to consider the possibility of translation or cultural differences in how the question was asked. Paralleling the trend in Mexico, among those who filled out the USA-based survey in Spanish, the prevalence of binge eating was relatively similar across FS levels. This could suggest language-based differences or, alternatively, it might further bolster the earlier argument, as a greater proportion of those filling out the Spanish survey may be of Hispanic or Latinx descent and therefore remain outside the context of high-income, English-speaking countries.

Individuals who perceived their weight as “just about right” exhibited the lowest prevalence of self-induced vomiting and the weakest association with FS status. Individuals who perceive themselves as “just about right” likely feel less societal pressure to alter their bodies compared with other groups, which may explain the lower prevalence of self-induced vomiting across FS statuses. In contrast, a similar pattern was not seen for binge eating. The weakest association between FS status and binge eating was found among individuals who perceived themselves as “obese,” yet this group exhibited the highest prevalence of binge eating. It is possible that other risk factors, such as body dissatisfaction and internalized weight stigma, may be more prominent predictors of risk in this high-risk group, making the impact of FI relatively less important. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between different predictors of risk and patterns of association when studying eating disorders and FI.

There are both strengths and limitations of the present study. Strengths include the large, international sample of diverse participants across multiple survey years, which enhanced the generalizability of findings and facilitated the examination of moderation by key factors—analyses that prior studies have not had the statistical power to conduct. However, limitations should also be noted. For example, samples were not recruited by using probability-based sampling, though sample weights based on country-specific census data were used to maximize external validity. The cross-sectional and self-report nature of the data is an additional limitation of the study.

Given the high prevalence of FI [ 4 ] and the large economic and social burden of EDs [ 42–44 ], understanding that the strong, positive, dose–response relationship between FI and ED behaviors occurs cross-nationally is compelling for both public health investigation and intervention. It also highlights the pervasive and robust association between FI and ED behaviors [ 18 , 45 ], regardless of culture, geo-location, and governmental/social support structures. Efforts to improve the accessibility and availability of nutritious foods for individuals facing FI are a global issue with potentially far-reaching implications beyond physical health.
target: A link has been established between food insecurity and eating disorder (ED) pathology, but most research on this topic has occurred in the USA. This study examined associations and potential moderators of associations between food security (FS) levels and ED behaviors cross-nationally.Repeated cross-sectional data representing 104 881 adults 18–100 years of age in Australia, Canada, Mexico, the UK, and the USA came from five waves (2018–22) of the International Food Policy Study. Participants completed the Household Food Security Survey Module and reported on past-3-month binge eating and self-induced vomiting to control weight. Associations between past-year household FS level and ED behaviors were examined with adjusted modified Poisson regression models. Interactions with potential moderators were also tested.Marginal, low, and very low FS were associated with elevated prevalence of both ED behaviors. Compared with households with high FS, binge eating was 1.34, 1.54, and 1.73 times as prevalent in households with marginal, low, and very low FS, respectively. Associations were stronger for self-induced vomiting; compared with households with high FS, self-induced vomiting was 2.40, 7.10, and 11.98 times as prevalent in households with marginal, low, and very low FS, respectively. Moderation results revealed meaningful differences by some factors. For example, associations were weaker in Mexico and stronger among ethnic minorities and participants with children.Results support cross-sectional associations between FS and ED behaviors, with a particularly strong link for self-induced vomiting.
