inputs:
Pain and pain-related diseases are among the leading cause of disability and disease burden worldwide [ 1–3 ]. With global population ageing, this burden continues to escalate, as pain prevalence peaks in late middle and older age [ 4 , 5 ]. Disadvantaged socio-economic conditions have been associated with increased pain and worse pain-related outcomes [ 5–8 ]. Part of this social gradient can be explained through behavioural [ 9–11 ] or psychosocial mechanisms [ 11–17 ]. Unhealthy behaviours—more common among those with lower socio-economic conditions—can both contribute to and result from pain. Studies, mostly from Europe, show that behaviours such as smoking and physical inactivity partly explain these associations [ 9–11 ]. Psychosocial mechanisms have also been highlighted, including the roles of depression, anxiety, and stress [ 11–17 ].

Among the proposed underlying mechanisms, the effect of sleep-related disorders on pain has been a focus of growing interest [ 18 , 19 ]. It has been previously shown that, compared with individuals in more socio-economically advantageous conditions, those with a lower educational level, occupational position, and economic difficulties are more likely to experience sleep problems [ 18 , 20–24 ]. The relationship between sleep and pain has been described as bidirectional, though there is greater support for sleep impacting pain than vice versa [ 18 , 25 , 26 ]. Given the socio-economic inequities in sleep and sleep being a risk factor for pain, this highlights the importance of better understanding the extent to which the socio-economic inequities in pain are explained by sleep quality and duration. However, to date, only two studies—one from the UK and one from the USA—have evaluated the contribution of sleep to socio-economic inequities in pain as assessed by neighbourhood socio-economic conditions, reporting mixed results [ 12 , 27 ]. Both studies are cross-sectional and use traditional mediation methods (e.g. difference methods) [ 12 , 27 ], which limits understanding of the direction of associations and direct and indirect effect estimates.

No study to date has evaluated the mediating role of both sleep quality and duration—key risk factors for pain [ 18 ]—on socio-economic inequities in pain by using individual-level socio-economic indicators from both childhood and adulthood. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by using a counterfactual mediation model in a prospective cohort study from Switzerland.
### Study population

We used data from the CoLaus|PsyCoLaus study—a population-based cohort of adults of European origin living in the city of Lausanne, Switzerland [ 28 ]. Briefly, a representative sample was collected through a simple, non-stratified random sampling of 19 830 individuals (35% of the source population) aged between 35 and 75 years. The study was initiated in 2003 ( n = 6733), with the first follow-up conducted in 2009–2012 ( n = 5064) and the second follow-up in 2014–2017 ( n = 4881) [ 28 ]. For the present analysis, we used data from the first (when pain assessment was initiated) and second follow-up phases; the first follow-up is therefore considered the baseline for this study.

The inclusion criteria required participants to have both sleep and pain data. A total of 2586 participants completed measures of sleep at baseline, of whom 1719 also completed pain assessments in the follow-up ( Supplementary Fig. 1 ). The analysis of chronic pain included 1687 participants, excluding 32 participants with missing chronic pain data. The analysis of pain severity included 699 participants who reported experiencing pain and had pain severity data at follow-up. For analyses related the participant’s own occupational position, analysis was restricted to 1066 participants who reported working at baseline. Supplementary Table 1 details the sample size and exclusion/inclusion criteria for each analysis.

### Exposures: socio-economic indicators

We used four indicators of socio-economic conditions assessed at baseline as the main exposure variables. Childhood socio-economic conditions, commonly indicated by the father’s occupational position, was classified into three main categories by using the European SocioEconomic Classification framework [ 29 ]: ‘high’ (higher professionals/managers, lower professionals/managers, higher clerical), ‘intermediate’ (small employers and self-employed, farmers, lower supervisors, and technicians), and ‘low’ (lower clerical, sales workers, skilled/unskilled workers). Adulthood socio-economic conditions included self-reported education, occupational position, and income. The highest level of attained education was classified as ‘high’ (university education), ‘intermediate’ (higher secondary education), and ‘low’ (lower secondary education or lower). Participants’ occupation was categorized as for the father’s occupation. Monthly household income before social charges had six response options used as income categories: >13 000, 9500–13 000, 7000–9500, 5000–7000, 3000–5000, and <3000 CHF (Swiss francs; 1 CHF = 1.15 US$ in March 2024).

### Mediators: sleep measures

Baseline sleep quality was quantified based on the validated Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)—a 19-item questionnaire evaluating sleep patterns over the previous month [ 30 ]. The PSQI includes seven components of sleep, including sleep quality, latency, efficiency, duration, disturbances, daytime dysfunction, and use of sleep medications/aids, with each scored from 0 to 3. The overall PSQI score was obtained by summing these scores and the final score ranged from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating poorer sleep quality. We also created a binary sleep quality variable by using a PSQI score cut-off point of >5 as ‘poor sleep quality’—a value that reflected clinically significant sleep disturbances with sensitivity and specificity of >85% [ 30–33 ]. Sleep duration was self-reported as the average number of hours of sleep per night and categorized using physiological cut-offs into short (<6 h/night), recommended or normal (6–8.5 h/night), and long (>8.5 h/night) [ 34 , 35 ].

### Outcome: pain measures

The presence of pain, chronic pain, and pain severity were assessed at follow-up by using a self-administered questionnaire involving an 11-item pain inventory previously validated in a French population [ 36 ]. The presence of pain was measured by using the question: ‘Currently, do you suffer from one or more pains felt every day? (yes/no).’ Participants who reported experiencing pain were asked: ‘How long have you had pain that you feel every day? (<3 months/≥3 months).’ We defined chronic pain as pain lasting for ≥3 months and coded as ‘yes’ versus ‘no’ (no pain or pain lasting for <3 months). Among participants with pain, the pain severity was evaluated by using three questions from the Brief Pain Inventory on a validated numeric rating scale ranging from 0 = no to 10 = worst imaginable pain; participants reported whether pain varied in severity during the day and indicated the highest, lowest, and average pain severity during the last week [ 37 ]. The mean pain severity score was the mean of these values.

### Covariates

Potential confounders were selected based on known associations with the exposure, mediators, and outcomes, and those that did not lie on the causal path, identified by using a directed acyclic graph ( Fig. 1 ). We included age (continuous), sex (men/women), and country of birth (Swiss-born/non-Swiss-born) as potential confounders.

### Statistical analyses

We used linear regression for continuous dependent variables (sleep quality, pain severity score), logistic regression for binary dependent variables (pain, chronic pain, sleep quality), and multinomial logistic regression for the categorical dependent variable of sleep duration. All estimates [odds ratios (ORs) and beta coefficients with 95% confidence intervals (CIs)] were adjusted for age, sex, and country of birth. First, we analysed associations between baseline socio-economic conditions and follow-up pain; second, those between baseline socio-economic conditions and sleep; and third, those between baseline sleep and follow-up pain. Socio-economic indicators were modelled as ordered variables, hypothesizing a linear effect on the outcome [ 38 , 39 ]. A Cochran–Armitage test showed no departure from the linear trend. A priori, a Wald test provided no evidence of effect modification by age and sex.

We used counterfactual mediation methods to examine the extent to which the association between each socio-economic indicator and pain outcomes was mediated by sleep measures that fulfilled the criteria for mediation (based on the previously mentioned three sets of analyses) ( Fig. 1 ). Counterfactual mediation analysis enables the decomposition of the total effect of socio-economic conditions on pain into direct and indirect components, even in the presence of interactions and non-linearities, overcoming limitations of traditional approaches (e.g. difference-of-coefficients or product-of-coefficients methods) [ 40 , 41 ]. For counterfactual mediation, two regression models were fitted: (i) a model that predicts pain outcomes based on socio-economic indicators, sleep measures, an interaction term between them, and confounders; and (ii) a model that predicts sleep measures based on socio-economic indicators and confounders. Regression coefficients from these models were used to estimate the NDE (natural direct effect—the effect of socio-economic conditions on pain via pathways that do not involve sleep measures), NIE (natural indirect effect—the effect of socio-economic conditions on pain operating through sleep measures), and MTE (marginal total effect—the total effect of socio-economic conditions on pain) [ 38 , 42 ]. Subsequently, the proportion of the association between socio-economic conditions and pain that is mediated by sleep was computed (PM: proportion mediated). Confidence intervals were computed through percentiles from bootstrapping with 10 000 simulations [ 43 ]. We use the term ‘effects’ as commonly used in mediation research; however, this does not imply that causality can be inferred from our findings.

A priori, we decided not to adjust for baseline pain, as it is a mediator in the causal pathway between socio-economic conditions and follow-up pain ( Fig. 1 ) and such adjustment would have introduced overadjustment or collider bias, leading to biased estimates [ 44–46 ]. To show this issue, in analyses of baseline socio-economic conditions or sleep with follow-up pain, we additionally adjusted for baseline pain and compared the results with those of the main analyses. We also did not adjust for other pain risk factors, including psychological factors and health-related behaviours, as these also lie on the causal pathway between socio-economic conditions and pain [ 8 , 44 , 47 ]. Analyses were undertaken by using Stata 16 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).
Our analytical sample included 1719 participants [52.0% women; mean age (SD) = 60.1 (9.1) years] with a mean (SD) follow-up of 3.8 (0.4) years ( Table 1 ). Most participants reported their father’s occupation as intermediate (23%) or low (54%) and their educational level as intermediate (66%) or high (26%). Approximately a quarter of participants had a low occupational position (26%) and 17% reported income levels of ≤5000 CHF. The mean PSQI score was 4.1 (SD = 2.8) and 44% had a PSQI score of ≥5. Normal sleep duration was reported by 86% of the participants, while 5% had long and 9% had short sleep durations. At follow-up, 47% reported having pain and 40.8% reported having chronic pain. Among those with pain, the mean pain severity score was 3.6 (SD = 1.7).

Individuals with low socio-economic conditions were more likely to report pain and have worse pain severity compared with more socio-economically advantaged individuals ( Supplementary Table 2 ). Low occupational position and household income were also associated with chronic pain, whereas father’s occupational position and education showed no such associations. These effects were attenuated after further adjustment for baseline pain, highlighting the potential introduction of overadjustment bias ( Supplementary Table 3 ).

Low socio-economic conditions, across all four indicators, were associated with continuous PSQI scores; however, only household income was associated with low sleep quality when using the PSQI score as a binary variable ( Table 2 ). While no associations were evident between the father’s occupational position and sleep duration, strong associations were observed between low education, household income, and short and long sleep durations. Low occupational position was also associated with short sleep duration.

Both the PSQI score and poor sleep quality were associated with all pain outcomes, while short sleep duration was associated with pain and chronic pain and not pain severity ( Table 3 ). These associations were attenuated after further adjustment for baseline pain ( Supplementary Table 4 ).

Based on the results from the previous sets of analyses, counterfactual mediation was conducted where socio-economic indicators were associated with pain outcomes, with sleep measures, and where sleep measures were associated with pain outcomes. Thus, Table 4 presents counterfactual mediation models for associations between socio-economic indicators and pain, chronic pain, and pain severity, mediated by the PSQI score (continuous) or short sleep duration. Low educational level (OR MTE 1.49; 95% CI: 1.00–2.18), occupational position (1.63; 95% CI: 1.19–2.46), and household income (1.71; 95% CI: 1.16–2.56) were associated with pain, with the PSQI score mediating 30%, 21%, and 45% of these associations, respectively. Low occupational position (1.63; 95% CI: 1.11–2.30) and household income (1.63; 95% CI: 1.11–2.69) were associated with chronic pain, with the PSQI score meditating 20% and 51% of these associations, respectively. All socio-economic indicators were associated with pain severity, with the PSQI score mediating 15% of the association with the father’s occupation, 9% with education, and 16% with household income. The MTE of low education on pain was 1.65 (95% CI: 1.05–2.46), with short sleep duration appearing to mediate 31% of the association. The effects of own occupation position and household income on pain were not mediated by short sleep duration. Finally, the MTE for chronic pain was 1.59 (95% CI: 1.07–2.60) for low education and 1.75 (95% CI: 1.15–2.78) for low household income, with short sleep duration mediating these associations by 36% and 37%, respectively. The effect of occupational position and chronic pain was not mediated by short sleep duration. The results of the counterfactual mediation analysis for sleep measures not meeting the mediation criteria are presented in Supplementary Table 3 .
A main strength of our study includes using four different indicators to capture socio-economic conditions across the life course, measuring both sleep quality and quantity, and measuring pain in terms of chronicity and severity. The counterfactual mediation method enabled us to more accurately examine the mediating role of sleep compared with traditional methods [ 55 ].

There are also important limitations. The CoLaus|PsyCoLaus comprises individuals of European origin living in a wealthy country, likely contributing to relatively low exposure to adverse socio-economic conditions. While the PSQI has been validated across populations, it has not been validated in a Swiss population. Our analysis included participants with and without baseline pain; given that pain is a common issue among adults and older adults, excluding participants with pain limits generalizability and substantially reduces statistical power [ 56 ]. The relatively small sample size for pain severity analyses also limited the statistical power to detect smaller effects. Our findings may be subject to selection bias and limited generalizability, as analyses were restricted to participants with complete baseline sleep and follow-up pain data, possibly underestimating inequities. Missing data on own occupational position were extensive and those with incomplete data tended to have lower educational and income levels, suggesting that associations with pain outcomes and the mediating role of sleep measures may have been underestimated. The lack of mother’s occupational data is another limitation, although, given the cohort’s age and historical context, the father’s occupation likely captured much of the early-life socio-economic conditions. The father’s occupation and education were retrospectively reported, capturing early-life socio-economic conditions with a strong theoretical temporal link with adulthood sleep measures. However, individual occupation position and income were measured concurrently with sleep, limiting temporal inference [ 57 ]. The lack of longitudinal early-life data also prevents ruling out reverse causation.

Our analysis relies upon strong assumptions of no unmeasured confounding between the exposure, mediators, and outcomes. While we adjusted for several confounders based on prior research on health inequities, unmeasured confounding remains possible. Potential unmeasured confounders include neighbourhood characteristics, job conditions, and early-life health, and mediator–outcome confounders (i.e. behavioural and psychosocial factors) [ 8 ] not assessed in this study. These sources of residual confounding could bias estimates in either direction, with underestimation or overestimation of the observed associations. Proper adjustment for mediator–outcome confounders affected by the exposure would require advanced modelling beyond the scope of this study. Further research is therefore needed to better understand the behavioural and physiological mechanisms underlying pain exacerbation in a detrimental socio-economic context.
The institutional Ethics Committee of the University of Lausanne approved the CoLaus|PsyCoLaus study (reference 16/03). The study was performed in agreement with the Helsinki Declaration and its former amendments, and in accordance with the applicable Swiss legislation. All participants gave their signed informed consent before entering the study.
discussion:
Using counterfactual-based mediation analysis, we showed that sleep quality as measured by using the PSQI score mediated socio-economic inequities in pain, chronic pain, and pain severity scores. Although uncertainty around the percentage mediated was high, sleep quality explained 30% of the educational, 21% of the occupational, and 45% of the income inequities in pain; 20% of the occupation and 51% of the income inequities in chronic pain; and 15%, 9%, and 16% of the father’s occupation, educational, and income inequities in pain severity, respectively. Additionally, we found that short sleep duration explained 31% of the association between education and pain as well as 36%–37% of both the education and income inequities in chronic pain.

A large body of evidence suggests an association between different socio-economic indicators and pain experience and severity, aligning with our findings [ 8 , 48 ]. All socio-economic indicators were associated with a continuous PSQI score, but not with a binary variable for overall sleep quality when using a PSQI-score cut-off of 5 (except for income). Despite this cut-off showing high sensitivity (89.6%) and specificity (86.5%) for identifying sleep disorders, a systematic review found that its validity varies substantially across clinical and non-clinical samples [ 49 ]. We also found strong associations between education, occupational position, and household income with suboptimal sleep duration, with stronger associations for short sleep than for long sleep, consistently with previous studies [ 20–24 , 34 , 35 , 50 ]. Low socio-economic conditions are linked to financial hardship, job-related psychosocial stress, shift work, poor living conditions, lack of social support, and loneliness, leading to chronic and mental stress, which in turn negatively influences both sleep quality and quantity [ 34 , 50 ].

Our results also confirm the association between sleep quality and pain outcomes, aligning with results from a systematic review of longitudinal and experimental studies [ 18 ]. We also found that short, but not long, sleep duration is associated with increased odds of pain experience and chronic pain but not with pain severity. Previous studies have reported associations between short and long sleep durations with different pain measures, with greater support for short sleep duration impacting pain than long sleep duration [ 18 , 51 ]. Short sleep duration may be a result of complex social, behavioural, and/or physiological conditions. In lower socio-economic groups, longer working hours, greater job demands, and shift work may contribute to shorter sleep duration [ 35 ]. Physiological mechanisms linking sleep quality and quantity to pain include elevated pro-inflammatory markers, alterations in the function of dopamine, and changes in psychological affects (e.g. moods, anxiety) [ 18 , 52 ]

Considering the mediating role of sleep measures, the only two available studies examined neighbourhood-level socio-economic inequities in pain and reported mixed results [ 12 , 27 ]. No prior studies have examined the mediating role of sleep quality and duration on the association between individual-level socio-economic indicators and pain measures. We found that the association between adulthood socio-economic conditions and pain experience was substantially mediated (19%–51%) by sleep quality (continuous PSQI scores). Similar results were found for chronic pain, with PSQI scores mediating the occupation and income inequities in pain by 20% and 51%, respectively. The mediation role of sleep quality and short sleep duration was greatest for the association between income and pain, likely because the association with income was the strongest compared with other socio-economic indicators. Financial hardship may contribute to stress, anxiety, uncertainty, and neighbourhood conditions (e.g. noise), impacting sleep [ 53 , 54 ]. The results support the need to address sleep inequities, especially income-related. Of note, short sleep duration mediated the education inequities in pain by 31% and education and income inequities in chronic pain by 37%, but showed no mediation when other socio-economic indicators were used. These results highlight that sleep quality and short sleep duration partially mediate the socio-economic inequities in specific pain outcomes.
In this study, we found that sleep quality and short sleep duration partially mediate the socio-economic inequities in pain, chronic pain, and pain severity. The results from this study support early intervention in sleep quality and duration, where indicated, among socio-economically disadvantaged individuals as part of an integrated approach to reducing pain inequities. Beyond targeted sleep interventions, addressing broader structural drivers—such as education, income security, and working conditions—may have a wider and more sustained impact on reducing inequities in pain.
target: Sleep-related problems exhibit strong social patterning and are associated with pain; however, their mediating role in socio-economic inequities in pain remains largely unknown. We aim to assess the extent to which life course socio-economic inequities in pain experience and severity are mediated through sleep quality and duration.We used data from 1719 individuals [52.0% women; mean age 60.1 years (SD 9.1)] from the Swiss CoLaus|PsyCoLaus study, with both sleep measures at baseline (2009–2012) and pain measures at follow-up (2014–2017). Life course socio-economic conditions were assessed by using the father’s and individual’s occupational position, educational level, and income. Potential mediators included self-reported sleep quality (measured by using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, ranging from 0 to 21, with high scores indicating poorer sleep quality) and duration (short <6 h/night; normal 6–8.5 h/night; long >8.5 h/night). Presence of pain, chronic pain, and pain severity were assessed by using a self-administered questionnaire. We estimated age, sex, and country of birth with adjusted β coefficient, odds ratio, and proportion mediated by using counterfactual mediation analyses.Pain and chronic pain were reported by 47% and 40.8% of the participants, respectively. Among 699 participants with reported pain severity data, the mean pain severity score was 3.6 (SD 1.7) (scale ranging from 0 = no to 10 = worst imaginable pain). Sleep quality explained 30% of the educational, 21% of the occupational, and 45% of the income inequities in pain; 20% of the occupation and 51% of the income inequities in chronic pain; and 15%, 9%, and 16% of the father’s occupation, educational, and income inequities in pain severity, respectively. Short sleep duration explained 31% of the education inequities in pain and 37% of the education and income inequities in chronic pain.This study suggests poor sleep quality and short sleep duration partially mediate socio-economic inequities in pain. The role of other potential mediators at individual and societal levels should be further investigated.

Vegetation and peat fires are expected to increase under climate extremes [ 1–3 ]. Studies have projected increases in the frequency and intensity of fires in the future [ 1 , 4 ] and the impact on exposed populations could vary by region based on socioeconomic disparities [ 5–7 ]. The severity of fires differs by various factors, including climate, such as the El Niño phenomena [ 8–10 ], vegetation, human activities, and land use [ 2 , 11 ]. Southeast Asia is a region of concern, as different areas within it comprise varying characteristics of the aforementioned factors [ 12 , 13 ]. In previous decades, the region has experienced among the worst fire-related particle exposures [ 5 ].

There are 14.9 million hectares of peatland in Indonesia, of which ∼18% are located in the province of Central Kalimantan [ 14 ], where peat fires are a major air-pollution issue [ 2 , 15 , 16 ]. Peat fire is characterized by its nature of smoldering in the peat layer underground and flaming up under dry and flammable conditions [ 17 ]. Extremely high levels of particulate matter (PM) have been reported due to smoke haze [ 18–20 ] and these affect the air quality regionally. The complicated combination of climate conditions and fire characteristics, such as moisture, temperature, biomass types, and smoldering or flaming types of fires, leads to emissions of different forms and chemical constituents [ 21–25 ]. While several studies have quantified the health impact attributable to smoke haze in Southeast Asia [ 10 , 26 , 27 ], challenges remain in providing epidemiological evidence in this region [ 28 ].

Epidemiological studies have demonstrated adverse health effects associated with exposure to ambient PM [ 29 ], including those caused by different sources and chemical constituents [ 30 ]. Short-term exposure to smoke haze can lead to increased risks in both respiratory mortality [ 31–34 ] and morbidity [ 31 , 35–43 ], but evidence from tropical peatlands remains scarce. Several epidemiological studies in Southeast Asia were conducted in areas located downwind of peat fires during southwest monsoon seasons [ 32 , 43–46 ] and agricultural burning seasons [ 42 ], where increased respiratory hospitalization due to fire-PM was pronounced [ 42 , 43 ]. However, fire intensity might not exactly reflect levels of smoke exposure [ 34 , 45 ]. Detailed studies on smoke haze, with and without considering fire activities, would be beneficial in elucidating the differential impact of different haze conditions.

Previous studies have used smoke-haze indicators [ 32 , 34 , 35 , 45 ], cut-off levels of PM [ 42 , 47 ], air-quality indices [ 46 ], and combinations of several definitions [ 42 , 43 ] to classify a haze day and whether it is affected by local or distant burnings. This may be due to the diverse characteristics of local activities, fires, and smoke from different types of vegetation or land, as well as climate conditions [ 28 ]. Some studies have also reported adverse respiratory effects of fires comprising larger areas [ 34 ] and in the post-fire period [ 41 ]. In addition, the toxicity of components derived from peat fires may differ from those of other vegetation types [ 25 ] and pollutant concentrations can vary by distance [ 18 ] and time since ignition [ 48 ]. This suggests the need to consider fire characteristics and duration when assessing the impact on health.

This study aims to examine the association between smoke haze and respiratory-related visits to primary healthcare centers in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. Specifically, the effects of haze according to the presence of fire activity, duration of haze, and lag patterns were assessed.
### Study settings

Two second-level administrative subdivisions in the province of Central Kalimantan in Indonesia—Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency—were investigated ( Fig. 1 ). These subdivisions had populations of 293 457 and 134 499, respectively [ 49 ]. The study period spanned from 2015 to 2019, which included several major smoke-haze episodes in the region.

### Data sources

Health data included daily respiratory visits to public primary healthcare centers—community clinics, known as puskesmas (short for “ Pusat Kesehatan Masyarakat ”) in Central Kalimantan. Handwritten records of visits to puskesmas were transcribed into English and digital forms and aggregated into daily counts. Due to data-collection feasibility, data quality, and data-availability limitations, 18 puskesmas were non-sampled, whereas data from one puskesmas was excluded. Data from six puskesmas were included for analysis. Puskesmas were grouped by subdivision— Puskesmas Kereng Bangkirai, Puskesmas Menteng, and Puskesmas Tangkiling in Palangka Raya City, and Puskesmas Bereng, Puskesmas Bukit Rawi, and Puskesmas Pulang Pisau in Pulang Pisau Regency.

Due to the limitations of ground-measured PM 10 (particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter <10 μm) data, satellite data from Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) and Advanced Himawari 8 Imager (AHI) were used to estimate the PM 10 concentrations. PM 10 was estimated by using Equation (1) . However, both cloud and haze can affect AOD values through surface reflectance and aerosol scattering. Therefore, the AOD values were adjusted by incorporating albedo values using Equation (2) ( R 2 =0.91). Details are elaborated in Supplementary Note S1 :

Fire hotspot counts were retrieved from satellite data obtained from MODIS active fire data in the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) [ 50 ]. Daily total fire hotspot counts were aggregated by subdivision.

Daily mean temperature and dew-point data were obtained from the ERA5-Land database [ 51 ]. Data were aggregated by subdivision. The daily relative humidity was derived from temperature and dew-point data [ 52 , 53 ].

### Haze-day definitions

The effects of extreme air pollution were investigated based on the haze and its conditions: (i) with or without fire activity and (ii) the duration of continuous haze days. This was applied to investigate the difference in respiratory risks under exposure to haze from active burning activities. Haze-day definitions used in the present study were as follows.

Meanwhile, a duration indicator was derived to represent different lengths of continuous days of haze. For each haze definition, haze days occurring consequently for 1 – 3 days were coded as ‘1’, 4 – 14 days as ‘2’, and ≥15 days as ‘3’.

### Statistical analysis

This study was performed with a space-time-stratified case-crossover design [ 54 , 55 ]. A conditional quasi-Poisson regression model [ 56 ], allowing for overdispersion, coupled with a distributed lag non-linear model [ 57 , 58 ] was applied for each subdivision. Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the main model. First, a different smoothing spline for temperature was applied—a natural cubic spline for moving average temperature lag 0–3 with three degrees of freedom (3 df). Second, we adjusted for relative humidity by using a natural cubic spline for moving average relative humidity lag 0–3 with 3 df. Third, different lag lengths were tested—lag 10, 14, and 21 days. Fourth, due to an apparent cluster of Puskesmas Bukit Rawi with the other puskesmas in Palangka Raya City, a sensitivity analysis was performed by grouping Puskesmas Bukit Rawi into Palangka Raya City (i.e. four puskesmas in Palangka Raya City, and two remaining in Pulang Pisau Regency). Finally, we tested the model without removing strata with zero cases.
During the study period, there were a total of 32 824 visits to puskesmas due to respiratory health outcomes, with daily average visits ranging from 1.8 ( Puskesmas Bukit Rawi) to 9.4 ( Puskesmas Menteng) cases ( Table 2 ). Of these, 71.4% were visits within Palangka Raya City. With variations across puskesmas , there were apparently higher trends of respiratory visits during July to October, and higher peaks especially in 2015 and 2019 ( Fig. 2A ). The daily average PM 10 concentration ranged from 66.1 to 86.1 μg/m 3 ( Table 3 ). There were two extreme peaks of PM 10 concentrations: one in 2015 (1303 μg/m 3 ) and another in 2019 (870 μg/m 3 ) ( Fig. 2B and C ).

The use of different haze definitions yielded different counts of total haze days and durations ( Table 3 ). There were more non-fire-haze days in Palangka Raya City (57.1%), but more fire-haze days in Pulang Pisau Regency (66.4%). Figure 2B and C demonstrates that most days with extremely high PM 10 concentrations in Pulang Pisau Regency were fire-haze days, whereas those observed in Palangka Raya City, including smaller peaks of PM 10 concentration, were mostly non-fire-haze days. The durations of fire-haze days were noticeably longer in Pulang Pisau Regency ( Table 3 and Fig. 2B and C ). When fire- or non-fire-haze days not specified, the longest duration of haze was observed in Puskesmas Bereng, located in Pulang Pisau Regency (75 days).

The effects of haze days on adverse respiratory outcomes appeared to differ in each subdivision by the haze definition used ( Fig. 3 ). The effects of haze days were pronounced in Pulang Pisau Regency, mainly contributed by fire haze. A null association was observed for the effects of haze days based on all three definitions in Palangka Raya City. Meanwhile, in Pulang Pisau Regency, haze days imposed an overall 36.6% [95% confidence interval (CI): 10.2%, 69.3%] increased risk of respiratory visits, with evidence observed for fire-haze days [74.4% (95% CI: 18.9%, 164.6%)] but not non-fire-haze days [26.3% (95% CI: –9.4%, 76.0%)]. There was no differential effect observed between a fire-haze and a non-fire-haze day.

Nonetheless, Fig. 4 shows that haze effects were sensitive to different definitions by duration. In Palangka Raya City, no haze effects were observed for short and moderate durations, but a reduced risk was observed when the haze duration was ≥15 days [–29.7% (95% CI: –43.9%, –11.7%)]. For Pulang Pisau Regency, prolonged durations were associated with an increased risk of respiratory visits. This pattern was clear when using both haze- and fire-haze-day definitions, with the highest risk observed when the duration of haze was ≥15 days [haze: 82.8% (95% CI: 31.7%, 153.7%); fire haze: 88.1% (95% CI: 13.8%, 210.8%)]. Although this pattern was observed for fire-haze days in Palangka Raya City, the effects were not significant. In both subdivisions, non-fire-haze days yielded non-significant associations, with apparently higher risk in Pulang Pisau Regency.

Different lag patterns of haze-related respiratory outcomes were observed in each subdivision, though evidence was weak ( Fig. 5 ). Non-fire haze followed an “n”-shaped lag pattern in both subdivisions, while the fire-haze lag pattern varied by location, with Pulang Pisau Regency showing a “u”-shaped lag pattern. The “n”-shaped lag pattern in Palangka Raya City was consistent for all-haze and non-fire-haze days when different durations were examined ( Supplementary Fig. S1a–c ). The lag patterns in Pulang Pisau Regency were also consistent throughout different durations.

When different lag lengths were tested, the risks remained only at shorter lags in Pulang Pisau Regency, while no changes were observed in Palangka Raya City ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Sensitivity analyses, which involved altering the lag structures for temperature, adjusting for relative humidity, modifying the puskesmas groupings, and without removing strata with zero cases, yielded consisted results, confirming the robustness of the main model ( Table 4 ).

discussion:
Our study provides valuable insight into the respiratory health effects of smoke haze, with a focus on the presence of fire activities and haze duration in two subdivisions in Central Kalimantan (Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency), Indonesia, from 2015 to 2019. The findings indicate that haze days pose a higher risk of adverse respiratory outcomes, consistently with a large body of epidemiological evidence [ 28 , 31 ], although some differences were noted when different haze definitions were used [ 28 ]. Haze characteristics, such as with or without local fire activities [ 42 ] and the duration of continuous occurrence [ 45 ], play an important role in elucidating the risk patterns. The risk of respiratory visits to puskesmas during smoke haze was prominent in Pulang Pisau Regency, which was mainly characterized by fire haze, but not in Palangka Raya City. With contrasting lag patterns, however, differential effects by fire- or non-fire haze remain inconclusive.

In Southeast Asia, haze can comprise both “fire” and “smoke” characteristics, hence different methods have been used when addressing its health effects [ 28 , 43 ]. We observed a pronounced risk of respiratory visits in Pulang Pisau Regency, especially on fire-haze days, but there was no significant difference between fire- and non-fire-haze days. This could be explained by the increased spread of haze-affected areas [ 34 ], the timing and severity of the burning [ 41 , 45 , 48 ], and the level of development of the subdivision [ 59 ]. When duration was considered, the pattern of increasing risk when the duration increased was observed for fire haze in both subdivisions. However, null associations were observed on haze days (Definition-1) with short and moderate durations in Palangka Raya City, while prolonged durations showed a reduced risk. If healthcare is assumed to have been equally accessible in both subdivisions during haze episodes, then this would affirm the idea that respiratory risk was higher in areas characterized by fire-haze days, which might potentially comprise different toxicities [ 25 ] and intensities [ 34 ] of pollutants.

It is also possible that healthcare access differed by area during haze periods, especially during prolonged and severe haze periods. Affected populations that encountered acute and severe health illnesses triggered during haze may have gone to hospitals instead of puskesmas , as essential medical resources are limited at puskesmas . According to one study, respiratory visits to primary healthcare centers increased during haze in urban/city areas, suggesting the possibility of better healthcare access in urban/city areas [ 59 ], consistently with the reduced risk observed over long durations of haze in Palangka Raya City. However, implementation of the national insurance policy in Indonesia since 2017 might have changed the population behavior, promoting visits to puskesmas under the subsidy, but this could not be explained by the previous study [ 59 ], which was conducted prior to 2017. Furthermore, better healthcare access in urban/city areas or unequally distributed health preventive measures may have led to the reduced risk during prolonged haze in Palangka Raya City. For example, during extreme haze, ‘ Posko Karhutla ’ is declared an affected area. Mobile clinics [“ Posyandu ” (“ Pos Pelayanan Terpadu ”), literally interpreted as ‘integrated service post’] are mobilized by the government as an extension of primary healthcare centers. In addition, oxygen houses are provided by the government and independent organizations. These may have resulted in a lower number of recorded puskesmas visits, though this cannot be confirmed in our study.

Haze characteristics should be considered while interpreting risk patterns over durations. Notably, fire haze exhibited increasing risk when the duration increased, as observed in both Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency. For Pulang Pisau Regency, characterized by fire haze, haze (Definition-1) days exhibited the same ascending trend. However, fire-haze and non-fire-haze durations in Palangka Raya were short, suggesting that the longer duration of haze (Definition-1) was mainly contributed by a combination of short durations of both fire and non-fire haze ( Fig. 2B and C ). This may explain why a negative association was observed for long durations (≥15 days) of haze (Definition-1), resembling those of short-duration fire haze, even though a high risk with large uncertainty was observed for long-duration fire haze. Furthermore, haze characterized by fires demonstrated “u”-shaped lag patterns. Higher risks at shorter lags suggest the possibility of a trigger based on a sudden intense increase in air particles released from smoke or fires [ 48 ]. Meanwhile, the lowered risk in middle lags and higher risk in later lags could be explained as follows: first, residents may have taken preventive measures, such as reducing outdoor activities; second, puskesmas may have reached the daily capacity of visitors; and third, additional mobile clinics may have been set up temporarily during extreme haze. Nonetheless, there was no significant change in lag patterns over varying durations. More studies will be needed to clarify these relationships.

Smoke pollutants are potentially detrimental to respiratory outcomes, when they are both near [ 42 , 48 ] and distant [ 43 , 60 ] to the burning location, while toxicity depends on the burning conditions of underground peat [ 25 ]. Smoke pollutants remain detrimental even after being transported over distances [ 24 , 43 , 60 ]. Palangka Raya City is located downwind of Pulang Pisau Regency during the southwest monsoon, which is a dry season that favors fire ignitions and spread. As observed in our study, major haze episodes occurred during this monsoon season (July to September in 2015 and 2019). Therefore, the high PM 10 concentrations in Palangka Raya City may contain some transported pollutants from fires in upwind areas, playing a role in the notably high respiratory risk during haze days, independently of local fire activity. Consistently with this, Pulang Pisau Regency is a major burning area in Central Kalimantan [ 61 , 62 ], although burnings could be dominant in Palangka Raya City irregularly, particularly due to prescribed fires [ 63 ].

The use of primary healthcare visit data and the assessment of haze effects based on different characteristics offer crucial information to clarify the effects of haze on respiratory health in this region. Nonetheless, this study has several limitations. First, we could not ensure that all cases of adverse respiratory outcomes have been captured. This is due to two reasons: (i) only six puskesmas were included in this study due to the limitation of data availability and (ii) there was no information on the maximum visit capacity in puskesmas or on the number of cases in mobile clinics or hospitals. Second, it remains unclear whether there were any changes in puskesmas visits due to the implementation of the national insurance policy in 2017. Third, fire hotspot counts were used as a proxy for fire activity and to define fire-haze days. Exposure may have been attenuated if the fires had occurred in underground peat, which is not being captured in fire counts. However, our findings suggest no evidence of such differential effects. Haze by Definition-1, a more conservative definition, should always be examined.
The findings of this study suggest inconclusive effects of smoke haze on respiratory visits to primary healthcare centers. While strong evidence was observed in the area mainly characterized by fire haze, the varying risk patterns in different subdivisions and durations suggested the need for further investigation, with considerations of the haze characteristics.
target: Smoke haze is a common air-pollution issue in Southeast Asia. Studies have suggested an elevated respiratory risk due to smoke-haze exposure. However, relevant studies have applied different exposure assessments in addressing haze effects and there is no unified definition of haze due to differences in its characteristics by location. The present study aimed to examine the effects of haze on respiratory health outcomes by analysing local fire activity and duration.Data for daily respiratory visits in Central Kalimantan were collected at local primary healthcare centers (‘ puskesmas ’) during the period spanning 2015–2019, encompassing two major haze episodes in the region. Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter <10 μm and fire hotspot counts were used to determine haze days, including fire-haze and non-fire-haze days. A space-time-stratified case-crossover design was used through a conditional quasi-Poisson regression model to examine the effects of haze vs. non-haze days in each subdivision, with lags of up to five  days, for different haze definitions and durations.The risk of respiratory visits was prominent during haze days but varied by haze characteristics. There was a 36.6% (95% confidence interval: 10.2%, 69.3%) and 74.4% (18.9%, 164.6%) increased risk of respiratory visits in Pulang Pisau Regency during haze and fire haze, respectively. The risk was pronounced when the haze was characterized by longer durations.Our findings suggest inconclusive effects of haze on respiratory visits to primary healthcare centers, although they appeared to be prominent in the area mainly dominated by fire haze. Haze characteristics should be analysed carefully for differences in risk patterns according to location.

Although the prevalence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) varies across populations [ 1 ] and diagnostic methods [ 2 , 3 ], it has markedly risen over recent decades [ 4–6 ], with a pooled prevalence of 32.4% [95% confidence interval (CI): 29.9–34.9] and incidence of 46.9 cases per 1000 person-years in adults [ 3 ]. Men are more susceptible to developing NAFLD than women (70.8 vs. 29.6 cases per 1000 person-years) [ 3 ].

NAFLD, associated with a sedentary lifestyle, low physical activity, excessive calorie intake, and unhealthy diet [ 7 ], is considered a hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome [ 8 , 9 ] and a leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [ 10 ]. In South Korea, a study reported NAFLD prevalence of 33.6% among 25 947 participants, by using abdominal ultrasonography data, over a median follow-up of 7.5 years [ 11 ]. The HCC incidence was 23.1 vs. 0.9 per 100 000 person-years for those with and without NAFLD, respectively [ 11 ]. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, gamma-glutamyl transferase, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) level, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) level, and triglyceride level, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for NAFLD-associated HCC was 16.73 (95% CI: 2.09–133.85) [ 11 ]. Similarly, a study found an association between nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and HCC (HR: 3.49; 95% CI: 1.23–9.86) in a Japanese cohort with biopsy-confirmed NAFLD [ 12 ]. Recently, NAFLD was also linked to gastrointestinal cancer [ 9 ], cardiovascular diseases [ 1 ], and disability [ 6 ].

Given the lack of approved drugs for NAFLD treatment [ 13 ], researchers are exploring preventive strategies, focusing on personal traits such as phenotype [ 14 ] and lifestyle [ 13 ], and environmental exposures such as air pollutants and endocrine-disrupting chemicals [ 15 ]. According to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, high systolic blood pressure, smoking, and ambient fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) pollution were the top three risk factors for age-standardized attributable disability-adjusted life years in East Asia [ 16 ], including Taiwan. These findings emphasize the importance of raising awareness and the critical need to mitigate exposure to ambient PM 2.5 pollution and other risks.

Air pollutants, particularly PM 2.5 and traffic-related pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) and carbon monoxide (CO), pose significant health risks. PM 2.5 —fine particulate matter that is ≤2.5 μm in diameter—infiltrates alveoli and enters the bloodstream [ 17 , 18 ], increasing morbidity and mortality in respiratory infections, cardiovascular diseases, and type 2 diabetes [ 19 ]. Motor vehicle combustion is the primary source of ambient NO 2 [ 20 ] and CO [ 21 ]—both traffic-related air pollutants. NO 2 exposure is linked to pediatric asthma [ 22 ] and respiratory mortality [ 23 ], while short-term CO exposure is associated with increased hospital visits for myocardial infarction [ 24 ] and higher cardiovascular and respiratory diseases mortality [ 25 ].

Recent studies exploring associations between NAFLD and air pollution, particularly PM 2.5 , have yielded inconsistent results [ 26–28 ]. Some longitudinal studies reported positive associations between PM 2.5 exposure and NAFLD incidence [ 29 , 30 ] or fatty liver index [ 31 ]. Others identified proximity to major roadways [ 28 ] and NO 2 exposure [ 30 ] as NAFLD risk factors. Differences in study designs, exposure levels, PM 2.5 components [ 32 ], and NAFLD definitions may account for these discrepancies.

In Taiwan, efforts to mitigate air pollution have lowered PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO levels over recent decades [ 33 , 34 ]. Despite these improvements, epidemiological studies investigating associations between traffic-related air pollutants and NAFLD incidence remain limited. Using a time-dependent Cox proportional-hazards model, this study investigates the association of NAFLD incidence with PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure.
### Participants

Participants were selected from the MJ Health Research Foundation database, which collects health examination data and lifestyle information through questionnaires. The dataset included health records from company-provided and voluntary examinations for individuals and families [ 35 ]. From 135 399 screened participants, inclusion criteria were: health examinations conducted between 1996 and 2016; age of ≥20 years at enrollment; no history of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or thyroid disease; [ 5 ] no history of gastrointestinal surgery; absence of NAFLD or liver cirrhosis on baseline ultrasonography; no reported alcohol consumption or hepatitis; and availability of at least two health examination records. Participants were required to have a registered address in Taiwan, excluding eastern regions (∼0.6% of the cohort) due to sparse air quality monitoring stations [ 33 ]. Individuals who relocated during follow-up were excluded due to challenges in assessing accurate cumulative exposure. Additional exclusions were participants with incomplete covariate data. Finally, 62 660 participants were included. Supplementary Figure S1 presents the selection process flowchart.

### NAFLD definition

Fatty liver disease and cirrhosis were diagnosed through abdominal ultrasonography by experienced physicians at the MJ Health Screening Center [ 36 ]. NAFLD was defined as “fatty liver” or “fatty liver with focal sparing,” excluding liver cirrhosis cases.

### Exposure evaluation

Daily PM 2.5 and NO 2 levels were estimated by using a hybrid Kriging land-use regression (LUR) model involving an extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm [ 37 , 38 ] and CO levels were estimated by using LUR-XGBoost [ 39 ]. Models utilized daily air pollutant data from 68 fixed-site monitoring stations in western Taiwan. Meteorological variables, greenness, culture-specific emissions (e.g. temples, Chinese restaurants), proximity to the nearest power plant, garbage incinerators, and industrial parks were predictors for PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO [ 37–39 ]. Additionally, levels of co-pollutants such as SO 2 and O 3 were determined [ 37–39 ]. Daily ambient PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO levels were estimated with the aforementioned models and mapped at 50 m × 50 m resolution in ArcGIS. Personal exposure levels were based on residential township. Model performance (10-fold cross-validation) showed R 2 values of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.84, with root mean square error (RMSE) values of 4.73, 2.04, and 0.15 for PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO, respectively [ 37–39 ]. The exposure window was defined as the 3-year average before each health examination during follow-up.

### Covariates

Demographic data [ 3 , 5 , 28 , 30 ] were obtained through self-administered questionnaires, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), marital status (single/divorced/separated/widowed or married/cohabitating), educational level (junior high school or lower, senior or vocational high school, college degree, or master’s degree or higher), annual household income (<13 333, 13 333–40 000, or >40 000 USD) [ 40 ], smoking status (never, secondhand/former, or frequent smoker/daily smoker), sleep duration (<6, 6–8, or >8 hours/day), regular exercise (never/little, sometimes/1–4 h/week, or frequently/daily/>4 h/week), and fried-food consumption (none/little/≤1 portion, 2–3 portions, or ≥4 portions/week).

Given that NAFLD typically coexists with metabolic disorders [ 10 , 11 , 41 ], metabolic indicators, including abdominal obesity, hypertension, elevated fasting glucose, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL-C, and high LDL-C, were adjusted for. Waist circumference and blood pressure were nurse-measured, while biochemical data (triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, fasting glucose) were analysed by using a Toshiba C8000 analyser [ 36 ]. Metabolic indicators were defined by using established criteria [ 42 ]. Abdominal obesity: waist circumference of ≥90 cm (Asian men) or ≥80 cm (Asian women). Hypertension: systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥85 mmHg, or use of antihypertensives. Elevated fasting glucose: ≥100 mg/dL or hyperglycemic medication use. Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥150 mg/dL or medication use. Low HDL-C: <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women) or medication use. High LDL-C: <130 mg/dL. Initial metabolic status was used in the analysis, as air pollution exposure may influence these indicators [ 43 ].

### Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics characterized participants and air pollutant levels. Spearman’s correlation established a matrix for all pollutants. For participants developing NAFLD, event time was the first NAFLD record; for others, the last examination before loss to follow-up or 31 December 2016 was right-censored.

Time-dependent Cox proportional-hazards models were used to calculate HRs and 95% CIs for NAFLD incidence. Covariates significant in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models. Two-pollutant models assessed changes after adjusting for another pollutant. Adjusted HRs per interquartile range (IQR) increase in PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO were computed. Sensitivity analyses were stratified by sex and modifiable behaviors (smoking, sleep duration, exercise, and fried-food consumption). Robustness was further validated by using augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW), combining inverse probability of censoring weighting with multiple imputations for a high censoring rate [ 44 ]. Model fit was assessed via Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC). All analyses were performed by using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).

Taiwan spans ∼36 000 km 2 , with a population of 21.5–23.5 million during 1996–2016 [ 45 ]. Participants were recruited from townships averaging 53.3 km 2 (range: 0.9–247.3 km 2 ). Supplementary Figure S2 shows Taiwan’s population density and the cohort distribution.
Between 1996 and 2016, 18 959 incident NAFLD cases were identified over 357 392 person-years (incidence: 53.0 per 1000 person-years).

 0.30), while a strong correlation was noted between NO 2 and CO ( r =
 0.86). Supplementary Figure S3 depicts the geographical distributions of 3-year average of air pollutants and the proportion of new NAFLD cases. PM 2.5 levels increased from northern to southern Taiwan, while NO 2 and CO levels were higher in densely populated areas ( Supplementary Figure S2A ).

### Associations between individual characteristics and NAFLD incidence

Table 2 presents crude HRs showing associations between individual characteristics and NAFLD incidence. Baseline demographics are shown in Supplementary Table S1 . Participants developing NAFLD were predominantly ≥45 years old, men, with BMI of ≥24 kg/m 2 , married/cohabitating, or had unhealthy behaviors. Secondhand/former smokers, frequent smokers, sleep duration <6 h/day, exercise ≤4 h/week, higher fried-food consumption (≥2 portions/week), and those with any metabolic indicator assessed in this study showed increased NAFLD risk.

### Associations between exposure to ambient air pollutants and the incidence of NAFLD

Single-pollutant models adjusted for age, sex, and BMI ( Table 3 , Model 1) showed significant associations between 3-year average PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure, and NAFLD incidence. Further adjustments for marital status, education, smoking, sleep, exercise, fried-food consumption ( Table 3 , Model 2), and initial status of metabolic indicators ( Table 3 , Model 3) yielded adjusted HRs that were consistent with those of Model 1. Model 3 demonstrated the best fit based on lower AIC and BIC values. Adjusted HRs were 1.04 (95% CI: 1.02–1.05) per 7.4-μg/m 3 PM 2.5 increase, 1.06 (95% CI: 1.04–1.09) per 8.5-ppb NO 2 increase, and 1.16 (95% CI: 1.13–1.19) per 0.27-ppm CO increase. Two-pollutant models confirmed the significance of each pollutant when adjusted for another. Exposure–response curves are shown in Supplementary Figure S4 .

Table 4 presents adjusted HRs using median 3-year pollutant levels as cut-offs: ≤30.2 μg/m³ for PM 2.5 , ≤21.6 ppb for NO 2 , and ≤0.56 ppm for CO. Compared with participants residing in areas with low levels of both PM 2.5 and NO 2 , those in areas with high levels of both pollutants had an adjusted HR of 1.25 (95% CI: 1.19–1.31). Similarly, compared with participants in areas with low levels of both PM 2.5 and CO, the adjusted HR was 1.12 (95% CI: 1.07–1.17) for those in areas with low PM 2.5 but high CO, and 1.28 (95% CI: 1.22–1.33) for those exposed to high levels of both pollutants.

### Sensitivity analyses

Associations stratified by relocation status ( Supplementary Table S2 ) remained significant among participants who stayed in the same township throughout follow-up or during the 3 years prior to their health exam, with slightly stronger effects in the latter group. Stratification by quintile-based township area ( Supplementary Table S3 ) showed that associations were maintained in smaller townships; however, in larger areas (≥62.70 km 2 ), associations for PM 2.5 and NO 2 were attenuated, whereas those for CO remained significant. Robustness analyses considering a high censoring rate (65.7% censored before 2016) confirmed consistency with primary findings ( Supplementary Table S4 ), supporting their validity.

Figure 1 depicts associations of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure with NAFLD incidence stratified by sex and modifiable behaviors (smoking, sleep, exercise, and fried-food consumption). Participants with unhealthy behaviors were more susceptible to NAFLD when exposed to PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO.
The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the National Taiwan University Hospital (approval number: 202002093RIND). The requirement for informed consent was waived.
discussion:
This population-based cohort study highlights significant associations between long-term exposure to PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO, and NAFLD incidence among participants without alcohol consumption.

Several metabolic indicators (abdominal obesity, hypertension, elevated fasting blood glucose, and dyslipidemia) were adjusted for ( Table 3 , Model 3), given the established coexistence of NAFLD with metabolic disorders [ 10 , 11 , 41 ]. Our findings align with Sun et al. , who reported a positive link between PM 2.5 and NAFLD by using the fatty liver index, derived from triglycerides, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, BMI, and waist circumference [ 46 ].

With a mean follow-up of 5.7 years, our findings support the 3-year average as a reliable exposure metric. Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 demonstrate consistent results for various exposure windows (1-, 3-, and 5-year averages) and this finding aligns with prior studies using various exposure windows [ 25 , 28 , 30 ]. Furthermore, our observed NAFLD incidence (53.0 cases per 1000 person-years) closely matches the pooled estimate by Riazi et al. (46.9 cases per 1000 person-years) [ 3 ], confirming the validity of our exposure metric.

As in most follow-up studies, there is a possibility of loss to follow-up. Moreover, participants in the MJ cohort are invited annually for health check-ups, though the actual timing of health examinations varies among individuals. Supplementary Table S7 presents stratified analyses based on follow-up interval length to address potential differences in population characteristics. Results consistently showed significant associations between each pollutant and NAFLD incidence, regardless of the interval length.

Emerging evidence highlights the role of air pollution in NAFLD, with pollutant levels and regional variations influencing risk. In the UK Biobank study, detrimental PM 2.5 ranged from ∼9.7 to 10.9 μg/m³, and NO 2 from 26.4 to 38.7 μg/m³ (∼14.0 to 20.6 ppb, converted at 25°C) [ 29 ]. In contrast, our study identified unique risk patterns from pollutant combinations. Participants living in areas with both high PM 2.5 (>30.2 μg/m³) and NO 2 (>21.6 ppb), low PM 2.5 but high CO (>0.56 ppm), or both high PM 2.5 and CO were at increased risk of NAFLD ( Table 4 ). These differences might be attributable to regional variations in PM 2.5 composition, such as copper and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, linked to hepatic steatosis and lipid metabolism gene expression in experimental studies [ 31 ].

Recently, observational studies have linked NAFLD incidence with residential proximity to major roadways [ 27 ] and NO 2 exposure [ 25 , 29 ], highlighting traffic-related air pollution. This is the first study to longitudinally examine CO exposure and NAFLD incidence. While low CO levels may be cytoprotective, high levels can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase, disrupt mitochondrial metabolism, and induce oxidative stress [ 47 ]. These mechanisms align with our findings.

The strengths of the study include the focus on Taiwan’s densely populated western regions; the evaluation of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO; and the novel association identified between CO exposure and NAFLD. Additionally, culture-specific emission sources, such as temples and Chinese restaurants, were incorporated into the air pollution modeling. More importantly, based on our findings and those of previous studies [ 25 , 30 ], we recommend health promotion strategies to mitigate the effects of air pollution on NAFLD, including reducing fried-food consumption, quitting smoking, ensuring sufficient sleep, and engaging in physical activity. While our study incorporated cultural and behavioral factors, high-resolution models such as 3D GEOS-Chem enable more precise neighborhood-level exposure estimates [ 48 ]. Future research should integrate detailed regional emission inventories to refine exposure assessments and better analyse small-scale sources.

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, participants potentially had higher socioeconomic status [ 40 ] and greater health consciousness than the general population, which may limit generalizability. Nevertheless, the population density closely resembles Taiwan’s distribution ( Supplementary Figure S2 ), ensuring some degree of representativeness. Second, study participants were selected from the MJ cohort based on abdominal ultrasonography and absence of baseline NAFLD-related conditions, with those missing key covariate data (e.g. lifestyle factors and metabolic indicators) excluded ( Supplementary Table S8 ). Additionally, 65.7% were censored before 2016, raising further concerns regarding representativeness as well. However, the major outcome of this investigation, NAFLD, was obtained by measurement, i.e. abdominal sonography, and not by the capturing of an event, such as cardiac events [ 49 ]. Therefore, the observed outcome might not be related to the censoring. As suggested by Lesko et al. [ 49 ], the follow-up time should be censored at participants' last recorded encounter, reducing concerns of bias due to loss to follow-up, especially in a group of health examinees. This is supported by the AIPW analysis ( Supplementary Table S4 ) , which showed consistent results with the primary findings, supporting the robustness of our study despite substantial attrition. Third, while polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in PM 2.5 are hypothesized to induce hepatic steatosis [ 31 ], our study did not explore this aspect. Instead, we included industrial parks in the air pollution exposure assessment. Future research should examine the long-term effects of specific PM 2.5 components. Fourth, using township-level residential data to estimate personal exposure may have introduced bias due to exposure misclassification, which is inevitable in air pollution studies. This issue relates to the resolution of exposure assessment. High-resolution models, such as 3D GEOS-Chem, have been proposed to provide more precise neighborhood-level exposure estimates [ 48 ]. In this current investigation, township was used as the exposure unit, rather than the exact address. We took into consideration the working and commuting possibilities and opted to use a slightly broader exposure geographic location. Despite this limitation, our exposure model demonstrated reasonably good performance in terms of R 2 and RMSE. To further evaluate the robustness of our findings, we conducted additional analyses (Supplementary Tables S3). Future studies should incorporate higher-resolution exposure data, such as personal air quality monitors or detailed indoor and occupational exposure assessments, to further refine estimates.

In conclusion, long-term exposure to PM 2.5 and traffic-related air pollutants, such as NO 2 and CO, is associated with an increased incidence of NAFLD. These associations, confirmed in two-pollutant models, are particularly relevant for regions with high NAFLD prevalence and air pollution, such as Asia and developing countries.
target: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) affects approximately one-third of adults and may progress to advanced fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Epidemiologic studies linking air pollution to NAFLD incidence remain limited. This study examined associations between long-term exposure to ambient air pollution and NAFLD incidence.The study included 62 660 adults in Taiwan undergoing health examinations from 1996 to 2016. NAFLD was diagnosed through liver ultrasonography; individual characteristics and medical history were obtained from questionnaires. Residential township data estimated exposure to fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), and carbon monoxide (CO). Time-dependent Cox regression was conducted to assess associations between air pollution and NAFLD incidence.The overall NAFLD incidence was 53.0 cases per 1000 person-years. Adjusted models showed positive associations between air pollutants and NAFLD. Compared with low exposure to both PM 2.5 and NO 2 , the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) [95% confidence interval (CI)] for high exposure to both was 1.25 (1.19–1.31). Similarly, compared with low exposure to both PM 2.5 and CO, the adjusted HR (95% CI) was 1.12 (1.07–1.17) for low PM 2.5 and high CO, and 1.28 (1.22–1.33) for high exposure to both.Long-term exposure to PM 2.5 and traffic-related air pollutants, including NO 2 and CO, may increase the risk of developing NAFLD.
