Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are a major public health issue, responsible for 74% of global deaths, with 77% of all NCD mortality occurring in low- and middle-income countries [ 1 ]. Cardiovascular disease (CVD), cancers, chronic respiratory disease (CRD), and diabetes are regarded as major NCDs, affecting most of the population aged 30–69 years [ 1 ]. These conditions often require long-term, sometimes lifelong, treatment and follow-up to maintain the health status of patients. Disruption in access to routine healthcare services for their management may increase morbidity and mortality, affecting the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 3) of ensuring healthy lives and minimizing premature deaths due to NCDs.

In late December 2019, a novel coronavirus disease emerged in China and had spread to >77 countries by March 2020. The World Health Organization identified this disease as COVID-19 and declared it a pandemic [ 2 , 3 ]. In response, most nations instituted strict controls, including lockdowns, social isolation, and travel restrictions (isolations and quarantine), anticipating its quick spread. These measures led to partial or complete disruption of preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services for NCDs and other health issues [ 3 ]. The disruption had a serious effect in low-income countries, which already had limited capacity and where people had limited access to affordable, quality care [ 4–6 ]. Management of the pandemic itself necessitated ad hoc changes to meet the surge in patient volumes, including the suspension of routine primary health services, cancellation of scheduled treatments, and the reallocation of healthcare resources and personnel to COVID-19 wards [ 7 ]. These adaptations, compounded by the unavailability of public transportation induced by lockdown measures, further exacerbated access limitations to essential health services during the crisis. Furthermore, lockdowns caused economic losses, making it harder for patients to pay for and use services [ 5 , 6 , 8 ], thus reducing their follow-up visits and medication adherence [ 9 ]. In addition to these factors, public fear of infection and the stigma associated with infected or suspected cases have resulted in a decrease in healthcare utilization, particularly for routine, elective, and preventive visits [ 4 , 5 ].

The consequences of limiting access to preventive and therapeutic services for NCDs—including increased mortality, poor mental health, and post-lockdown effects on chronic diseases—due to strict pandemic measures have been widely discussed in the literature [ 4 , 5 , 7 , 8 , 10 ]. However, evidence from low- and middle-income countries, which were disproportionately affected by the pandemic and subsequent stringent control measures including lockdowns, remains underexplored. Nepal, a low-income country with limited healthcare resources, implemented a nationwide lockdown from 24 March to 14 August 2020, restricting all kinds of travel and border closure. The healthcare, already grappling with challenges such as poverty, illiteracy, inadequate infrastructure, shortage of trained professionals, cultural barriers, political instabilities, and geographical obstacles to providing quality care, experienced further compromises in service delivery [ 11 , 12 ]. These limitations were reflected in increased mortality and morbidity indicators for NCDs—mainly CVD, CRD, cancer, hypertension (HTN), and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [ 4 ]. In Nepal, deaths from amendable causes—such as hypertensive diseases, diabetes mellitus, kidney disease, and other conditions—have been rising, accounting for about two-thirds of total deaths in 2015 [ 13 ]. While mortality and morbidity are influenced by multiple factors, many of which lie outside the healthcare system, access to high-quality healthcare services remains crucial for managing and preventing these amendable NCD-related deaths [ 14 , 15 ]. Meanwhile, a systematic assessment of these impacts in Nepal in relation to health service disruption attributed to stringent containment measures remains unavailable. We therefore aimed to analyse the effects on services for CVD, CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD by using a robust epidemiological design, controlling for time-invariant confounders, long-term trends, and the seasonality of selected NCDs.
We conducted interrupted time series (ITS) analysis by using monthly counts of outpatient department visits for selected NCDs (CVD, CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD) to evaluate the impacts of lockdown on health service utilization after controlling for time-invariant confounders, seasonality, and long-term trend affecting the population-level distribution of these diseases [ 16 , 17 ]. We used the reference period of lockdown implementation from March 2020 to August 2020 as the primary intervention period to assess the situation during the COVID-19 pandemic. The main health outcomes in this study were outpatient department visits for CVD (cerebrovascular and coronary heart diseases), CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD, and the utilization of free services for patients with selected NCDs. The database we used defines CVD as including the following heart-related conditions: ischemic heart disease, vascular heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, cardiac arrest, heart failure, congestive heart failure, stroke, and other cardiac-related conditions [ 18 , 19 ]. HTN is both a non-communicable disease and a major metabolic risk factor for cardiovascular and kidney diseases. In our source datasets, these conditions were recorded separately; therefore, we analysed them independently. The free health service scheme, implemented by the Nepal government, aims to provide financial relief to individuals facing severe and financially burdensome diseases such as CVD, cancer, renal failure, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, head and spinal injury, sickle cell anemia, and stroke. For this study, we have included data of patients receiving free health services for selected CVD (defined earlier), CKD, and cancer only. We evaluated the impact of lockdown by estimating the percentage change in the number of outpatient department visits and the utilization of free services as the function of intervention implementation.

### Data collection and management

The observation period spanned 33 months, from July 2018 to April 2021 (corresponding to the Nepali calendar dates of Shrawan 1, 2075 to Chaitra 30, 2077), encompassing 20 months before and 13 months after the lockdown implementation. Monthly data on outpatient department visits for patients with NCDs were retrieved from the Integrated Health Information Management Section (IHIMS), Department of Health Services of the Ministry of Health and Population (MoHP), Nepal. The IHIMS, under the Policy, Planning, and Monitoring Division of Nepal’s Department of Health Services, manages routine health data from the ward level, the smallest administrative unit, to the federal level through predefined processes [ 20 ]. It collects, verifies, and processes data from both the public and private sectors to maintain a centralized data bank. The Department of Health Services publishes the annual health report by using data generated by IHIMS [ 19 ]. As the annual report and data are published at the end of the fiscal year, we were unable to obtain additional data for analysis. Data were then checked for duplication and inconsistencies by using Microsoft Excel before being imported into R-software for further analysis. COVID-19 data were extracted from daily reports published by MoHP and imported into Excel 2010.

### Statistical analysis

We used descriptive statistics to summarize the number of monthly hospital visits for selected NCDs, namely CRD, CVD, cancer, CKD, and HTN. We utilized a scatterplot of the time series to illustrate the outpatient department visits for selected NCDs before and after the lockdown period. The association between hospital outpatient department visits and lockdown implementation was estimated by using a quasi-Poisson regression model to account for overdispersion. We controlled the models for seasonality by using Fourier terms, incorporated an indicator variable for the time to control long-term effect, and included a 1-month lag of residuals in the model to control residual autocorrelation. The final model to compute the acute effect of lockdown on health service utilization was defined by using the following equation:

In this model, y t represents the outpatient department visits of each selected NCD patient at time t ; β 0 is the intercept; exp ( β 1 ) denotes the change in outpatient department visits with respect to the change in unit time; exp ( β 2 ) indicates the change in number of outpatient department visits during lockdown period; and β 3 indicates the slope of change following the intervention (interaction between time and intervention). Fourier terms were determined by using Quasi-Akaike Information Criterion. The intervention start point was defined as 25 March 2020, when the government of Nepal officially announced the lockdown. The pre-intervention period spanned from mid-July 2018 to mid-March 2020 ( T = 1 to T = 20) and the post-intervention period was from 25 March 2020 to 13 June 2021 ( T = 21 to T = 33), encompassing 20 months pre intervention and 13 months post intervention.

The estimated percentage of immediate change and the average annual change in the secular trend were calculated by using the coefficient of the lockdown indicator ( β 2 ) and the interaction term between time and the lockdown indicator ( β 3 ) in the model, respectively. We calculated the number of averted outpatient department visits by subtracting the actual outpatient department visits from the predicted number without the influence of the lockdown.

We tested the model fit by plotting residuals, autocorrelation functions, and partial autocorrelation functions. All statistical tests were two-sided and a P -value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed by using R v4.0.1 ( http://www.R-project.org ). All data analyses were conducted in 2022.
This study analysed the outpatient department visits and the utilization of free services for selected NCDs by using data retrieved from IHIMS, Nepal. A total of 3 985  500 outpatient department visits were recorded in the 20 months before the COVID-19 pandemic compared with 2 745  395 visits during the pandemic, indicating an overall 31.1% reduction in outpatient department visits, as shown in Table 1 . Similarly, the utilization of free services decreased by 12.5%, from 51 054 cases pre pandemic to 44 661 cases post pandemic. Among individual NCD categories, the major decline in outpatient department visits was observed for cancer (50.2%), followed by CVD (45.2%) and CRD (32.6%). CKD and HTN experienced smaller declines of 16.7% and 27.5%, respectively. Free service utilization also declined, with the largest reductions seen in CVD (37.8%) and CKD (19.9%), while cancer services experienced a relatively smaller decrease of 6.7%.

Figure 1 illustrates trends in outpatient department visits for patients with chronic NCDs before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. CRD and HTN consistently accounted for the highest number of outpatient department visits, showing a sharp decline after the onset of lockdown in March 2020, followed by a gradual but incomplete recovery. CVD and CKD exhibited similar patterns, showing significant drops post lockdown and slower recovery rates. Cancer visits were the least frequent and showed the most substantial decline, with minimal rebound.

Figure 2 shows an ITS analysis of monthly outpatient department visits for patients with NCDs. The graph compares the expected number of outpatient department visits for each NCD during the post-lockdown period to the observed number of outpatient department visits. The grayed-out area on the white background reflects the period of the COVID-19 pandemic. The figure demonstrates that, after lockdown, there was a dramatic decrease in the rate of outpatient department visits by all studied NCDs, including cancer, CRD, HTN, CVD, and CKD. While the expected and observed lines for CRD, CKD, and HTN are almost parallel, those for CVD and cancer appear to be slightly out of alignment. The slope of the outpatient department visit rate before and after the lockdown appears to be similar, indicating that the lockdown caused an immediate drop in outpatient department visits, but that the rise in outpatient department visits has followed the same trajectory as before.

The results for the effect of the lockdown are summarized in Table 2 , reporting the relative risk (RR) when comparing the periods before and after lockdown. The model shows evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic has affected outpatient department visits for cancer and CVD. There was a 73% [RR 0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.089–0.808] decrease in outpatient department visits for CVD and a 64% (RR 0.36, 95% CI: 0.175–0.745) decrease in outpatient department visit for cancer patients. Though an immediate reduction in outpatient department visits was observed, the model lacks adequate evidence to show the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on outpatient department visits for CRD (RR 0.89, 95% CI: 0.651–1.228), HTN (RR: 1.004, 95% CI: 0.64–1.575), and CKD (RR 0.589, 95% CI: 0.231–1.501). This signifies that outpatient department visits for HTN, CRD, and CKD remained almost constant before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Figure 3 shows the trend of services utilization under the free health service scheme by patients for major NCDs (CVD, CKD, and cancer) before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The number of patients utilizing services for CKD remained relatively high and did not show a significant decline during the COVID-19 waves; there was consistently high utilization, even during the COVID-19 periods, which might have been due to the requirement for the continuity of care for CKD such as dialysis. The utilization of services for heart disease and cancer declined during the COVID-19 periods.

Figure 4 shows an ITS analysis of the monthly utilization of free health services for NCDs. The graph compares the expected numbers for service utilization for each NCD during the post - lockdown period to the observed numbers for service utilization. The grayed-out area on the white background reflects the period of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Though an immediate reduction in the utilization of free services was observed, Table 3 shows that the model lacks adequate evidence to show the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the utilization of free services for cancer (RR 1.76, 95% CI: 0.45–7.05), CVD (RR 0.37, 95% CI: 0.06–2.11), and kidney disease (RR 1.45, 95% CI: 0.69–3.01).
Our study has several strengths, including a robust quasi-experimental design that effectively teases out the association between lockdown enforcement and the disruption of healthcare service utilization nationwide by using official data from the IHIMS, MoHP. However, this study has several limitations. First, the analysis was conducted at an aggregate level rather than on an individual basis, and it only covers the first lockdown phase. Second, we assumed lockdown implementation as a discrete, point-in-time intervention rather than an intervention period over a period of time. This assumption may oversimplify the nature of the lockdown, potentially underestimating or misrepresenting gradual or phase effects that occurred throughout the enforcement period. Consequently, the observed changes in healthcare service utilization may not fully account for varying levels of lockdown stringency or compliance over time. A sequential analysis that includes all pandemic waves would offer a clearer picture of the overall impact. Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term effects of these disruptions on patient outcomes.
The study was approved (registration number: 692/2021 P) by Nepal Health Research Council, Government of Nepal, with a waiver for informed consent.
discussion:
This study reveals a notable decline in the number of outpatient department visits and the utilization of free healthcare services for NCDs immediately following the COVID-19 lockdown in Nepal. The data strongly suggest a significant impact of the lockdown on outpatient department visits for cancer and CVD. Specifically, there was a marked reduction in visits for these conditions, indicating that the lockdown had a substantial effect on healthcare access and utilization for these diseases.

We also observed a decrease in outpatient visits for CRD, HTN, and CKD; however, the statistical evidence was insufficient to definitively attribute these changes to the lockdown. While trends in the utilization of free services for cancer, CKD, and CVD showed variations before and after the lockdown, none of these changes was statistically significant. This lack of significance suggests that the observed differences might be attributed to random variation rather than a definitive effect of the lockdown on service utilization.

Our findings are consistent with a systematic review of 17 cancer studies and 14 cardiovascular studies that were conducted primarily in the region of Southeast Asia, which reported a 30%–40% reduction in outpatient department services during the pandemic [ 21 ]. Additionally, a study conducted across multiple hospitals in India also observed decreased hospital visits and treatment for NCDs during the pandemic, despite having adequate resources and infrastructure [ 22 ]. This aligns with our findings, highlighting that, even in countries with well-established healthcare systems, outpatient department visits and service utilization for NCDs were significantly affected by the pandemic. In contrast, a time - series analysis from China reported a reduction in hospital visits for respiratory diseases, but found no significant effect on outpatient department visits for CVD [ 23 ]. Although our study found no significant impact on service utilization for NCDs, the general trend of reduced service utilization during the pandemic is consistent with those of other reviews and studies. These have shown reductions in all aspects of NCD care, including screening, diagnosis, treatment, palliative care, and follow-up management [ 21 ]. Similar findings from retrospective studies in Croatia and China attributed reductions in hospital and outpatient services to factors such as lockdowns, the reorganization of hospital operations, the rationing of medical resources, and public reluctance to seek care due to infection risks [ 11 , 12 ]. These factors likely contributed to decreased access to services and travel restrictions during the pandemic.

Given the essential role of primary care in the prevention and management of NCDs, the impact of the pandemic on healthcare access has exacerbated challenges in managing these chronic conditions. Regular follow-ups and adherence to medication are crucial for managing NCDs effectively. The disruption in these services underscores the need for continuity of care as part of pandemic preparedness, ensuring that chronic conditions are managed appropriately despite public health measures and the direct impacts of the pandemic [ 24 ].
The COVID-19 pandemic reduced outpatient department visits and utilization of free health services for NCDs, especially cancer and CVD. The lockdown likely disrupted medication adherence and physical activity, potentially leading to complications and advanced disease stages. These reductions in service access may have resulted in delayed diagnoses and suboptimal treatment. It is crucial for the health system to maintain continuous care for NCD patients during pandemics.
target: The implementation of restriction and mitigation measures to contain COVID-19 infection led to a significant disruption in the delivery of essential health services. However, the ramifications of the immediate COVID-19 containment policies on healthcare service utilization for major non-communicable diseases (NCDs)-related cases, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains unknown.We used an interrupted time series study design, fitted with quasi-Poisson regression models, to assess the impacts of the nationwide lockdown on hospital visits for NCDs, namely cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic respiratory disease (CRD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), cancer, and hypertension (HTN)-related cases, in Nepal. A total of 33 months of nationwide outpatient department visits data for NCD cases between July 2018 and April 2021, 20 months before and 13 months after the enforcement of the nationwide lockdown, were included in the final analysis.Compared with the expected level, there was an estimated 73% [relative risk (RR) 0.269, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.089–0.808] decrease in outpatient department visits for CVD and a 64% (RR 0.361, 95% CI: 0.175–0.745) decrease for cancer. Although an immediate reduction in outpatient department visits was observed, the evidence was not conclusive to determine the true effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on outpatient department visits for CRD (RR 0.89, 95% CI: 0.651–1.228), HTN (RR 1.004, 95% CI: 0.64–1.575), and kidney disease (RR 0.589, 95% CI: 0.231–1.501).We estimated that the nationwide lockdown implemented in response to the COVID-19 pandemic affected hospital visits for patients with CVD and cancer. However, the available evidence was not conclusive enough to determine the impact of COVID-19 on outpatient department visits for the other NCDs analysed, namely HTN, CRD, and CKD.

A large body of literature has documented associations between childhood household dysfunction and health [ 1–6 ], behavioural [ 5 , 7 , 8 ], and socioeconomic [ 9 , 10 ] outcomes. Household dysfunction includes a diverse range of events occurring within the family, such as parental substance use, mental health problems, union dissolution, and incarceration [ 11 ]. These experiences commonly co-occur, and a dose–response relationship robust to covariate adjustment between the total number of the indicators and the studied outcomes is typically found [ 1–3 , 11 ].

A central methodological limitation in previous research is that most studies do not assess unobserved confounding in these associations. Such confounding might arise from genetic factors. Studies often include similar indicators measured from both parents and their children, many of which have a genetically heritable component, including psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and criminal behaviour [ 12–15 ]. Observed parental and offspring indicators may also be expressions of underlying heritable factors, such as personality traits or externalizing disorders [ 12 , 13 , 15 ], and many of the indicators of childhood household dysfunction also have shared genetic determinants [ 16 , 17 ]. Confounding may also arise from socioeconomic factors that have an intergenerational component [ 18 , 19 ] and are associated with indicators of household dysfunction [ 20 ]. Finally, children may impact parental outcomes [ 21–23 ]. For instance, children’s psychiatric diagnoses may be associated with subsequent parental diagnoses, partly due to parental distress [ 24 ].

Previous studies on child maltreatment have used, e.g. twin designs [ 25 ] and Mendelian randomization [ 26 ] to adjust for unobserved familial confounding, whereas studies on household dysfunction indicators, such as parental divorce or mental health problems, have addressed this issue using, e.g. children-of-twins and adoption designs [ 27–30 ], or molecular genetics designs, such as polygenic risk scores together with single nucleotide polymorphism based heritability [ 22 , 30 ]. The results from these studies indicate that these experiences have a direct association with offspring mental health outcomes, net of genetic confounding [ 30 ]. However, these associations depend on specific exposure-outcome pairs, e.g. the association between parental mental health problems and offspring mental health problems is less confounded than the associations between parental criminality and offspring mental health [ 22 ], and parental divorce is an environmental risk factor for externalizing but not internalizing disorders [ 27 ].

A common approach of adjusting for unobserved confounding is also a sibling fixed effects design, which accounts for an average of 50% of co-segregating genes and the environment shared by the siblings [ 31 ]. Several studies have used this approach to study childhood household dysfunction and showed that the associations between the exposures and outcomes largely attenuate in sibling comparisons [ 32–34 ]. Similar findings have been reported in studies using sibling comparisons to study child maltreatment [ 25 ] and adverse childhood experiences, a combination of maltreatment and household dysfunction [ 35–37 ].

However, a key caveat of the sibling fixed effects design is that the estimates are based only on information from siblings who are differentially exposed to the indicator of interest [ 31 ], but many of the childhood household dysfunction indicators are typically shared between siblings, especially if they are measured as ever experienced during childhood. A workaround for this problem is to compare outcomes between discordantly exposed cousins. This design accounts for 12.5% of the co-segregating genes of the cousins and, in addition, for those environmental factors that are shared by the cousins [ 38 , 39 ]. Cousin comparisons have not been widely used to study the outcomes of multiple household dysfunction indicators, except for three Swedish studies, which showed that the population-level estimates of the associations between household dysfunction and neurodevelopmental disorders [ 32 ], substance use [ 34 ], and drug use [ 40 ] attenuate between 20% and 30% [ 32 , 34 ] or more [ 40 ] in cousin comparisons.

In this study, we use cousin comparisons to assess unobserved confounding in the associations between childhood household dysfunction and multiple outcomes in emerging adulthood. Based on previous research on childhood adversities [ 1–3 , 11 ] and data availability, we included parental psychiatric and substance-attributable hospitalizations, death, prison sentence, union dissolution, and social assistance as household dysfunction indicators. We assess six outcomes in emerging adulthood, which we expect to be associated with household dysfunction based on previous research [ 1 , 8 , 10 ]: hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders and substance use, psychotropic medication, not being in education, employment or training (NEET), and violent and property crime arrests. We assess the associations between single household dysfunction indicators and the outcomes since the amount of unobserved confounding may differ by specific exposure-outcome constellations [ 22 ]. We expect there to be unobserved familial confounding in all the associations, but more in the associations between similar parental and offspring variables. We also study the well-known dose–response relationship between the parental indicators and the outcomes. Given the accumulation of multiple exposures with intergenerational associations, we expect to find more unobserved confounding in the associations between multiple indicators of household dysfunction and the outcomes than between single exposures and the outcomes.
The study is based on register data on all individuals born in Finland in 1987–2000 and residing in Finland at age 14 ( n = 854 082). We excluded those without full observations between ages 0–14 ( n = 9049) and those without information on biological parents at birth ( n = 9046). The final analytical sample size was 835 987. To identify cousins, we included the first-born children of each mother in the data, and defined cousins as sharing the same maternal grandparents but having a different mother. In total, we identified 87 500 first-born full cousins, nested within 40 898 maternal grandparents.

For all the parents and their children, annual information on sociodemographic variables, mortality, police-reported crime, and criminal convictions was obtained from Statistics Finland. These data were linked with inpatient hospital episodes and specialized outpatient visits from the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare and psychotropic medication purchases from the Social Insurance Institution of Finland.
### Household dysfunction

We included parental substance-attributable and psychiatric inpatient episodes, death of either parent, unconditional prison sentences, union dissolutions, and social assistance (a means-tested last-resort financial assistance) as indicators of household dysfunction. All indicators were measured as ever experienced between ages 0–14, using data from both biological mothers and fathers. Detailed descriptions of the data sources and definitions are available in Supplementary Table S1 .

### Outcomes

Hospital-presenting substance use and psychiatric disorders, violent and property crime arrests, psychotropic medication purchases, and being NEET for at least 2 consecutive years were considered as outcomes in emerging adulthood ( Supplementary Table S2 ). We followed the study participants for these outcomes from 1st January of the year they turned 15 years old until the date of the outcome, death, or emigration or the end of 2020 (2019 for medication purchases), when the participants were aged 20 to 33. For NEET, exact months and days of the event were unavailable; therefore, we used the last day of the first NEET year of the 2-year NEET period as the event date. We had labour market data until 2019, but since we defined NEET as consisting of at least 2 consecutive NEET years, we ended the follow-up for this outcome in 2018 as no one could become NEET in 2019 with this definition.

### Observed confounders

Statistics Finland’s data on parental education, region of residence, birth order, maternal age at birth, sex, and an indicator for two-parent family were included as observed confounders ( Supplementary Table S3 ). These variables were measured at age 0.

### Modelling approach

We used Cox regression to examine the associations between each indicator of childhood household dysfunction and each outcome. For every association, we fitted a crude model, and a model adjusted for observed confounders using the population-level data. Cluster-robust standard errors were used to account for correlation between full siblings.

We then used the data on the 87 500 first-born full cousins and conducted cousin comparisons with stratified Cox models. The cousins within each grandparent dyad shared the same baseline hazard and were compared to each other only. The estimated associations were mostly derived from discordantly exposed cousins and thus the number of informative strata differs by exposure. The cousin comparisons were adjusted for all observed confounders except birth order, which did not vary between the cousins.

We assessed the accumulation of the household dysfunction indicators by summing up all the binary indicators, with a cut-off at four. The sum score was used as a categorical covariate in the confounder-adjusted models, both in total population and in the cousin comparison framework. All the analyses were conducted with Stata 17.

To assess whether our results are driven by prevalent outcomes, we repeated our main analyses by excluding individuals whose first outcome occurred before the start of follow-up (age 15). We also examined the co-occurrence of the household dysfunction indicators by calculating a tetrachoric correlation matrix of the variables, and then by conducting an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on this matrix.
### Descriptive characteristics

Parental union dissolution and social assistance were the most common indicators of household dysfunction ( Table 1 ). Of the outcomes, psychotropic medication purchases were the most common (26%), followed by 2-year NEET (23%) and hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders (17%) ( Supplementary Table S4 ). All outcomes were more common among those exposed to household dysfunction ( Table 1 , Supplementary Table S4 ). Outcome rates and proportions by confounders are presented in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 . The descriptive characteristics were similar in the cousin population ( Supplementary Tables S7–S10 ), except that the mothers were younger due to the inclusion of only first-borns.

Both the exposures and outcomes had overlaps ( Figs 1 and 2 ). Forty-seven percent of individuals experiencing any of the household dysfunction indicators had at least two, and 49% of those with any of the outcomes had at least two. The most common co-occurring household dysfunction indicators were social assistance and union dissolution ( Fig. 1 ), and the most common co-occurring outcomes were psychotropic medication purchases, NEET, and hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders ( Fig. 2 ).

### Single indicators of household dysfunction

Parental psychiatric hospitalization was associated with increased hazards of all the outcomes in the population-level models, with hazard ratios (HRs) ranging between 1.4 and 1.9 ( Table 2 , P -values in Supplementary Table S11 ). The covariate-adjusted associations were attenuated by 6%–15% (on average 9%) in the cousin comparison. The largest attenuation was observed for crime-related outcomes and psychotropic medication ( Table 2 , Supplementary Table S12 ). The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from the cousin comparison overlapped with the intervals from population-level covariate-adjusted models for all outcomes, except psychotropic medication purchases.

The HRs varied between 1.5 and 2.2 in the population-level covariate-adjusted models ( Table 1 ). The estimates were attenuated by 4%–21% (on average 11%) in the cousin comparison, the most for offspring property crime arrest ( Table 2 , Supplementary Table S12 ). This association was the only one where the CIs of the HRs from the cousin comparisons did not overlap with the population level CIs.

The HRs ranged between 1.3 and 1.7 in the covariate-adjusted population models ( Table 2 ). In the cousin comparison, the effect sizes were of similar magnitude for most of the outcomes ( Table 2 ). The largest attenuation (19%) was observed for hospital-presenting substance use ( Supplementary Table S12 ). The CIs between the cousin comparison and the covariate-adjusted population model overlapped in all the associations.

In the population-level adjusted model, the HRs ranged between 1.6 and 2.5 ( Table 2 ). In cousin comparisons, the hazards were attenuated by 1%–39%, on average 22%. The largest attenuations were observed for offspring substance use and crime-related outcomes, followed by psychotropic medication purchases. In these associations, there was no overlap in CIs between the population-level model and the cousin comparison. In general, both the effect sizes and attenuation after adjustment for unobserved confounding were the largest for this exposure.

This exposure was associated with 40%–85% increased risk of the outcomes in the adjusted population-level model. These estimates were attenuated by 6%–21% (on average 13%) in the cousin comparisons, most for hospital-presenting substance use and property crime. The 95% CIs from population-level model and cousin comparisons only overlapped in the association between the exposure and offspring hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders.

The HRs for social assistance ranged between 1.6 and 2.1 in the covariate-adjusted models. These estimates were attenuated by 9%–22% (on average 14%) in the cousin comparison, the most for offspring property crime. The 95% CIs from population-level model and cousin comparisons only overlapped in the association between social assistance and offspring hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders.

### Accumulation of household dysfunction

A gradient between the number of household dysfunction indicators and the hazards for all outcomes was observed at the population level and in the cousin comparisons ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S13 ). The distributions of specific indicators across the sum score categories are presented in Supplementary Fig. S1 . The associations between one, two, three, and four or more household dysfunction indicators and the outcomes were on average 8% (range 4%–17%), 14% (4%–25%), 20% (11%–34%), and 18% (1%–34%) smaller in the cousin comparisons than in the population-level models, respectively ( Supplementary Table S13 ). The largest attenuations were observed for offspring property crime arrest, followed by violent crime arrests and hospital-presenting substance use. In around half of the comparisons, the CIs from cousin comparisons and population-level models overlapped.

### Additional analyses

Excluding the individuals with outcomes before the start of follow-up did not have a major impact on the results ( Supplementary Table S14 and Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 ). The factor analysis of the household dysfunction indicators ( Supplementary Tables S15 and S16 ) pointed towards the exposures belonging to one general adversity domain, but with parental death and to some extent union dissolution as outliers.
discussion:
In this study, we demonstrated the well-known associations between multiple indicators of childhood household dysfunction and multiple outcomes in emerging adulthood, and the dose–response relationship between the exposures and the outcomes [ 1–11 ]. Our approach allowed us to compare the magnitude of these different association in a well-characterized data with consistent measurement and no loss to follow-up over time. We also extended previous research by using cousin comparisons to assess unobserved confounding in these associations, an approach seldom used in previous research on childhood household dysfunction (for exceptions, see Refs. [ 32 , 34 , 40–42 ])

Based on previous studies [ 22 , 30 , 32 , 34 ], we expected to observe familial confounding in all the associations, and, indeed, in nearly all the exposure-outcome associations, the estimate from the cousin comparison was lower than the estimate from the population-level model. On average, the estimates attenuated by about 12%, but the range of attenuation was wide, from null to 39%. In over half of the associations, the CIs from the population-level model and cousin comparison overlapped, indicating uncertainty in the difference between the estimates. This might partly relate to the loss of statistical power in the cousin comparisons as the overlap occurred less frequently with the most common household dysfunction indicators (social assistance and union dissolution).

Due to the intergenerational components of the exposures, we expected to find more familial confounding in the associations between similar parental and offspring variables than in the other exposure-outcome associations. Such a pattern did not clearly emerge from the data. Regarding the dose–response relationship, we expected to find more familial confounding in the associations between higher number of exposures and the outcomes, which was confirmed.

Across the single exposures and the sum score of the exposures, the largest attenuations between the population-level model and the cousin comparison were observed in the associations between the exposures and offspring violent crime, property crime and hospital-presenting substance use, which might relate to higher degree of heritability and genetic correlation between these outcomes [ 14 , 43 , 44 ]. The larger amount of unobserved familial confounding also led to less of an overlap between the CIs from the population-level models and the cousin comparisons. The difference between the population-level model and the cousin comparison was especially clear for property crime.

Of the specific exposures, the associations between parental prison sentence and the outcomes seemed to exhibit a larger amount of familial confounding, which is likely related to the very high prevalence of different psychiatric, personality, and substance use disorders as well as socioeconomic disadvantage among Finnish prisoners [ 45 , 46 ]. Parental death seemed to differ from the other household dysfunction indicators, which was also observed in the factor analysis: the estimates from cousin comparisons were very close to estimates from population-level models for all outcomes, except offspring substance use.

### Methodological considerations

Although the cousin comparison addresses some of the problems of concordant exposures within nuclear families, it only accounts for approximately 12.5% of co-segregating genes and those environmental factors that are shared on the extended family level. Therefore, both genetic and social confounding in these associations is likely to remain. Second, we did not assess the shares of confounding attributable to environmental or genetic factors, which would require extending the cousin comparison to a children-of-siblings or children-of-twins [ 27–29 ] design. Third, due to the non-collapsibility of HRs [ 47 ] and inflation of measurement error in family-based designs [ 48 ], part of the attenuation observed between different models might be artificial. Fourth, register data only include relatively severe exposures and outcomes, and our results might not extend to associations between less severe exposures and outcomes. On the other hand, our results are based on objectively assessed conditions with long-term follow-up, little attrition, and no response biases.

Our observations highlight the need for prevention and intervention programmes at different societal levels. Since some of the associations between specific indicators and the outcomes were less confounded, preventing these experiences might decrease the risk of adverse outcomes at the population level [ 22 ]. Second, since most of the associations seemed to exhibit some level of unobserved confounding, and since some of the experiences might be hard to prevent, targeted support for children exposed to household dysfunction in early life are also needed to mitigate the negative consequences of these experiences [ 49 ]. Potential opportunities for evaluation and intervention may present themselves when parents are in contact with healthcare or other authorities, such as social services or the judicial system, but also in more routine settings, such as primary care [ 50 ]. Due to the broad range of both the exposures and outcomes, it seems evident that multidisciplinary intervention efforts are required.
target: Childhood household dysfunction is a well-known risk factor for adverse medical and social outcomes. However, less is known about the extent to which such associations are affected by unmeasured familial confounding.This cohort study is based on Finnish register data on birth cohorts 1987–2000 ( n = 835 987). We considered parental hospital-presenting substance use and psychiatric disorders, prison sentences, death, means-tested social assistance, and union dissolution at ages 0–14 as indicators of childhood household dysfunction. The study participants were followed from age 15 until the end of 2020 for hospital-presenting psychiatric disorders and substance use, psychotropic medication purchases, violent and property crime arrests, and not being in education, employment, or training. The associations were estimated using Cox regression, and cousin comparisons were used to account for unmeasured confounders shared within extended families ( n = 87 500).All the exposures were associated with the outcomes in the population-level models, with hazard ratios ranging from 1.3 (95% confidence interval 1.3–1.4) to 2.5 (2.4–2.6). The associations attenuated in the cousin comparisons, on average 12% but with a wide range from −2% to 39% [hazard ratios ranging from 1.2 (1.1–1.4) to 1.9 (1.6–2.3)]. A dose–response relationship between the exposures and the outcomes was observed in the population-level models and the cousin comparisons, with attenuated associations in the latter.Our findings show systematic associations between childhood household dysfunction and subsequent outcomes. Unobserved confounding likely creates upward bias in these associations, but the extent of this confounding depends on the specific exposure-outcome pairs.

Gastric cancer (GC) remains one of the most common cancers worldwide [ 1 ]. Evidence increasingly indicates the effectiveness of endoscopic screening in reducing GC mortality [ 2–4 ]. Since 2002, South Korea has implemented nationwide GC screening for individuals aged 40 and older, and both individual-level and population-level studies have indicated that this program reduced GC mortality [ 3 , 5 ]. As encouraging evidence accumulates, an increasing number of countries are considering implementing organized GC screening programs to reduce GC burden [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. Yet, one critical aspect of GC screening’s effect remains unresolved.

In addition to lowering mortality, GC screening is anticipated to prevent new cases by detecting and treating precancerous lesions [ 8 ]. However, the effect on GC incidence remains unclear, with conflicting findings from a limited number of individual-level studies [ 8–10 ]. South Korea’s pioneering screening program offers an opportunity for population-level analysis. Data from South Korea show that the age-standardized incidence of GC initially remained stable and later slightly declined during the screening period [ 11 ]. But disentangling the true effect of the screening program from other confounding factors and secular trends, especially given that national cancer data only began in 1999 [ 12 ], presents a significant challenge.

This study bypasses that limitation by using a quasi-experimental design and nearly three decades of high-quality data from the Seoul Cancer Registry (established in the early 1990s) to evaluate the impact of the screening program on GC incidence. By analyzing real-world data in complex settings, this study provides actionable insights for policymakers.
### Research setting

In 1999, the Korean government launched a screening program for GC targeting low-income Medical Aid recipients. In 2002, the Korean National Cancer Screening Program (KNCSP) was expanded nationwide to include the National Health Insurance beneficiaries, resulting in almost universal coverage for all Korean citizens [ 5 ]. The KNCSP offers biennial screening for individuals aged 40 years and older, with a choice of upper gastrointestinal (UGI) series or endoscopy [ 13 ]. Two key trends have occurred since its implementation. First, national surveys indicate that the screening participation rate rose from 39.2% in 2004 to 77.5% in 2023 [ 14 ]. Second, the screening modality used has shifted dramatically. Among all screenings performed, the proportions conducted by endoscopy increased from 31.15% in 2002 to 72.55% in 2011 [ 13 ]. By 2019, nearly 90% of GC screenings were performed using endoscopy [ 15 ]. Details on the GC screening program are described in the Supplementary Methods .

### Study design

We used the synthetic control method (SCM) [ 16 ] to construct a synthetic control for Seoul by deriving a weighted average of multiple control registries without intervention. Weights were determined through a data-driven approach that minimized differences in age-standardized GC incidence between Seoul and the synthetic control prior to screening implementation. The SCM assumes that if the treated registry and constructed control registry have similar long-term GC incidence trajectories, they are likely influenced by similar driving factors and should continue to follow similar trends unless disrupted by an intervention, such as the start of screening in Seoul. Thus, any observed differences after the implementation start can be reasonably ascribed to the intervention.

This study was exempt from ethical review because it only used aggregated data.

### Outcome data

The primary outcome measure was age-standardized GC (International Classification of Diseases code: C16.0-C16.9) incidence among people aged 40 years or above. We obtained annual age-specific GC incidence rates for Seoul from the Seoul Cancer Registry (1993–2020), which covers 18% of South Korea’s total population. Control registry data were extracted from the Cancer Incidence in Five Continents (CI5) Plus database [ 17 ]. The CI5 plus database provides updated annual incidence rates from high-quality cancer registries. The primary quality indicators CI5 uses are the percentage of microscopic verification (MV%) and the percentage of cases registered by death certificate only (DCO%), where higher MV% and lower DCO% indicate better quality. The data were last updated in November 2024 and include records up to 2017. Age-standardized rates were calculated using the World Health Organization standard population age structure [ 18 ]. The main SCM analysis covered 1993–2017, while alternative analyses with only Seoul’s data extended to 2020, depending on data availability.

### Control registry selection

Control registries without organized GC screening programs were included in the donor pool based on the following criteria: (i) having GC incidence data for each year during the study period; (ii) being a single, primary registry. To prevent double-counting, we excluded combined registries [like “Thailand (four registries)”] or sub-registries (like “USA, California, Los Angeles: White”) when their individual or parent-level registries were available; (iii) reporting over 100 GC cases in 1993; (iv) having complete report of age-group specific population numbers. Supplementary Fig. S1 shows the selection procedure for the donor pools. Following these criteria, 30 registries met these criteria, and final control weights were assigned using data-driven processes as described in the statistical analysis section.

### Statistical analysis

The original SCM proposed by Abadie and Gardeazabal [ 19 ] in 2003 is designed to interpolate the outcomes of control units to prevent irrational counterfactuals. A requirement of this approach is the “convex hull” criterion, meaning the outcome of the treated units must remain inside the distribution of the control data. South Korea, however, has one of the highest rates of GC incidence in the world [ 20 ], which is insufficient to fulfill the convex hull condition [ 21 ]. Therefore, we applied the flexible SCM approach developed by Bonander [ 16 ], which relaxes the requirement for control weights to sum to one while imposing a penalty on extrapolation to avoid unrealistic estimates. Details on the construction of the synthetic control are in the Supplementary Methods .

We assessed pre-treatment fit by plotting the difference in GC incidence between Seoul and the synthetic control for all pre-treatment years. We calculated average post-intervention rate ratios (RRs) and their associated 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The average RR during the post-intervention period was estimated by dividing the treated unit’s average outcome values by the synthetic control’s average GC incidence for the same period. A three-fold cross-fitting method was applied to produce the final debiased estimate and its 95% CIs [ 16 ]. We also calculated the rate difference and RRs in each year during the post-intervention period. To assess whether the observed effects for Seoul could occur by chance, a placebo test was conducted by repeating the SCM for each control registry as if it were the intervention unit [ 3 ]. We then plotted the differences between observed and counterfactual trends for each control registry and Seoul to observe whether the effect for Seoul became distinct after the screening, suggesting it was unlikely due to randomness.

Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of our findings. First, we performed the negative control outcome analysis by repeating the SCM among people aged 35–39, who did not undergo screening. If a difference in post-intervention trend is also observed for this population ineligible for screening, the observed effect in the main analyses may be due to other factors than screening. Second, we conducted the leave-one-out examination for each weighted control unit to test the influence of each single control registry’s weight. Third, the pre-intervention period was refined from 1993–2001 to 1993–98 to mitigate overfitting risks. The fit between Seoul and the synthetic control during the validation period (1999–2001) was assessed. A good fit during this period would confirm the SCM’s predictive validity for Seoul in the absence of the GC screening program.

We also employed various alternative methods. First, we borrowed the idea of the difference-in-differences (DID) analysis to account for background secular trends in incidence. This analysis compared the change in log age-standardized GC incidence between the pre- and post-intervention periods for the screening target population against the corresponding change observed in a non-eligible control population (aged 20–39). The resulting estimate (β), which is on the log scale, was converted to a relative percentage change for interpretation using the standard transformation ( e β - 1 ) * 100 % ⁠ . Second, following the method by Gangnon et al. [ 22 ] we conducted a modified age-period-cohort (APC) analysis [ 22 ] to evaluate screening’s impact on GC incidence by including a screening period function. The population and GC case data from the Seoul Cancer Registry were used to fit the negative binomial log-linear regression. The screening function allowed us to estimate the effect of screening on GC incidence. We also estimated the GC incidence without screening, which was derived as the sum of the age, period, and cohort effects. Details on the two alternative methods are in the Supplementary Methods . Data analyses were performed using R version 4.3.2.
The synthetic control was made up of 19 control registries, with Belarus emerging as the primary contributor ( Supplementary Table S1 ). The pre-intervention fit between Seoul and the synthetic control was good, showing similar decreasing trends in both ( Fig. 1 ). Following the initiation of the screening program, GC incidence in Seoul remained relatively stable compared to the decreasing trend in the synthetic control, showing a relatively higher rate with an average post-intervention RR being 1.11 (95% CI: 0.99–1.24). Notably, the magnitude of this difference was not static; it peaked in 2011 (at a relative 26%) and subsequently decreased ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S2 ). During the pre-intervention period, the disparities between the synthetic control and Seoul were relatively minor compared to post-implementation differences ( Fig. 1A ). The post-intervention differences between the synthetic control and Seoul became markedly pronounced after 2005, as evident from the placebo tests ( Fig. 1B ).

Sensitivity analyses consistently demonstrated the robustness of our findings. Negative control outcome analysis showed no post-intervention differences in GC incidence in 35–39-year-olds who did not undergo screening ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). This suggests that factors other than GC screening remained relatively stable and did not alter GC incidence. Excluding each weighted control registry had minimal impact on the base case analyses, and also when excluding the primary contributor, Belarus ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). To validate the SCM’s ability to model Seoul’s underlying GC trend, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by restricting the pre-intervention period to 1993–1998. The resulting synthetic control accurately tracked Seoul’s actual declining incidence during this 1999–2001 validation period ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ). Furthermore, post-intervention differences between 2002 and 2017 resembled the main results, further corroborating the validity of our findings.

The naive DID analysis compared the change in GC incidence from the pre- to post-intervention period between the screening population and the population aged 20–39 years. This analysis showed that the implementation of screening was associated with a 9.4% relative increase in GC incidence in the screening group, after accounting for the underlying trend observed in the population aged 20–39 years ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ). Additionally, the effect trend indicated by the modified APC analysis aligned with the SCM results. The effect expanded over time, peaking at an RR of 1.14 (95% CI 1.03–1.28) between 2008 and 2012, but subsequently declined, showing a negative effect of 0.89 (95% CI 0.71–1.11) between 2018 and 2020 ( Fig. 2A ). Correspondingly, the observed GC incidence after screening was initially relatively higher but decreased from 2018 to 2020 compared to the estimated rate without screening ( Fig. 2B ).
discussion:
Using population-based cancer registry data and a quasi-experimental design, our SCM analysis found that Seoul’s screening program initially increased GC incidence compared to the synthetic control, peaking at a 26% difference in the tenth year. In the final years of the SCM analysis, this gap began to narrow. These findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. The trend was also consistent with our alternative APC model, which used an extended dataset for Seoul. The APC analysis suggested the narrowing trend continued and reversed into a reduction by the fifteenth year.

Researchers have long focused on the impact of GC screening on GC mortality [ 2–4 ], leading to a growing consensus regarding its beneficial effect in reducing mortality rates [ 6 , 7 ]. However, the effect of screening on GC incidence has received limited attention [ 9 ], despite its importance in providing a complete picture of the benefits and potential harms associated with screening programs. Insights from other cancer screenings, which have been more thoroughly investigated, underscores the importance of examining incidence separately, even when the benefit on mortality is well-established. For instance, colorectal cancer (CRC) screening has demonstrated a reduction effect on cancer incidence by the removal of precancerous lesions [ 23 ]. Conversely, breast cancer screening has been associated with increased cancer incidence due to overdiagnosis, which can lead to unnecessary medical interventions and psychological stress for patients. It should be noted that overdiagnosis still exists in CRC screening, despite its proven net reduction in CRC incidence [ 24 ]. These findings suggest that the impact of cancer screening on incidence is complex and can be distinct from its effect on mortality.

Published individual-level analyses regarding the effect of endoscopic screening on GC incidence showed mixed results [ 8–10 ]. A meta-analysis that included only four studies did not find the association between endoscopic screening and GC incidence [ 9 ]. However, two cohort studies conducted in high-GC-incidence regions of China observed that endoscopic screening reduced non-cardia GC incidence, but not cardia GC incidence, in the screened group compared to the unscreened group, after adjusting for age and sex [ 8 , 10 ].

Several factors may contribute to uncertainty and pose research challenges. First, screening initially inflates incidence rates by detecting prevalent disease, requiring a long-term follow-up to ascertain the ultimate effect. Second, endoscopic screening may allow for endoscopic resection of visible dysplasia, potentially reducing GC incidence. Endoscopic screening can also facilitate the detection and treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection, thereby preventing GC incidence. However, unlike CRC screening, where even low-risk polyps can be removed during colonoscopy, few treatments are available for atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia during GC screening. Subsequent surveillance and treatment may be necessary, and even after curative removal of gastric dysplasia, there is a risk of metachronous gastric carcinoma.

The impact of a screening program on GC incidence, as assessed in this study, shows an even more complex dynamic when examining cross-sectional rates from a population perspective compared to cumulative incidence rates from a single cohort perspective. An initial rise in incidence is expected due to detecting asymptomatic GCs. The growing participation rates in the Korean GC screening program may further amplify and prolong this relative increase [ 14 ]. Additionally, the proportion of screenings conducted by endoscopy, known for its higher sensitivity compared to UGI series, has steadily increased [ 13 , 25 ]. Supporting these trends, the percentage of early-stage GC grew from 39% in 2001 to 73% in 2016 [ 26 ], suggesting that the increase in incidence is primarily attributable to early-stage GC detection. However, the potential for overdiagnosis in GC screening also warrants consideration [ 27 ]. Overdiagnosis in GC screening has rarely been investigated [ 27 ] and cannot be excluded as a possibility.

We also observed a diminishing relative increase of GC incidence after 2011, followed by a subsequent reduction effect. This pattern may suggest a compensatory drop following early detection or a potential preventive effect of screening. Given that our population is dynamic rather than fixed, and our outcome measures annual population incidence rates rather than cumulative incidence, we cannot discern these potential screening effects on GC incidence, as well as inferring which one dominates. The ultimate impact of screening on GC incidence remains uncertain, and randomized controlled trials are needed for conclusive determination.

A key strength of this study is its population-level evaluation of GC screening, which facilitates evidence triangulation. We confirmed the robustness of our primary SCM by extensively validating its predictive fit against observed GC trends using both a hold-out validation period ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ) and a negative control population ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). We further employed methodological triangulation with APC and DID analyses. While these alternative models have more significant limitations than SCM in our case, particularly the naive DID, they corroborated the SCM’s findings and allowed us to analyze recent data from 2018 to 2020 that the SCM could not.

Our study has several limitations. First, the basic idea behind SCM is that once the synthetic control reproduces the treated unit’s pre-intervention outcome trajectory, it implicitly adjusts for all observed and unobserved factors influencing the outcome. As a result, adding explicit covariates is optional, because the synthetic control is already, by construction, comparable to the treated unit. Still, incorporating covariates can further strengthen the analysis [ 28 ]. In our study, we did not include covariates such as Helicobacter pylori infection rate due to limited data availability. Second, the increase in opportunistic GC screening in South Korea over time [ 29 ] might lead to an overestimated direct effect of the organized screening program on GC incidence. However, the start of the organized screening program might have had an indirect effect of improving coverage and quality of opportunistic screening. Third, we cannot discern the specific contributions of screening by UGI series or endoscopy to the observed effects. While UGI series was the main modality in the program’s early years, it was soon replaced by the more sensitive endoscopy.

As more countries consider organized GC screening or surveillance [ 4 , 6 , 7 ], South Korea’s GC screening program offers practical insights, but its generalizability requires caution. Endoscopy capacity is central to the screening and diagnosis of GC. In South Korea, the number of endoscopic examinations for GC increased 20-fold in the decade following the program’s start [ 30 ]. Such an increase will lead to substantial costs and infrastructure hurdles for countries with limited endoscopic infrastructure or gastroenterologists. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an immediate surge in GC diagnoses following a screening program, which will significantly burden treatment services. This necessitates a prompt healthcare system response, likely increasing demand for endoscopic submucosal dissection, which requires investment in training and infrastructure [ 31 ]. Finally, programs must address potential inequities in access to screening, diagnosis, and treatment to ensure effectiveness and avoid worsening health disparities [ 32 ].
This study found a higher GC incidence in Seoul, South Korea, after the organized GC screening program compared to the synthetic control. The magnitude of the difference expanded and peaked in the tenth year after the program’s start, then began to narrow. The alternative APC analysis indicated that the increase might finally reverse into a reduction effect. Healthcare sectors should anticipate an immediate increase in care demands following GC screening implementation. Future studies that comprehensively evaluate GC screening, reporting both mortality and incidence outcomes, are needed to assess the overall effectiveness and to investigate the potential for overdiagnosis, which remains an understudied possibility in GC screening.
target: Evidence of gastric cancer (GC) screening’s impact on GC incidence remains limited. In 2002, South Korea started a nationwide GC screening program. This study uses a quasi-experimental design to evaluate the effect of the program on GC incidence in Seoul.Using a flexible synthetic control method (SCM), we estimated the impact of GC screening on age-standardized GC incidence in Seoul. Annual age-specific GC incidence data were obtained from the Seoul Cancer Registry and Cancer Incidence in Five Continents Plus database. Post-intervention trends in GC incidence between Seoul and the synthetic control were compared to estimate average rate ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Several sensitivity and alternative analyses were performed, including a modified age-period-cohort (APC) analysis.The screening program was associated with a higher GC incidence in Seoul compared to the synthetic control, with an average post-intervention RR of 1.11 (95% CI: 0.99–1.24). After 2002, the start of the screening program, there was a noticeable increase in the post-intervention differences between Seoul and the synthetic control, which peaked in 2011 (RR 1.26), and then began to fall. The results were robust across sensitivity analyses and alternative analyses. The modified APC analysis indicated that after initially expanding and then diminishing, the effect eventually reversed, resulting in a reduction in incidence.These findings suggest that healthcare sectors should anticipate an immediate increase in care demands following GC screening implementation. While a subsequent reduction in GC incidence is expected, the potential preventive impact remains inconclusive.
