In 2022, 22 million children missed their first dose of the measles vaccine compared to 19 million who had missed the same vaccine in 2019 [ 1 ]. Besides the recent COVID-19 pandemic [ 2 ], notable factors contributing to delayed vaccination uptake included parental lack of information, difficult access to health facilities, lack of finance and parental support, and distrust in vaccines and vaccination programs [ 3 ]; health worker scarcity and inadequacies along the vaccine cold chain and vaccine supply affect vaccine coverage [ 3 ]; and, poor coverage rates for birth dose vaccines in the immediate postnatal period, with the pooled coverage rates for Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) being at 14.2% within 0–1 days following birth and a 1.3% pooled coverage rate for birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine [ 4 ]. A study in informal urban settlements in Nairobi, Kenya revealed a 67% full vaccination coverage by one year, a higher number of missed opportunities, and low coverage of routine childhood vaccination, primarily given at later ages [ 5 ]. In these settlements, 22% of fully immunized children received their vaccines out-of-sequence (receiving BCG, measles, pentavalent, and polio doses outside the recommended schedule) and 18% did not receive the pentavalent with polio vaccine, contrary to existing recommendations [ 5 ].

Untimely birth dose vaccine administration means the newborns remain unprotected from vaccine-preventable diseases in the period when they are most vulnerable to morbidity and mortality, requiring interventions to address this problem. Text message reminders might improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration as they keep individuals aware of vaccination schedules. Text message reminders are known to improve the completeness and timeliness of childhood immunizations in a cluster randomized trial at four primary healthcare facilities in Nigeria [ 6 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 131 studies found text message reminders increased antenatal care clinic attendance and timeliness of child immunization [ 7 ]. However, the current evidence comes from stable populations—populations without several of the additional barriers like low health service coverage and poor uptake of health services experienced by informal urban settlements. Therefore, there is uncertainty around the effectiveness of text message reminders in improving immunization uptake in an urban informal settlement as the populations are mobile. Mobile populations are at risk for untimely and incomplete vaccination as the majority are less familiar with health services, more likely to have insufficient resources to reach health facilities, and less likely to use the same health facility regularly among other plausible reasons. In-person reminders through lay community health workers (CHWs) are unlikely to reach most of the caregivers as they frequently change locations and are unavailable during routine work hours.

Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home. We leveraged the widespread use of mobile phones and text reminders as a low-cost intervention to nudge parents toward timely vaccinations, ultimately increasing immunization rates.

Accordingly, we evaluated the effectiveness of text message reminders in improving the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration (oral polio vaccine [OPV] 0 and BCG given at birth or within 2 weeks of birth) among newborns in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County, Kenya.
### Study design and setting

We conducted an open-label, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized pilot trial between December 2019 and April 2020 in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County in Kenya [ 8 ]. Viwandani is included in the Nairobi Urban Health and Demographic Surveillance System site [ 8 ]. The rationale for the trial design was based on the potential benefits of the intervention in improving the uptake of birth dose vaccines so withholding it from certain participants would be unethical, unacceptable, logistical inefficient, and inequitable. The trial site has a total population of 49 000 people, an annual birth rate of 16 per 1000 population, an infant mortality rate of 34.7 deaths per 1000 live births, and timely vaccination coverage of 22% [ 5 ]. Viwandani is composed of a mobile population [ 9 , 10 ], served by private health facilities and two public health facilities that provide free routine immunization services although both are located outside the area [ 5 ] and characterized by poor uptake of and access to health services, especially vaccination [ 11 , 12 ]. For this study, we considered eight villages that were divided into three blocks, with the first and second blocks having three villages each and the third block having two villages. This trial was not registered as it was a pilot.

### Participants, recruitment, and procedure

The study enrolled pregnant women residing in Viwandani who were in their second or third trimester. The participants were eligible if they met the following criteria; a pregnant woman owned a mobile phone and had no plans to relocate from the study village within six months of enrollment, and were willing to be enrolled and followed until two months after giving birth. The exclusion criteria were: pregnant women who had documented complications of pregnancy as assessed by health workers, women who planned to vaccinate their baby outside the Viwandani clinics, those who experienced adverse pregnancy outcomes during follow-up such as abortion, stillbirth, or early neonatal death, or those diagnosed with multiple pregnancies. Participant recruitment was conducted by lay CHWs targeting all pregnant mothers in their second or third trimester in the eight villages in Viwandani until the required sample size of mother–baby pairs was reached.

Enrolment into the intervention group was conducted sequentially through a public lottery randomization approach, two months apart, starting with block one (three villages), then block two (three villages), and lastly block three (two villages). Village assignment to any of the three blocks was done at random. The names of the blocks (cluster) were written on a piece of paper, sealed in an opaque envelope, placed in an opaque box, and thoroughly mixed. A village representative randomly selected an opaque sealed envelope without replacement, opened it, and revealed the assignment block for the village to the public. The blocks were thereafter randomly assigned to the intervention initiation time through a simple randomization approach. Here, the three blocks were randomly assigned to the intervention time using a computer-generated table of random numbers. By default, it was difficult to blind the study participants, investigators, and data collectors to the intervention so the trial was open-label.

### Baseline covariates

Trained lay CHWs used electronic/digitized forms installed on their mobile phones to collect data on the participant's background information, and data on the last menstrual period were abstracted from the antenatal care booklets upon obtaining informed consent. Mothers without ANC cards were asked to provide the data of their last normal menstruation period and if they did not know, they stated how many months their pregnancy had lasted and this was used to estimate their date of last menstrual period. The baseline data included socio-demographic variables such as maternal age, maternal level of education, marital status, household wealth tertiles (lowest, middle, and highest), and village name. Additional variables included calendar month and randomization block. Data on household characteristics including socio-economic status and childhood vaccinations were extracted from the Nairobi Urban Health Demographic Survey Surveillance database and then merged with the data collected through the digital platform using a unique household identification number.

### Intervention vs. control periods

The intervention was text message reminders provided to all participants in a phased manner, with the transition from the control period to the intervention period being every two months. In general, the intervention involved an interaction between lay CHWs, pregnant women, and healthcare workers using a mobile phone application linked to a central registry. Two lay CHWs selected from each village were trained to register all pregnant women in their second or third trimester using a mobile phone. The lay CHWs captured demographic variables of the pregnant women including age of gestation, expected date of birth, preferred health facility for delivery, and the village of residence at registration, and relayed the data to a central database. This triggered automated reminder messages to pregnant women through their mobile phones, lay CHWs, family members, or a friend about when the women were expected to deliver.

At delivery, lay CHWs documented the date of delivery of the child and submitted the data to the central database. The participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period. The first text message reminder was sent upon registration, the second was sent two weeks before the expected delivery date, and the last was sent on the expected date of delivery. At the vaccination point, the child's vaccination status was updated by lay CHWs or health workers, and the data were again relayed to the central server. Both lay CHWs and the health facilities received bi-monthly reports about newborns who were due for vaccination to appropriately plan for vaccination services.

During the control period, participants received the standard maternal, newborn, and child health care package provided by health workers. Among others, the routine antenatal care package comprised four visits, enabling pregnant women to receive health education on nutrition, vaccination, birth preparedness, and complication readiness; testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), syphilis, malaria, including blood grouping, and cross-matching; deworming using albendazole; access to ferrous sulfate and folic acid to prevent anemia; and malaria prophylaxis using sulphadoxine and pyrimethamine tablets. At birth, the babies are offered free vaccinations at the facility of delivery. Both private and public health facilities free vaccine from the government provided they are accredited as a vaccination center. In Viwandani several private facilities are not accredited to vaccinate babies but two public facilities and a few private ones offer vaccinations.

### Outcome

The primary outcome was the timely administration of birth dose vaccines, namely BCG and OPV. We created three binary indicators of whether a newborn received OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG.

Timely administration of birth dose vaccine was defined as receipt of the birth dose vaccines by the newborn at birth or within 2 weeks of delivery. The data were collected through cross-sectional surveys from a random sample of participants who received the text message intervention.

### Statistical methods

We hypothesized the intervention would improve the timely administration of birth dose vaccines from 22% under routine immunization [ 5 ] to 45%. Considering 0.04 intra-cluster correlation coefficient [ 13 ], a fixed cluster size of 12 children, and a 0.8 autocorrelation coefficient, a total of 479 mother–baby pairs were needed to achieve 80% statistical power at a 5% significance if the drop-out was 20% [ 14 ].

We summarized categorical data as frequencies and percentages, and numerical data as mean and standard deviation. We stratified baseline categorical data by the trial arm and performed Chi-squared tests to assess covariate balance. For numerical data, mean differences between the trial arms were tested using the Student’s t -test as the data were normally distributed. We applied the intention to treat analysis principle to compare the outcomes between the intervention and control periods. The trial outcome was binary but common (more than 10%) so the odds ratio would overestimate the intervention effect so the risk ratio is recommended [ 15 , 16 ]. We used a generalized linear mixed effects Poisson regression model with random intercepts, exchangeable correlation structure, and robust standard errors. Using random intercept accounted for between-cluster variability in the baseline outcome. We identified theoretically relevant baseline covariates a priori, including maternal age, maternal level of education, calendar time, and household wealth tertile. We adjusted for these covariates, clustering at the village level, and calendar time to control for temporal confounders.

We reported the findings as adjusted risk ratio (aRR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, United States) was used for sample size computation and data analysis.
### Participant characteristics

Table 1 presents the distribution of participant characteristics between the intervention and control periods. The participants were similar regarding age categories ( P = .560), level of education ( P = .210), and wealth tertile ( P = .620) but different regarding marital status ( P = .02).

### Participant recruitment per block and time

Table 2 shows the mother–baby pairs recruited in each block and at each time point between the intervention and control periods. Overall, 491 mother–baby pairs who had received the intervention at various time points and also had complete data were included, which is slightly higher than the computed sample size. The rationale for over-recruitment in certain blocks was to compensate for the lower numbers of mother–baby pairs in the other blocks and to maintain the statistical power.

### Distribution of outcomes between intervention and control periods

Differences in the timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration were observed for all the vaccines, whether separately or combined ( Table 3 ). During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG administration were 93%, 92.7%, and 92.1% compared to 80.9%, 81.6%, and 77.9% during the control period, respectively ( P < .001).

### Effect of the intervention on the timely administration of birth dose vaccines

Table 4 summarized the effectiveness of the intervention on the study outcomes. During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0 administration (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and OPV or BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43) tended to improve compared to the control period, adjusting for other factors.
Ethical review and approval were from the Amref Institutional Review Board (Amref ESRC P538/2018). We obtained additional permits and approvals from the National Research Commission and participating health facilities. All participants gave written informed consent before involvement in the study.
discussion:
Our trial showed a trend toward improved timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the intervention period compared to the control period. The intervention effect was relatively larger for both OPV and BCG (19%) than separately for OPV (16%) and BCG (14%). The improvement in the timely administration of birth dose vaccines has public health and clinical significance as it contributes to reducing childhood-preventable diseases, including morbidity and mortality. Our findings are consistent with previous studies that show text message reminders improve health outcomes and health services utilization [ 6 , 7 ]. Prior randomized trials also revealed that text message reminders are effective in improving the utilization of recommended first-year vaccinations [ 17 ], primary care attendance [ 18 ], and antenatal and postnatal visits and all recommended first-year vaccinations [ 17 ], including HIV testing and maternal retention in care during the first 8 weeks following delivery in Kenya [ 19 ].

Timely initiation of vaccination in the first year of life is crucial as transplacental immunity declines rapidly over time thereby posing a significant risk for neonatal morbidity and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases. Since vaccination coverage and timeliness are the two most important factors affecting population-level protection against preventable diseases, our findings illustrate that text message reminders could be an additional tool for improving vaccination coverage in an urban informal settlement in Kenya and similar settings.

The trend toward better timeliness in birth dose vaccines during the intervention period might be explained by the low intervention intensity as only three standardized text message reminders were sent to the participants and the shorter transition time between the intervention and control periods. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 88 randomized trials from 17 countries with nearly 1.7 million participants showed that incentives and increased access to immunization services are the most promising tools to improve vaccination uptake in low-income countries [ 20 ].

Therefore, our findings suggest text message reminders could be combined with incentives and/or approaches to increase access to vaccination services to improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccines. For example, text message reminders could be combined with improved routine immunization access, outreaches, or incentives. Future research should assess such intervention packages [ 20 ]. Lastly, the possibility of the John-Henry effect cannot be ignored—during the control period, the participants might have changed their behavior by working hard to compensate for not being offered the intervention hence impacting the intervention effect [ 21 ]. Interpretations of our findings should consider these issues, and the data should be considered preliminary for larger randomized trials.

Our trial has several strengths. The trial is among the first to demonstrate the use of text message reminders in improving the administration of birth dose vaccines in an urban informal settlement in Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa. We employed a rigorous trial design to demonstrate a cause–effect relationship. The pragmatic trial was conducted in a real-world setting as the usual service providers implemented the intervention. Therefore, scaling up the intervention would not pose a major challenge as contextual factors were not manipulated. However, there are limitations. First, we lack data on specific barriers and facilitators to intervention uptake. The data would have strengthened the findings including informing scalability. Second, the findings are limited to birth dose vaccines and might not apply to all childhood vaccines. Third, the findings are limited to a shorter intervention period so the long-term intervention effects remain unknown.

Fourth, the post-estimation intra-cluster correlation coefficient was very tiny, suggesting that the variation in outcomes within the clusters is relatively low compared to that between the individuals across the entire study population. This reduces the trial's statistical power in detecting the intervention effect when the clusters are taken into account, making it difficult to detect treatment effects at the cluster level. However, a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial was relevant for ethical and logistical reasons, including controlling for temporal/time trends or other external factors that might influence the outcome. Lastly, we do not have data on contamination so we could not estimate the per-protocol effects of the intervention.
In this pilot randomized trial, text message reminders improved the timely administration of birth dose vaccines among newborns in an informal urban settlement. These findings suggest that text message reminders might serve as an additional tool for improving the timeliness of administering vaccines and improving the performance of vaccination programs in an informal urban settlement.
target: We evaluated the effectiveness of text message reminders on the timely administration of birth dose vaccines among newborns in Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County, Kenya.In a pilot stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial, we sequentially randomized pregnant women to receive text message reminders or routine care. Three standardized text messages were sent notifying pregnant women to take their newborn for vaccination at birth during the intervention period. No text messages were sent during the control period but vaccinations were provided as standard practice in Kenya. The primary outcome was timely administration of birth dose vaccines—oral polio vaccine (OPV 0) and Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) administered at birth or within 2 weeks of birth.Among 491 newborns (355 intervention period versus 136 control period), timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the respective intervention and control periods were as follows: OPV 0 only (93.0% vs. 80.9%), BCG only (92.7% vs. 81.6%), and OPV 0 or BCG (92.1% vs. 77.9%). Timeliness of birth dose vaccine administration showed a borderline improvement in the intervention period than the control period: OPV 0 only (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG only (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and both OPV 0 and BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43).This trial showed that text message reminders can improve the timely administration of birth dose vaccines among newborns in an urban informal settlement and can be used as an additional tool for improving the timeliness of administering vaccines in such settings.

inputs:
Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and influenza are respiratory tract infections that may cause severe morbidity and mortality. COVID-19 has so far led to >7 million deaths since 2019 [ 1 ], while seasonal influenza or “flu” causes 290 000–650 000 deaths annually [ 2 ]. Although most episodes of COVID-19 or influenza do not require medical attention, their severity and case-fatality increase among individuals affected by chronic non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, metabolic, neurodevelopmental, liver, or hematologic diseases, as well as among those with immunosuppressive conditions or treatments (such as HIV, receiving chemotherapy or steroids, or malignancy) [ 2 , 3 ]. High-risk groups also include pregnant women and, for influenza, young children [ 4 ].

Vaccination is critical to the prevention of hospital admissions and deaths due to both diseases. Whereas the influenza vaccine has been available since the 1940s and its adoption by countries was gradual, the development and global deployment of COVID-19 took place rapidly from 2020 onwards, leading to >13.5 billion doses being administered [ 5 ]. Such a success story was made possible by unprecedented scientific collaborations, extensive prior research, and substantial public funding, which enabled vaccine development to be completed in record time while maintaining high safety standards. New versions of influenza and COVID-19 vaccines are regularly being developed as both viruses continue to circulate and mutate [ 6 ].

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all individuals, with booster doses recommended every 6–12 months for high-priority adults >50 years old [ 2 , 7 ] or who present comorbidities or immune deficiencies [ 8 ], health workers with direct patient contact, and children and pregnant women [ 9–11 ]. For influenza, WHO recommends annual vaccination for pregnant women, children aged 6 months to 5 years, people aged >65 years, people with chronic medical conditions, and health workers [ 2 ].

Flu vaccination has been offered in Brazil since 1999 [ 12 ]. In 2024, the Ministry of Health recommended the vaccine for all individuals aged ≥6 months to achieve universal coverage [ 13 ] rather than restricting immunization to priority groups, as was the case in the past. Yet, national vaccine coverage as of July 2024 had only reached 44% among priority groups (pregnant and puerperal women, older adults, children, and native people living in reservations), according to official data [ 14 ].

Brazil started COVID-19 immunization in January 2021, with the Ministry of Health recommending two doses for children <5 years of age and one dose for all others, except for immunocompromised persons, who should receive three doses. The recommendation also includes annual booster doses for priority groups such as Indigenous people and persons with comorbidity, and 6-monthly doses for immunocompromised people aged ≥5 years, pregnant or puerperal women, and persons aged ≥60 years [ 15 ]. Based on official data from 19 January 2021 to 22 March 2023, national coverage with at least one COVID-19 vaccine was 88%, while 82% were fully vaccinated with all recommended doses. The Johns Hopkins vaccine tracker estimated the one-dose coverage as 89%, with Brazil ranked fifth among Latin American countries [ 16 ].

COVID-19 vaccine coverage varies among the country’s regions, being lower in municipalities with lower education levels, higher proportions of Afro descendants, high income, and worse health service indicators [ 17 ]. Economic and educational inequalities in influenza vaccine coverage were also reported by some authors but not by others [ 18 , 19 ].

The nationwide EPICOVID19 study, conducted in Brazil in 2020, consisted of four repeated serological survey waves assessing the presence of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and focusing on monitoring the pandemic expansion in the country. The surveys were conducted in 133 sentinel cities in all 26 Brazilian states and the Federal District [ 20 ], by using probability sampling within each city. In 2024, the EPICOVID 2.0 study was implemented, using the same methodology, to evaluate the impact of the pandemic in Brazil, including measuring the coverage of COVID-19 and influenza vaccines. In addition to coverage, reported reasons for non-vaccination were studied, as were regional and socio-demographic inequalities in coverage levels.
Methodological details of the EPICOVID 2.0 study are available in a companion publication [ 21 ].

### Study design and sampling

A nationwide survey in Brazil was conducted between 11 March and 3 June 2024 in 133 sentinel cities from the 26 Brazilian states and the Federal District. According to the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), those cities were the most populated cities in the country’s 133 intermediary regions. Multistage sampling was employed. First, 25 census tracts were selected with probability proportionate to size in each sentinel city. Second, 10 households were randomly selected within each tract, using maps and household listings made available by the IBGE. Third, one individual was randomly chosen from a list of all household members and, in the case of refusal, a second individual was randomly selected. If this individual refused, then the interviewer proceeded to the next household on the right side of the original house. The field team recorded refusals and household replacements.

### Data collection

Data were collected simultaneously throughout the country by a team of surveyors working for a company with substantial experience in previous surveys commissioned by the Brazilian Ministry of Health. A smartphone app was used in data collection and uploading [ 21 ].

The sampled individuals answered a face-to-face questionnaire. Vaccine uptake was assessed through the questions “Are you vaccinated against COVID-19?” and “Are you vaccinated against flu?”. For COVID-19, those who answered yes were also asked how many doses they took (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or more). We described the prevalence of ≥1 dose, ≥2 doses, and ≥4 doses. Interviewers also asked about how the information received on the COVID-19 vaccine affected the respondent's attitude (“avoids the vaccine,” “indifferent,” or “seeks the vaccine”).

Information on explanatory variables included the geographic region of residence (North, Northeast, Southeast, South, or Center-West) and socio-demographic variables: self-reported skin color (in Portuguese: branco, preto, pardo, amarelo, or Indigenous; respectively White, Black, Brown, Asian, and Indigenous), sex (female or male), age in years (0–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80+), and years of schooling (0–4, 5–8, 9–12, 13+). Four groups of religious affiliation were included in the analyses: none, Catholic, evangelical, and others. To assess the socioeconomic position of households, we calculated a wealth index based on principal component analysis of a set of household characteristics and assets (computer, internet access, color television, air conditioning, motor vehicles, cable television, number of bathrooms, and number of residents per bedroom), similar to what is done for Demographic and Health surveys [ 22 ].

### Data analysis

Initial analyses described the sample in terms of the geographic and socio-demographic variables and vaccine coverage. For COVID-19, three variables were calculated (≥1 dose, ≥2 doses, and ≥4 doses), while, for influenza, the variable referred to having ever been vaccinated (yes or no). In the unadjusted analyses, vaccine coverage was stratified according to the explanatory variables, with point estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) being presented. Significance was by tested using chi-squared tests for heterogeneity and for linear trends in proportions.

Poisson regression models were also run to estimate the prevalence or coverage ratios of COVID-19 and influenza vaccines according to the explanatory variables. First, an unadjusted model was run, followed by a multivariable regression in which explanatory variables were gradually included according to a postulated hierarchical model with three levels: (i) geographic region and demographic variables (skin color, sex, and age); (ii) socioeconomic (religious affiliation, years of schooling, wealth); and (iii) vaccine information. Further analyses explored intersectionalities between sex and four other explanatory variables: age, skin color, wealth index, and schooling. Poisson regression was then used to estimate the Wald test for the interaction terms.

We calculated the sampling weights to represent the target population by using data from the IBGE, which included population size, sex, age, and race/color for each city. Specifically, we considered the distribution of sex, age, and ethnicity for each of the 133 cities (based on the 2022 census) [ 23 ] and compared it with the same distribution in the EPICOVID 2.0 survey. The population size was also accounted for by dividing it by the number of interviews ( n = 250) conducted in each city. These quotients were then multiplied to calculate the final survey weights.

All statistical procedures were run on Stata 18. Sampling weights were accounted for by using the “svyset” command, with the city as the stratification variable and the census sector as the primary sampling unit. All subsequent analyses were conducted by using the “svy” command in Stata, which adjusted for the complex survey design by accounting for stratification, clustering, and within-city correlations.
The 33 250 interviews took place in 2024 (from 11 March to 3 June) in 133 urban areas. Of the initially contacted subjects, 7.5% refused to be interviewed and were replaced to complete 250 questionnaires per city. All results shown below were obtained from the weighted analyses, but unweighted results are also presented in the Supplementary materials and unweighted sample sizes in a companion paper [ 21 ].

Influenza vaccine coverage was 82.6% (95% CI, 81.6; 83.5) ( Fig. 1 ). Coverage with one or more doses of COVID–19 vaccines was 90.2% (95% CI, 89.5; 90.9). Two or more doses were received by 84.6% (95% CI, 83.8; 85.5) and four or more doses by 33.0% (95% CI, 31.6; 34.4) of the sample. Most individuals received three doses.

Table 1 shows the unweighted distribution of the sample. The region with the highest proportion of interviews was the Northeast (31.6%), followed by the Southeast (24.8%). Most of the sample were female (62.0%) and almost half reported having Brown skin color (49.4%). The modal schooling category was 9–12 years (47.2%) and, as expected, ∼20% of the individuals were classified in each wealth quintile. Catholic religion was the most prevalent (45.7%), followed by evangelicals (28.6%); the latter accounted for 5.1% of the sample, mainly spiritism (1.8%) and African rites (1.5%). Due to the information received during the pandemic, most individuals (76.1%) decided to pursue the vaccine, followed by 13.6% who opted to avoid it and 10.6% who reported being indifferent.

Table 1 also shows the breakdowns by categories of the explanatory variables of coverage with 1+, 2+, and 4+ doses of COVID-19 and 1+ doses of influenza. In the text below, we focus on patterns observed for two vaccine indicators, namely 4+ COVID-19 doses and influenza vaccination. Unless otherwise stated, observed differences were highly significant.

The Southeast region had the highest coverage for both vaccine indicators, while the North and Center-West had the lowest coverage. COVID-19 coverage tended to increase with age, ranging from only 6.0% in those aged 0–19 years to >60% after the age of 60 years. In contrast, differences in influenza vaccine coverage were less marked, showing a U-shaped pattern, being higher in younger and older individuals. Women were 8.7% points (pp) more likely than men to be vaccinated against COVID-19, but there were no differences for the flu vaccine. Regarding skin color, White people had the highest coverage against COVID-19 and Indigenous individuals had the lowest coverage, with a difference of 7.2 pp ( P = 0.038), whereas there were no ethnic differences for the influenza vaccine.

There was a wide educational gap in COVID-19 coverage, with a difference of >20 pp between the highest and lowest schooling categories. A U-shaped pattern was observed for influenza, with lower coverage in the two intermediate groups. A positive socioeconomic gradient was observed for COVID-19 coverage with a gap of 9.4 pp among the top and bottom quintiles, but no significant differences were observed in influenza vaccine coverage ( P = 0.468). In terms of religion, Catholics and a small group of other religions showed the highest coverage levels, whereas evangelicals and those without a religion showed the lowest coverage. Differences between Catholics and evangelicals were wider for COVID-19 (15.1 pp) than for influenza (3.2 pp).

As expected, there was a strong association between how the information received on COVID-19 affected individual attitudes towards vaccination. Coverage with 1+ dose was 96.7% ( Table 1 ) and with 4+ doses was 40.4% among those who decided to seek the vaccine, compared with 61.2% and 7.9%, respectively, among those who mentioned avoiding the vaccine. Information on COVID-19 vaccination also affected influenza coverage, with a difference of 20.3 pp between seekers and avoiders.

Table 2 presents the reasons for non-vaccination for each vaccine. For COVID-19, the main reason was the lack of belief in this vaccine (32.0%), followed by concern about harmful consequences (27.4%). For influenza, the main reason was they did not belong to a priority group for vaccination (28.4%). Other reasons than those described in Table 2 accounted for ∼27% of the answers regarding both vaccines. The main groups of such reasons included lack of access to functioning health services (26 responses), illness at the time of vaccination (23), lack of information and interest (18), personal or cultural objections (17), emotional or psychological barriers (10), and lack of family support (7).

The co-coverage analyses ( Fig. 2 ) showed that 76.7% of the sample received at least one dose of both vaccines, 13.5% received only the COVID-19 vaccine, 5.9% received only the flu vaccine, and 3.9% received neither.

Unadjusted analyses and adjusted models are presented in Table 3 for four or more doses of COVID-19 and Table 4 for the influenza vaccine. Corresponding results for one or more doses and for two or more doses of the COVID-19 vaccine are presented in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 . For each category of the explanatory variables, coverage ratios are presented. As expected, coverage ratios ( Table 3 ) show similar patterns according to explanatory variables, as did coverage levels ( Table 1 ). The first model included adjustments for region, age, sex, and skin color. The adjusted ratios for the first three variables are somewhat attenuated compared with the unadjusted results, but similar patterns remain ( P = 0.001 or lower). For skin color, differences were no longer observed after adjustment for region, sex, and age. The second model added schooling, wealth, and religion to the earlier model; despite attenuation, a positive dose–response association with schooling persisted, but the association with wealth quintiles was no longer stepwise or significant. Evangelicals had markedly lower coverage than the other religions ( P < 0.001) and the ratio to nonreligious individuals became even more marked in the adjusted (CR = 0.69) than in the unadjusted (CR = 0.86) analyses. In the last level of the hierarchical model, the effect of vaccine information was adjusted for all other covariates and the associations were similarly strong, albeit attenuated, compared with those observed in the unadjusted analyses.

Unadjusted coverage ratios for the influenza vaccine ( Table 4 ) were also compatible with the coverage levels reported in Table 1 , with significant differences observed only for the country region, schooling, religion, and effect of the information received. These differences persisted in the adjusted analyses, except for schooling, for which the association disappeared, and for age, which became statistically significant after adjustment ( P –0.012) with lower coverage among individuals aged 20–24 years. In general, coverage ratios were lower for the flu vaccine than for 4+ doses of the COVID-19 vaccine, partly because the possible range of ratios is mathematically limited for high-coverage outcomes.

Lastly, we investigated the presence of intersectionalities between sex and four explanatory variables: age, schooling, wealth, and skin color ( Supplementary Table S3 ). Interaction P levels for COVID-19 vaccines (four or more doses) were significant for age and skin color. Women tended to show higher coverage than men in virtually all subgroups. Still, coverage among men aged ≥70 years was ∼7 pp higher than for women in the same age group, and coverage among Asian men was 14.6 pp higher. In all other categories of age, schooling, and wealth, coverage tended to be higher among women, except for boys and girls aged <20 years, who had similarly low coverage levels.

There were no significant interactions between sex and other variables regarding the influenza vaccine, but, in the poorest quintile and among the Indigenous, women seemed to be more likely to be vaccinated, whereas the reverse was observed in the two wealthiest quintiles. Because CIs are wide, these findings must be interpreted cautiously.
The study was approved by the School of Physical Education Ethics Committee at the Federal University of Pelotas (CAAE: 68382923.8.0000.5313) and by Brazil’s National Ethics Committee (CAAE 30721520.7.1001.5313). Written informed consent was secured from all participants, including parents of sampled children.
discussion:
Before discussing our results in detail, one should bear in mind the strengths and limitations of the study. This was the first nationwide study in Brazil with primary data collection measuring coverage with two priority vaccines. It was led by an experienced team that carried out a similar set of serological surveys in the same 133 cities during the peak of the pandemic, which resulted in the first description of how the pandemic moved around Brazil, with the highest initial antibody prevalence in the Amazon region and selected metropolises in the Southeast, then progressing to all country regions [ 24 ]. By relying on home interviews, the responders were not biased by access to telephones or the internet, and thus included individuals from different socioeconomic and ethnic groups. The final sample of >30 000 individuals allowed stratification by several explanatory variables with appropriate precision as well as analyses of intersectionalities.

The limitations of the study include restricting the sample to sentinel cities that constitute regional hubs, which are larger and tend to be more developed and have better health services than smaller cities. In addition, rural areas were not included; these account for ∼15% of the country’s population [ 25 ]. We could not collect information from household members who were either away at the time of the visit or refused to participate. Our sample had fewer children than was expected on the basis of the national population and White individuals and males were also underrepresented, possibly because these three groups were less likely to be at home when the visits took place. Weighting procedures were used to compensate for these differences in participation [ 21 ].

Our weighted analyses showed that COVID-19 vaccine coverage was 90.2% for at least one dose, 84.6% for at least two doses, and 33% for at least four doses. In March 2023, the estimate based on official vaccination records was 88.0% for one or more doses and 81.8% for two or more; these levels are very similar to those reported here, suggesting that the official figures, based on facility-reported doses, are highly reliable. According to the official data, Brazil ranked fifth among Latin American countries with the largest COVID-19 vaccination doses per 100 population [ 16 ].

However, the official estimates do not include coverage for four or more doses, which offer enhanced protection against evolving viral mutations. We opted for using coverage of at least four doses as the primary indicator of inequalities within the population, as more stringent health metrics tend to reveal disparities more effectively than less rigorous ones.

We found that influenza coverage was 82.6% in the whole sample, including doses received at any time in the past. Similar data from official sources are unavailable, as the reported coverage level of 44% corresponds to doses received in the past year and only for priority groups (pregnant and puerperal women, older adults, children, and native people living in reservations) [ 14 ].

An original finding resulted from the co-coverage analyses, showing substantial overlap between individuals who received both vaccines and revealing that only 3.9% of the sample failed to be immunized with either vaccine.

The Southeast region exhibited the highest vaccine coverage for both influenza and COVID-19, while the North and Center-West regions showed the lowest. Similar geographic gradients had been identified in earlier analyses of secondary data [ 17 , 26 ].

Several socio-demographic factors significantly influenced the vaccination rates. COVID-19 vaccine coverage increased with age, showing a particularly strong increase after age 60. This reflects the prioritization of older adults in the initial stages of the vaccine rollout in 2020, when uptake in this group was higher than for any other age range, which was soon followed by a reduction in mortality after age 60 [ 27 ]. In contrast, influenza vaccine coverage displayed a U-shaped pattern, with higher rates among younger and older individuals, in agreement with the priority given to young children and older adults [ 26 ].

Women demonstrated higher COVID-19 vaccination rates than men (8.7% age points higher)—a pattern that had also been reported in a secondary analysis of coverage with two or more doses [ 26 ]. In our study, the exception was among people aged ≥70 years, among whom male coverage was 7 pp higher than for females. The exact reasons for this inversion in the pattern are unclear, but a possible explanation is that older men are aware that COVID-19 deaths are more common for males than for females, and therefore may be more likely to seek the vaccine [ 28 ]. No sex gap was observed for the influenza vaccine.

White subjects exhibited the highest COVID-19 vaccination rates, while Indigenous individuals showed the lowest. Geographic [ 17 ] and individual-level [ 26 ] analyses of official data showed that White people were more likely to be vaccinated, with lower coverage among Black and Brown individuals. We were unable to find any nationwide studies of vaccination rates among Indigenous individuals with which our results could have been compared. Regarding the influenza vaccine, our results did not show any significant patterns.

Several authors have utilized national databases to show vaccine coverage inequalities according to education and wealth [ 17 , 26 , 29 ]. We found a substantial educational gap in COVID-19 vaccination rates, with a difference of >20%age points between the highest and lowest schooling categories. The positive gradient with schooling was attenuated in the wealth-adjusted analyses but remained significant. A positive wealth gradient existed for COVID-19 vaccination, which was no longer stepwise or significant in the adjusted model that included schooling as a covariate. In spite of the collinearity between the two explanatory variables, our results suggest that education is a stronger determinant of vaccine coverage than wealth.

The role of socioeconomic variables in determining influenza vaccination was unclear. Coverage showed a significant U-shaped association with schooling in the unadjusted analyses, which disappeared after adjustment. Wealth quintiles were not associated with flu vaccine coverage in any of the analyses.

The analyses of religious affiliation were particularly interesting. In a country that was once almost universally Catholic, the rapid expansion of evangelism has now reached ∼30% of the population. Evangelicals as a group tend to be strongly supportive of right-wing political parties, including the one led by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who is a spoken anti-vaccine person who states that he was never vaccinated [ 30 , 31 ]. Therefore, the findings that evangelicals are 16 pp less likely to be vaccinated against COVID-19 than Catholics is not surprising, and smaller studies in Brazil [ 32 ] and in England [ 33 ] pointed in the same direction. Moreover, lower vaccine coverage among evangelicals became even more accentuated after adjustment for covariates, including education and wealth, suggesting that the gap is not due to known confounding variables. Flu vaccine coverage, which is >80% in all subgroups, was still 3 pp lower among evangelicals than Catholics. The international literature suggests that religious affiliation, particularly Islam, is associated with lower childhood vaccine coverage [ 34 ] in some but not all countries, but we believe this is the first study to address evangelical affiliation.

The impact of information received regarding COVID-19 on vaccination decisions was significant, particularly in an era in which fake news is epidemic, including anti-science reports on the safety and efficacy of vaccines. Individuals who reported that the information received made them interested in seeking the COVID-19 vaccine had much higher coverage than those who interpreted the information as advice to avoid it. This pattern was unchanged by adjustment for covariates. Although the question was specific to information on the COVID-19 vaccine, a similar but less marked gradient was observed for the influenza vaccine, suggesting a spillover effect.

The main reasons for non-vaccination against COVID-19 were lack of belief in the vaccine (32%) and concerns about adverse effects (27.4%). For influenza, the most common—and understandable—reason was not belonging to a priority group (28.4%). Other factors contributing to vaccine hesitancy included limited access to healthcare services, illness at the time of vaccination, lack of information or interest, and cultural or psychological barriers.

Our results have direct implications for public health policies aimed at targeting specific subpopulations with renewed efforts to promote immunization, particularly ethnic and religious groups. The results also highlight the continued need to promote reliable, science-based information to the population and to strongly counteract false messages about vaccine safety and effectiveness.
target: This nationwide cross-sectional survey in Brazil investigated COVID-19 and influenza vaccination coverage and inequalities. Data from 33 250 interviews conducted between March and June 2024 in 133 sentinel cities revealed high overall coverage: 90.2% for at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine and 82.6% for influenza. However, significant disparities emerged. COVID-19 vaccination coverage increased with age, was higher among women and Whites, and strongly associated with higher education levels and wealth. Influenza vaccine coverage showed a U-shaped pattern by age and was lower among evangelicals compared with Catholics. Geographic variations were observed, with the Southeast region exhibiting the highest coverage and the North and Center-West the lowest. Co-coverage analysis indicated that 76.7% of participants received both vaccines. Reasons for non-vaccination included lack of belief in vaccine efficacy, concerns about side effects, and lack of access to healthcare. The findings highlight the need for targeted public health interventions to address vaccine hesitancy and inequalities in access, particularly focusing on specific subgroups such as evangelicals, Indigenous populations, and individuals with lower socioeconomic status.

### Genomic surveillance data

PHL and other laboratories perform WGS on a portion of specimens from confirmed COVID-19 cases [ 30 ] that are diagnosed among NYC residents, as previously described [ 4 , 31 ]. Weekly, starting on 12 August 2021, we determined the counts of each lineage assignment during a rolling 12-week period, ending on the most recent specimen collection date ( Table 1 ). Pango lineages, which represent the dynamic nomenclature applied to genetically distinct SARS-CoV-2 lineages [ 32 ], were assigned by using the pangolin software tool [ 33 ]. Initially, we used the PangoLEARN machine-learning model to assign a lineage name to each WGS result [ 33 ]. To improve lineage assignment stability, on 16 December 2021, we switched to the UShER method for placing new genome sequences onto a phylogeny [ 34 ].

Occasionally, as with XBB.1.5 and then XBB.1.16, a variant newly emerged during the rolling 12-week study period and quickly became the primary signaling node. In these instances, so as not to obscure more recently emerging variants, we reset the study period to begin after that variant stabilized as a percentage of sequenced cases. Once 12 weeks had elapsed since that stabilization, we returned to a rolling 12-week period. This is similar to an approach that is used to fine-tune a spatiotemporal cluster detection system when data in the temporal window and the baseline period are not comparable [ 35 ].

When a NYC resident tests positive for Salmonella infection, city and state laws require the laboratory to report the result and submit the patient’s isolate to PHL or the New York State Department of Health [ 36 , 37 ]. These laboratories conduct WGS on the isolates. WGS data (including serotype and cgMLST allele calls) and patient demographic data are uploaded to CDC PulseNet, where allele codes are assigned at the national level [ 11 ]. Allele codes are then populated in CDC’s System for Enteric Disease Response, Investigation, and Coordination (SEDRIC). In parallel, graduate student interns at the NYC Health Department attempt to interview all NYC residents with salmonellosis as soon as is feasible after the initial report to collect possible exposure information.

Weekly, starting on 16 November 2022, we downloaded from SEDRIC the allele codes for salmonellosis (typhoidal and non-typhoidal) for New York State residents, as additional parsing of patient addresses was necessary to restrict to NYC residents. We determined counts of each Salmonella allele code among NYC residents during a rolling 365-day period, ending on the most recent specimen collection date ( Table 1 ).

The population benefits of genomic surveillance might be inequitably distributed if particular groups are underrepresented in WGS results [ 38 ]. Underrepresentation might be a consequence of inequitable access to healthcare and laboratory testing, and, for SARS-CoV-2 infections, nonrandom sampling practices for sequencing [ 31 ]. We assessed WGS result availability for confirmed and probable cases [ 30 ] of COVID-19 and salmonellosis among NYC residents who were diagnosed during a 2-year period that ended in October 2023. We stratified by patient-level race or ethnicity and by the Index of Concentration at the Extremes—an area-based measure of economic and racial or ethnic segregation [ 39 ].

### Hierarchical tree files

Pango lineage notes were used to determine parent–child relationships for all detected SARS-CoV-2 variants [ 33 , 40 ]. For example, for the analysis that was conducted on 17 August 2023, all detected variants were descended from B.1. Thus, B.1 was designated as the tree root, which progressively branched into increasingly specific lineages, including the Omicron variant (i.e. B.1.1.529), culminating in more specific nodes, such as the Omicron subvariant EG.5.1.1. For recombinant lineages (e.g. XBB), in January 2024, we switched to assigning multiple parents, but in the earlier analyses that are presented here, we assigned the most recent common ancestor as the parent ( Table 2 ).

We designated ‘SAL’ as the tree root and each Salmonella serotype (e.g. Typhi, Enteritidis, Kottbus) as the second tree level. We appended the allele code, which can be up to six digits, to the serotype. Whereas laboratory scientists typically compare isolates manually by using allele ranges, we used allele codes because of the standardized hierarchical nomenclature. Isolates with more allele code digits in common have a lower number of allele differences ( Table 3 ).

### Prospective tree-temporal scan statistic

We conducted prospective analyses by using tree-temporal scan statistics [ 24 , 41 ] ( Table 1 ) in the free and open-source TreeScan TM software (Martin Kulldorff and Information Management Services, Inc., Calverton, Maryland). We searched for unusual increases that emerged over any recent time period at any node, from large phylogenetic branches to small groups of genetically indistinguishable isolates. Under the null hypothesis, for each variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is constant over time. Under the alternative hypothesis, for one variant or group of related variants, its proportion among all variants is higher during some recent period. Mathematical formulae for calculating the expected number of cases, excess cases, and relative risk are available in the TreeScan user guide [ 41 ].

For each node (candidate cluster), a likelihood ratio-based test statistic is calculated when the observed number of cases during the time window at the node exceeds the expected number. The candidate cluster with the maximum likelihood ratio test statistic is the cluster that is least likely to be due to chance under the null hypothesis of no node-by-time interaction, after adjusting for purely temporal variation and total node counts during the study period. For example, if a node has 5.4% of cases during the baseline period (i.e. prior to the cluster period) and there are 100 total cases with WGS results during the cluster period, then the expected number of cases during the cluster period at that node is 5.4.

Monte Carlo hypothesis testing is used to assess the statistical strength of clusters, controlling for the multiplicity of overlapping nodes and time windows evaluated. To create simulated datasets under the null hypothesis, case dates are shuffled and randomly assigned to the original nodes. The maximum likelihood ratio test statistic for each simulated dataset is calculated in the same way as for the observed dataset.

The maximum likelihood ratio for the observed dataset is ranked among those from the simulated runs under the null hypothesis, and a P -value is derived from this ranking as P = rank/(999 999 + 1) for the SARS-CoV-2 analyses [ 41 ]. For prospective analyses, a recurrence interval (RI) is calculated as the reciprocal of the P -value. For a weekly analysis frequency, this is further divided by 52 for the number of analyses per year. The RI represents the duration of weekly surveillance required for the expected number of clusters that are at least as unusual as the observed cluster to be equal to 1 by chance [ 42 ]. For example, when the null hypothesis of no clusters is true, then, during a 1-year period, the expected number of clusters with RI ≥ 365 days is 1. Supplementary Appendix S1 provides cluster-reporting details.

### Performance assessment

In the absence of national guidance for ways in which jurisdictions should select variants to monitor locally, we compiled illustrative examples of successes and challenges in using TreeScan results to focus attention on emerging variants during weekly analyses that were conducted during August 2021–November 2023.

We characterized clusters that were prospectively detected by using TreeScan during the first year of weekly analyses, from 16 November 2022 to 8 November 2023. We considered clusters to be “solved” if investigators identified a common food source, animal exposure, exposure site, or travel history that likely explained the association among cluster patients. Supplementary Appendix S2 provides further details about cluster definitions, cluster prioritization, and consideration of typhoidal clusters.
### Completeness and representativeness

Among NYC residents who were diagnosed during November 2021–October 2023, WGS was conducted for 7% of COVID-19 cases (151 944 of 2 266 600) and for 62% of non-typhoidal salmonellosis cases (1679 of 2722; Supplementary Table S1 ). Of 1068 salmonellosis cases with no allele code, 937 (88%) were probable cases with only a positive culture-independent diagnostic test result, 106 (10%) were culture-positive but had no isolate available for WGS, 5 (<1%) underwent WGS but failed quality control, and 20 (2%) were unique sequences that CDC’s naming algorithm could not match to an existing allele code. The median lag from specimen collection to allele code assignment was 22 days (interquartile range: 20–28 days). Of 1654 salmonellosis cases with an allele code assigned, 1322 (80%) had a fully or partially completed interview; interviews are necessary to collect information for identifying common exposures among cluster patients.

Patient demographic characteristics were similarly distributed between reported cases overall and the subset with WGS results. Distributions were within ±2.5% for every stratum of race or ethnicity and the Index of Concentration at the Extremes ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Although substantial proportions of patients lacked WGS results, there was no evidence of systematic underrepresentation during this period.

### SARS-CoV-2 illustrative examples

The analysis that was performed on 22 June 2023 searched for variants that were emerging during the 14, 15, 16, …, 27, or 28-day period that ended on 12 June 2023 ( Figure 1 ), across 200 nodes (excerpted in Figure 2 ). This analysis, with a computer running time of 4 minutes and 15 seconds, identified six SARS-CoV-2 variants emerging among NYC residents ( Table 4 ). Three of the six nodes were the same as in the prior week’s analysis ( Supplementary Table S2 ), including persistent, strong signals for XBB.1.16, XBB.2.3, and their subvariants. Of the newly signaling nodes, EG.5.1 (RI = 35 years) first signaled more strongly than its grandparent (XBB.1.9.2, Figure 2 ), with 11 specimens collected during 17 May–12 June 2023. EG.5 or EG.5.1 continued to signal for 13 consecutive weekly analyses, from 22 June to 14 September 2023, after which more specific subvariants (e.g. EG.5.1.6) began to signal more strongly.

The WHO designated EG.5 as a variant under monitoring on 19 July 2023 and a variant of interest on 9 August 2023 [ 43 ], 4 and 7 weeks, respectively, after our first EG.5.1 signal. During a period with many co-circulating variants and when EG.5 initially constituted a small number and percentage of cases with WGS results, the TreeScan analysis, trend visualization ( Figure 3 ), and dendrogram ( Supplementary Figure S1 ; see online supplementary material for a color version of this figure) led NYC Health Department officials to focus attention on this variant.

In the analysis that was performed on 20 October 2022, multiple BE.1.1.1 subvariants signaled for the first time, indicating delayed detection of BQ.1, BQ.1.1 (RI = 19 231 years for both nodes), and BQ.1.3 (RI = 2.4 years). In the concurrent UShER version update, a subset of cases had been reassigned to BQ lineages, revealing that BQ lineages, which descended from BE.1.1.1 [ 40 ], had been present for >1 month. Once the input data were updated, TreeScan analyses appropriately detected the emergence of BQ lineages.

The Omicron variant was first detected in NYC in clinical and wastewater samples that were collected in November 2021 and quickly became predominant [ 31 , 44 ]. While staff were urgently focused on the characterization of local effects on population health, TreeScan analyses provided confirmation that additional lineages that required attention and response were not emerging concurrently.

During the first year of analyses, on 128 serotypes, TreeScan detected 16 unique clusters in the primary analysis by using the specimen collection date as the temporal element and one additional cluster in the sensitivity analysis by using the upload date ( Table 5 ). TreeScan detects statistical anomalies, which must be investigated to distinguish true clusters from data-quality issues. Of the 17 clusters, two clusters were due to >1 isolate being sequenced from the same patient. These data-quality issues were identified by reviewing line lists and quickly resolved in SEDRIC. The remaining 15 clusters were plausibly outbreaks and worth epidemiological investigation. Of these 15 clusters, two were typhoidal and associated with travel to an endemic area. Of the 13 non-typhoidal clusters, two comprised family members with shared exposures, two reflected larger, interjurisdictional outbreaks, two were persistent strains that caused illnesses over a long time, and seven were unsolved. Of the 13 non-typhoidal clusters, one was detected at the third allele code digit so encompassed a broader allele range than rule-based cluster definitions. The remaining 12 clusters were detected to at least the fifth allele code digit (i.e. had a maximum expected difference of 4 alleles; Table 3 ), aligning with rule-based cluster definitions ( Supplementary Appendix S2 ). Of these clusters, nine were concurrently detected by PHL, two consisted entirely of isolates that were tested at other jurisdictions’ public health laboratories and so could not have been detected by PHL, and one was not concurrently detected by PHL because temporary technological issues disrupted portions of PHL’s cluster detection workflow.

Investigators considered TreeScan results to be helpful in focusing staff attention and investigation resources. For example, TreeScan clusters in NYC occasionally reflected concurrent, aberrant clusters across other jurisdictions, prompting multijurisdictional collaboration to identify common exposures. The TreeScan cluster at the third allele code digit alerted investigators to a local increase in Salmonella Javiana, spurring further investigation into possible subclusters. Moreover, in analysing isolates according to the location of residence, TreeScan detected clusters among NYC residents that otherwise might not have been detected because patients were tested by different laboratories. TreeScan also provided coverage when external technological issues disrupted certain processes at PHL.
The Institutional Review Board of the NYC Health Department determined this activity (No. 21–072) meets the definition of public health surveillance as set forth under 45 CFR§46.102(l)(2).
discussion:
By applying tree-temporal scan statistics prospectively to genomic surveillance data with a standardized hierarchical nomenclature, we automatically sifted through large quantities of data in minutes and generated weekly ranked shortlists of nodes with statistically unusual numbers of recent cases. This method flexibly evaluates all candidate clusters, across many degrees of genetic relatedness and date ranges. It dynamically accounts for any purely temporal trends, such as data lags or changes in WGS result availability, and minimizes false signals by adjusting for the multiplicity of nodes and cluster windows scanned. With real-time application to SARS-CoV-2 and Salmonella data, the NYC Health Department detected credible clusters for investigation and data-quality problems for correction.

### Limitations

WGS results were available for only 7% of COVID-19 cases and 62% of salmonellosis cases. After the federal COVID-19 public health emergency declaration ended in May 2023 and with reduced funding, specimen and sequence availability declined [ 45 ], which could have reduced population representativeness and delayed the detection of new variants. Additionally, although the NYC Health Code requires laboratories to reflexively culture certain enteric pathogens, including Salmonella [ 36 ], the widespread use of culture-independent diagnostic testing has reduced the proportion of salmonellosis cases with recovered isolates. Patients without WGS results cannot contribute their exposure histories to cluster investigations, making it more challenging to solve outbreaks. Improving population-based WGS data completeness, representativeness, and timeliness requires strengthening partnerships with clinics and submitting laboratories, as well as deepening investments in laboratory capacity and bioinformatics infrastructure, including applying culture-independent sequencing methods [ 46 , 47 ].

Where WGS results were available, the tree nomenclature imposed certain limitations. For SARS-CoV-2, assigning Pango lineages by using UShER allowed accurate and stable lineage assignments at the expense of timeliness. As in the BQ lineages example, delays in updating nomenclature to recognize new lineage designations resulted in delayed detection. For Salmonella , the signal-to-noise ratio to detect a new cluster was poor for allele codes that ended in ‘x’, as the underlying four-, five-, and six-digit codes were masked due to low genomic diversity that increased the within-code distance beyond the assignment thresholds. More broadly, we rely on a standardized nomenclature, with no consideration of genetic distances between tree nodes.

TreeScan should complement, not replace, other cluster detection approaches using laboratory-based data, such as by examining allele ranges [ 11 , 14 ]. Tree-temporal scan statistics could miss outbreaks where genetic or temporal clustering is weak. Zoonotic disease outbreaks, such as those associated with exposure to reptiles or backyard poultry, often involve multiple serotypes with large allelic diversity [ 15 ]. Patients’ isolates might be weakly clustered temporally for outbreaks due to persistent environmental contamination or following delays in accessing medical care or obtaining WGS results. Supplementary Appendix S3 provides additional minor limitations.
By decreasing the reliance on time-consuming, manual laboratory data review and by simultaneously analysing data not only by genetic relatedness, but also by temporal clustering, TreeScan analyses can help officials to focus limited investigative resources on emerging clusters and variants. Future work could apply this approach to additional pathogens [ 11 , 48 ], use additional hierarchical nomenclature systems, analyse additional pathogen characteristics (e.g. antimicrobial resistance patterns), and analyse state- and national-level data to support multijurisdictional outbreak response. Incorporating TreeScan as a free and open-source tool into analytical pipelines [ 49 ] could strengthen strategic frameworks for genomic surveillance [ 50 ], including in low- and middle-income countries.

Health departments should routinely apply multiple cluster detection methods to quickly detect different types of outbreaks. In NYC, spatiotemporal analyses have quickly detected outbreaks with strong geographic clustering before laboratory subtyping results became available. However, these methods could miss geographically diffuse outbreaks, such as those following exposure to a widely disseminated source, or outbreaks that affect only a few patients. Despite lags in subtyping data availability, such outbreaks could be detected more quickly by the application of tree-temporal scan statistics to WGS data. TreeScan thus fills an important gap in the public health practitioner’s automated cluster detection and monitoring toolkit.
target: The detection of communicable disease clusters in genomic surveillance data typically involves the application of rule-based signaling criteria, which can be arbitrary.
