The COVID-19 pandemic had substantial acute impacts worldwide, with more than 7 million deaths reported to the World Health Organization by December 2024 [ 1 ]. Mortality was particularly high in Brazil, representing 9.9% of all deaths worldwide in a country that accounts for 2.7% of the world’s population. This was due to a combination of unscientific political decisions, poor central coordination as different states and regions adopted variable approaches to prevention and case management, and conflicting public messages [ 2 ].

EPICOVID-19, a population-based serological survey carried out in four different waves during 2020 with a total of over 130 000 interviews in 133 Brazilian cities, showed that individuals with lower socioeconomic conditions, lower education, indigenous ethnicity, and black or brown skin colour were more likely to present antibodies against COVID-19 [ 3 ]. Other studies reported similar patterns in both high and low/middle-income countries [ 4 , 5 ].

Economic and social disruption due to the pandemic have profoundly impacted social, health, and economic outcomes among families, such as income reduction, unemployment, interruption of studies, and food insecurity [ 6 , 7 ]. During the pandemic, a six-country study (China, Japan, Italy, South Korea, UK, and USA) reported stronger impacts among individuals with low socioeconomic status [ 8 ]. In a systematic review, including studies from 27 countries, higher rates of dropouts and failures were reported among students from lower socioeconomic positions [ 9 ].

We aimed to describe how families were impacted by the pandemic in terms of income, employment, school attendance, food insecurity, and death of family members in a nationwide Brazilian population-based sample. Impact measures were stratified by socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, including indicators socioeconomic position and ethnicity. The rationale for stratification is provided by the importance of social determinants of health globally [ 10 ] and particularly in Brazil, which is one the most highly unequal countries in the world [ 11 ]. Our hypothesis was that the pandemic had a greater impact on population groups that were already more vulnerable at its onset, such as low-income families and households headed by women.
### Participants

Using the same sampling design as in the original 2020 study, 133 sentinel cities were selected throughout the country. The cities included Brasilia, 26 state capitals, and the largest cities in each of the country’s intermediate regions, as defined by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) [ 12 ]. In each city, a sample of 25 urban census tracts was drawn with a probability of selection proportionate to size, and 10 households were randomly selected in each tract. In each sampled household, all residents were listed, and one was randomly selected to be interviewed. If the sampled individual refused to be interviewed, a second one was sampled. If this individual also refused, the next household to the right was selected. A total of 33 250 participants were interviewed. Further details on the study methods have been described elsewhere [ 13 ]. Data were collected during May and June 2024.

### Outcomes

The following impact outcomes during the pandemic were studied: death of a family member due to COVID-19; decrease in family income; impact on work of a family member, defined as job loss (for those formally employed) or stopping working (for those in the informal sector); and impact on education, defined as any family member who stopped studying during the pandemic (analyses restricted to families with children or adolescents aged under 18). These three impact indicators referred to events or changes taking place during the pandemic. Household food insecurity during the pandemic was investigated using the Brazilian Food Insecurity Scale [ 14 ], which defines food insecurity at the household as one or more positive answers to eight questions. In addition, we analysed whether any household member had gone an entire day without eating due to lack of food. Food insecurity was assessed during the pandemic, rather than changes in food security compared to the pre-pandemic period.

### Procedures

The sampled individuals were invited to participate in the survey and informed about the objectives of the study, as well as its risks and advantages. Interviews were conducted only after the participant signed the free and informed consent form. The form was read when the selected individual was under 18 years of age; in this case, the child or adolescent either signed or fingerprinted the form, which a legal guardian also signed. The study represented minimal risk to health, being restricted to the application of a short questionnaire. Participants were informed that they could stop participating at any time during data collection.

### Data analysis

We used Stata 15 for the analyses. The prevalence of each outcome was described according to sociodemographic characteristics of the families, including region of the country, number and age distribution of family members, whether the family was headed by a woman, highest educational level of a family member, monthly family income, household wealth, and race/skin colour of the interviewee.

Household wealth was calculated through an index based on principal component analysis (PCA) of a set of household characteristics and assets (computer, internet access, colour television, air conditioning, motor vehicles, cable television, number of bathrooms, and number of residents per bedroom), similar to what is done for Demographic and Health surveys [ 15 ]. The first component of the PCA explained 37.8% of the total variance, and all variables had factor loadings above 0.4, except for internet access (0.24) and cable television (0.35). The wealth index was moderately correlated with reported monthly family income (Pearson’s correlation coefficient of 0.62), and both variables were retained in the analyses.

Information on race/skin colour—the official variable employed by the Brazilian classification—was not collected on each family member but only for the respondent. In consonance with the official classification used in Brazilian studies, the categories included (in Portuguese): branco, preto, pardo, amarelo, or indigenous; respectively white, black, brown, Asian, and indigenous [ 16 ]. Family income in the month preceding the interview was expressed in Brazilian minimum wages (∼US$250).

Proportions were compared using the Wald test. Prevalence ratios were estimated using Poisson regression. Sampling weights were employed to account for the sampling design (by using the ‘svyset’ command) and to reproduce the characteristics of the pooled set of 133 cities in terms of population size, sex, age, and race/colour, using the 2022 Census results [ 17 ]. All findings reported below resulted from the weighted analyses. Further details on weights are available elsewhere [ 18 ].

Equiplot graphs [ 19 ] were used to show inequalities in the outcomes according to wealth quintiles. The slope index of inequality (SII) was used to estimate the magnitude of income-related disparities [ 20 ]. The index ranges from −1 to +1, with negative values indicating higher levels of the outcome among the poor and positive values indicating the opposite.
Interviews were carried out in 33 250 households. Table 1 presents the distribution of households according to socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. Most households had a member with at least 9 years of schooling, a family income of up to three minimum wages, and were headed by a male.

Table 2 presents the five impact outcomes according to region, age, sex, wealth index, income, and race/skin colour. The death of a family member due to COVID-19 was reported in 14.7% [95% confidence interval (CI): 13.8%; 15.6%] of all households, being more common in wealthier and more educated families and in the North and Central-West regions. Reduced family income during the pandemic was observed in 48.6% (95% CI: 47.1%; 50.1%) of the households, with the highest prevalence in the North and Northeast and among families with current incomes of one minimum wage or less. About one of every three participants [34.9% (95% CI: 33.4%; 36.4%)] reported that they or someone in their household had lost their job or stopped working during the COVID-19 outbreak, this being more frequent in families whose income was three minimum wages or less. Concerning school attendance, 21.5% (95% CI: 20.1%; 22.9%) stated that a family member interrupted their studies during the pandemic. Food insecurity during the outbreak was reported in 47.4% (95% CI: 45.9%; 48.8%) of the families, and in 8.5% (95% CI: 7.7; 9.3), at least one adult failed to eat on one or more days due to lack of money (data not shown in Table). Food insecurity, work disruptions, and interruption of studies were more common among families earning one minimum wage or less, those led by women, and households with six or more residents. In contrast, white subjects were less likely to report food insecurity. Race/skin colour was not associated with the remaining outcomes. Table 3 describes outcomes according to race/skin colour stratified by family income.

Figure 1 shows that the widest absolute wealth inequality was observed for food insecurity, where prevalence in the poorest quintile was more than 30 percentage points higher than in the wealthiest quintile. For the death of a family member, the slope index of inequality (SII) was positive [0.08 (95% CI: 0.07; 0.10)], whereas for loss of income [SII: −0.16 (95% CI: −0.18 to −0.14)], impact on work [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.11 to −0.07)], school disruption [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.12 to −0.06)], and food insecurity [SII: −0.42 (95% CI: −0.43 to −0.4)], the slope index of inequality was negative, indicating greater disadvantage among the poorest. The lower SII estimate for food insecurity indicates that absolute wealth inequality was higher for food insecurity.
The study was submitted to the School of Physical Education Ethics Committee at the Federal University of Pelotas [CAAE: 68382923.8.0000.5313].
discussion:
Our large nationwide, population-based survey in Brazil documented important impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, 4 years after the initial cases in 2020. The impact included high frequencies of family deaths, income reductions, food insecurity, work, and schooling disruptions. The stronger impacts tended to affect already vulnerable groups, as discussed below.

The literature extensively documents the pandemic’s impacts on income, work, and schooling [ 21 ]. Our findings quantify the magnitude of such impacts in Brazil, as well as confirm the importance of disparities associated with region of residence, educational levels, income, wealth, gender, family composition, and ethnicity. In sequence, we discuss in greater detail our findings on food insecurity, family composition, and regional disparities, as well as on the apparently paradoxical inequalities in mortality at the household level.

Food insecurity was particularly frequent in low-income and female-headed families, those with six or more members and with children, and among indigenous populations. Almost two-thirds of the low-income families reported food insecurity; the SII value of 0.42 indicates a wide prevalence gap of 42 percentage points between the poorest and wealthiest households. Due to our cross-sectional design, we cannot assert that the reported levels of food insecurity were fully attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic, because such shortages might have predated the arrival of the virus in the country. Nevertheless, the literature suggests that insecurity increased during the pandemic. A United Nations report published in 2020 showed increases in global food insecurity, with particularly severe effects in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This was attributed to increased unemployment, loss of income, and disruptions in supply chains [ 22 ]. In Latin America, a cohort study in Mexico showed increased food insecurity from 41.6% before the pandemic to 53.8% during the pandemic period [ 23 ]. In Brazil, the impact was amplified by pre-existing inequalities, with the most vulnerable families facing rising rates of food insecurity and undernutrition. Food insecurity was also attributed to the ineffectiveness of social policies during the crisis, leaving millions at risk of hunger and extreme poverty [ 24 ]. Food insecurity may have long-lasting effects, as affected individuals may be more likely to suffer from post-COVID conditions, as reported in a Brazilian cohort study [ 25 ].

There were important regional differences within Brazil. The North (Amazon) and Northeast regions were the most affected by reductions in income, interruption of studies, and food insecurity. These two regions were affected by the pandemic’s fastest initial escalation in Brazil. In our original EPICOVID-19 survey carried out in 2020, the highest prevalence of antibodies against SARS-Cov-2 was initially observed in 11 cities along the Amazon River, after which prevalence increased rapidly in the Northeast [ 26 ]. In addition to the well-documented socioeconomic disparities among the Brazilian regions [ 27 ], factors such as the structure and organization of health systems and management of the pandemic may have played a role. Race/skin colour may also have played a role, as indigenous people—who are concentrated in the Amazon area—were amongst those with the highest levels of infection, hospitalization, and deaths during the pandemic, accentuating their pre-existing vulnerability to acute respiratory diseases, even before the pandemic [ 28 ].

Earlier studies showed that the North region also had the highest case fatality among all five regions of Brazil, both in indigenous and non-indigenous people [ 28–30 ]. Baqui et al . [ 31 ] hypothesize that the regional effect is driven by the increased burden of pre-existing comorbidity in the poorest regions and among the indigenous, leading to increased COVID-19 susceptibility and severity, compounded by unequal access to health care, including intensive care. We also investigated gender-related issues. Because impact outcomes were measured at the household level, it did not make sense to break them down according to the sex of the randomly chosen survey respondent. Instead, we examined gender inequality by comparing families according to the sex of the head of the household. Families headed by women, which represented 40% of the sample, were disproportionately affected by higher rates of food insecurity, income reduction, and interruption of studies. These findings were consistent with those of other studies worldwide that reported on individual-level outcomes. Women were more likely than men to experience negative work outcomes, such as permanent job loss and reduced income, or reductions in total hours worked, both for paid and unpaid work, thus aggravating pre-existing gender gaps [ 32–36 ]. Increased childcare needs due to school interruptions were also reported to impact women’s work. Regarding food insecurity during the pandemic, an Ethiopian study also reported higher levels in female-headed households [ 37 ]. A systematic review focused on pregnant women from different countries found that food insecurity during the pandemic ranged from 11% to over 80% [ 38 ], while a survey in the Amazon Region reported a prevalence of food insecurity of 57% also among pregnant women, with higher levels in large families and in low-income households [ 39 ]. Our findings also showed increased risks in large families for income reduction, work and schooling disruptions, and food insecurity.

Taken together, our findings suggest that pre-existing disparities exacerbated the impacts of the pandemic and likely affected subsequent recovery in terms of food security, education, income, and employment. In many LMICs, households have turned to agricultural work to compensate for job losses in the services sector, and informal work has substantially increased among the poorest [ 7 ]. As an upper-middle-income country, Brazil’s GDP fell 3.3% in 2020, which represented a record low annual decline in recent history. On the positive side, this decline was reversed after the pandemic [ 17 ].

Similar impacts on inequality were seen in some high-income countries, like UK [ 40 ] and Korea [ 41 ], where the pandemic accentuated socioeconomic disparities, especially affecting low-income workers and other vulnerable groups. Lastly, the interruptions in schooling may also aggravate inequalities and social exclusion [ 9 , 42 ].

We found that deaths of family members were more commonly reported in wealthier and more educated families. This finding persisted even after adjusting for sex, age, region, and skin colour. This was a surprising finding as—despite having universal healthcare—poor Brazilians still have lower access to complex health services and shorter life expectancies than their better-off counterparts [ 43 ]. Our finding also contradicts the Brazilian literature on the relationship between COVID-19 mortality and socioeconomic factors, which is mostly based on ecological studies correlating routinely collected mortality data with census-based economic indicators. Most such studies found higher mortality in poorer or more deprived areas of the country [ 31 , 44–48 ]. However, we were unable to find any individual-level study from Brazil on this association. Two observations may help explain our paradoxical findings. First, due to differential life expectancy according to socioeconomic position, wealthier families were more likely than poor households to include elderly members before the pandemic, and these persons were at the highest risk of COVID-19 death. Our current post-pandemic analyses showed that 37% of all households in the poorest quintile and 46% of those in the wealthiest quintile had at least one member aged 60 or older. Similarly, these proportions were 35% and 45% for family income brackets below 1 and over 5 minimum wages ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Such variability in age composition helps explain why wealthier households were more likely to report a death from a disease that primarily killed elderly people. Further analyses also showed that the sharpest socioeconomic increases in mortality were observed for the deaths of the parents of the respondents than for younger relatives (Supplementary Table S2). Another possible explanation is the higher prevalence of non-communicable diseases among the poorest [ 49 ], which may have led them to attribute COVID-19-related deaths to other pre-existing conditions.

Our study’s strengths include its standardized survey methodology and its large population-based sample, including over 100 cities spread throughout a country with 8.5 million km 2 . Yet, some limitations should be acknowledged. First, the time elapsed from the peak of the pandemic to the data collection date poses the risk of recall bias. However, the outcomes under study are objectively defined major events, such as death or unemployment, which reduces the likelihood of poor recall. Second, our sample was restricted to large cities that usually have better access to health care, and 15% of the national population living in rural areas were not included. Third, the higher proportion of negative outcomes in female-headed families might result from the death of a male head of household during the pandemic. For two reasons, we do not think this is a likely source of bias. We found that the proportion of households led by women in our sample was very close to that reported in the 2022 National Census [ 17 ]. In addition, reported deaths in the family did not vary according to the sex of the head of the household ( Table 2 ), and lastly, exclusion from the analyses of households where a spouse died due to COVID-19 (Supplementary Table S3) led to very similar results to those reported above. Lastly, we could not collect information from households whose members were away during the attempted visit or refused to participate.

In conclusion, substantial impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil were documented in terms of mortality, nutrition, income, work, and education. The pandemic disproportionately affected population subgroups that were already vulnerable before the pandemic, such as low-income, female-headed, and indigenous households, thus contributing to exacerbate pre-existing disparities. Our findings underscore the importance of developing and expanding targeted policies to address the needs of the most vulnerable and will contribute to their recovery. Further research should focus on effective interventions to reduce these disparities, including food security programmes, and education support for children from low-income households, and on preparedness to face future epidemics.
target: The COVID-19 pandemic imposed a substantial disease burden, yet few population-based studies assessed its long-term impacts on families. This study estimated the pandemic’s impact on family income, employment, school interruption, food insecurity, and death of family members in Brazil.Population-based household survey with 33.250 participants from 133 large cities in Brazil during May and June 2024. Households were selected using a multistage probability sampling design in each city.Among respondents, 14.7% [95% confidence interval (CI):13.8%; 15.6%] reported the death of a family member due to COVID-19; 48.6% (95% CI: 47.1%; 50.1%) experienced reductions in family income; 34.9% (95% CI: 33.4%; 36.4%) reported that at least one family member stopped working; in 21.5% (95% CI: 20.1%; 22.9%) of families, at least one member interrupted studies; and 47.4% (95% CI: 45.9%; 48.8%) experienced food insecurity during the pandemic. These outcomes were more frequent among families with low income and with six or more members, except for the death of a family member, which was more commonly reported in households with higher incomes and educational levels. Job losses, interruption of studies, and food insecurity were more common in families led by women. Indigenous people experienced a high prevalence of food insecurity.The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated social and economic inequalities, with most impacts disproportionately affecting the poorest families, those led by women, and indigenous people. Conversely, the death of a relative was more commonly reported among the wealthiest families that include a larger number of older members.

inputs:
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is defined as a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by age-inappropriate inattention or hyperactivity–impulsivity, or both [ 1 ]. In the long term, ADHD patients tend to show negative life outcomes including lower academic outcomes [ 2–5 ], higher criminal behaviour [ 6 ], financial distress [ 7 ], and suicide risk [ 7 , 8 ]. ADHD medication has been shown to ameliorate inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms in the short-term [ 9 ], so it is hypothesized it might have positive indirect effects on academic outcomes. To our knowledge, only the multimodal treatment of ADHD (MTA) randomized clinical trial (RCT) [ 10–13 ] has considered the long-term effect of medication on standardized achievement tests. The exploratory analysis found a small improvement for reading achievement scores.

The Cochrane review by Størebo et al. [ 14 ] suggested possible benefits of ADHD medication involved only teacher-rated behaviour and symptoms as well as parent-reported quality of life, while harms involved mostly sleep problems and decreased appetite. Similar results were found by a later review of non-randomized studies [ 15 ]. A recent crossover trial found that even in the short-term, the improved classroom behaviour and seat work productivity did not translate into improved learning [ 16 ]. A systematic review by Arnold et al. [ 17 ] found that in the case of long-term academic achievement, most studies evaluating pharmacological treatments reported benefits. However, another review considers these benefits to be educationally negligible, given the small effect sizes [ 18 ].

Observational studies complement results from such RCTs, especially their limited treatment durations, follow-up periods, or specific outcomes under study. For example, the Swedish national registry study of Jangmo et al. [ 3 ], which found that dispensations of ADHD medication had effects on grade point average, eligibility, and completion of upper secondary school and teacher assessment of performance, also in the long-term (three years). However, improvements in teacher assessed performance were not reflected in better standardized test scores. Likewise, the Danish registry study by Keilow et al. [ 19 ] leverages medication non-response as a natural experiment to estimate the effect of full or partial discontinuation of pharmaceutical treatment in grade point average. They found a negative effect of discontinuation of 0.22 SDs.

Recently proposed, the target trial framework helps avoid common ‘self-inflicted injuries’ in the causal analysis of observational data [ 20–24 ]. Researchers are required to explicitly state the hypothetical trial they want to emulate with an observational study, specifying eligibility criteria, treatment strategies, follow-up period, and a time-zero, among others. This prevents common pitfalls such as using post-treatment information for assignment, or estimating non-causal contrasts such as always-takers versus never-takers (rather than initiators versus non-initiators). To our knowledge, only a couple of applications to ADHD research exist: a study on ADHD medication initiation and mortality [ 25 ] and a study on the effect of diagnosis on quality of life [ 26 ].

In summary, evidence weakly supports the hypothesis that long-term medication will meaningfully improve academic achievement. Contrastingly, academic improvement might be one of the main drivers of parent’s decision to treat [ 27 ]. There is also evidence for the adverse effects of medication on children. Better quality of evidence is thus required so that clinicians, parents, and users can take informed decisions about the trade-offs at stake, and carefully analysed observational data can contribute to the body of evidence.

The present article’s main objective is to estimate the long-term causal effect of initiating ADHD medication on national test scores in the domains of English, numeracy, and reading in Norwegian children diagnosed with ADHD. The causal estimand corresponds to the intention-to-treat effect, i.e. an average treatment effect of initiation in a given period.

A secondary objective is to explore heterogeneity of the effects across the different domains of national test scores and subgroups.
This article follows the STROBE reporting guidelines for observational studies and the RECORD/RECORD-PE extensions for routinely collected health data [ 28–30 ], respectively. All code used for analysis is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/tvarnetperez/TTE_ADHD .

### RCT literature review

To our knowledge, the MTA trial [ 10–13 ] was the only pertinent RCT, though our available data were incompatible with its emulation. Thus, an ideal target trial following a pretest–posttest control group design was devised, which was adapted into the feasible target trial that our data allow.

### Data source

The study included person-, family-, and school-level variables, linked from multiple data sources: the Norwegian Prescription Database, the Norwegian Patient Registry, the Database for Control and Payment of Health Reimbursement, Statistics Norway, and the Medical Birth Registry of Norway.

### Target trial protocol

The protocol is summarized in the design diagram in Fig. 1 .

Eligibility criteria were evaluated only once for all participants, at time-zero. The study included Norwegian-born children diagnosed with ADHD by a specialist or across four general practitioner (GP) visits (reducing misclassification from symptomatic concerns). Children with diagnoses of severe comorbid disorders such as autism, epilepsy, and Down’s syndrome were excluded, as well as children who did not have any national test score at grade five. Children who were medicated before time-zero were excluded, i.e. a complete washout period. Figure 2 details the exclusion steps.

The ‘treatment’ or ‘as-started’ arm [ 22 ] corresponds to having been dispensed to their name an ADHD medication from a pharmacy in a grace period [ 21 ] between 365 and 455 days after their grade five national test. In the main analysis, this strictly means the intent to initiate a pharmaceutical treatment regime, whereas in the sensitivity analysis (with no-washout period), it can also mean to continue a regime.

The ‘control’ arm corresponds to not having been dispensed any ADHD medication from a pharmacy during the same grace period.

Randomization is emulated via model-based adjustment for potential confounders as measured until time-zero, i.e. baseline confounders.

We have defined time-zero as 365 days after the grade five national test. As can be seen in Supplementary Fig. S2 , 365 days after the grade five national test, 81.11% of children that would receive a diagnosis before the grade eight national test had already received it.

The follow-up period lasted until the (approximated) grade eight national test date, with an additional 30-day margin of error to tally children both diagnosed and medicated within the study period.

The outcomes are the standardized grade eight national test scores for all three domains: numeracy, reading, and English.

The ‘as-started’ effect, the target trial emulation equivalent of an ‘intention-to-treat’ effect [ 22 ].

A more general dataset containing 38 215 children was used to determine the time-zero cutoff (see Supplementary Fig. S2 ). This included dates of ADHD diagnosis for all children at any time.

Application of exclusion criteria except for washout period results in 12 541 observations. This is the dataset used for determining the grace-period cutoff (see Supplementary Fig. S3 ).

This eligible sample is further reduced into an analytic sample of 8458 observations by only considering children with a complete washout period—i.e. no ADHD medication use before time-zero and by listwise deletion of unimputed covariates, namely parents’ civil status at grades five and six (due to low cell count) and school ID at grades five and eight. The main analysis results and the descriptive tables are based on this dataset. The sensitivity analysis sample without the washout period exclusion results in 11 835 observations. Descriptive tables stratified by washout period are included in Supplementary Material, Section C .

Loss to follow-up (i.e. missing data in the posttest) was addressed through multiple imputation. Details are available in the shared analysis code.

Adjustment for observed confounders in the main analysis was done following a ‘pretreatment criterion’ [ 33 , 34 ]—based on domain knowledge, a set of baseline variables measured before medication dispensation initiation was selected. The covariates included in the BART term were: grade five national test scores for English, numeracy, and reading and respective missingness indicators; civil status of both mother and father at grades five and six; mother’s highest completed education; mother’s age at birth, pregnancy length, and parity; pupil’s sex and birth weight; birth year and month; a binary indicator for having at least one registration for ADHD for both parents; number of registered visits for an ADHD diagnosis, internalizing disorders, externalizing disorders, and any diagnosis prior to time-zero for both parents and the child, number of registered visits for sleep disturbances and specific learning problems prior to time-zero for the child, days medicated before time-zero, and a binary indicator for whether they had been medicated prior to time-zero (the latter two for the no-washout sample). The look-back period was at minimum six years and up to 12 years depending on the registry. Further variable descriptions are available in Supplementary Material, Section A .

All analyses were conducted using R version 4.2.3 [ 35 ], with the main analysis based on the package stan4bart [ 36 ].

### Sensitivity analyses

Our main sensitivity analysis includes the pupils that had taken ADHD medication before time-zero (i.e. no-washout period). In this manner, the target population of children diagnosed with ADHD is broadened. Additional sensitivity analyses, including negative controls [ 37 ] and proximal causal inference [ 38 , 39 ] are available in Supplementary Material, Section E .

Due to apparently conflicting results with previous studies, we conducted a post hoc informal replication of the analytic strategy of [ 19 ] on our data.
### Participants

The flow diagram in Fig. 2 summarizes the number of participants and respective exclusion criteria.

### Descriptive data

Descriptive statistics will be presented only for the washout sample. Table 1 shows frequencies across emulated treatment arm for different categorical variables. Emulated arms are relatively comparable—only medication variables have standardized mean differences exceeding an absolute value of 0.1.

Table 2 shows summary statistics for continuous variables. Standardized scores across all domains and for grades five and eight have a mean of around −0.5 SDs. This is expected, as scores are standardized relative to all children and our study sample concerns only children diagnosed with ADHD, which by definition involves negative academic impact [ 1 ]. There are few, if any, differences in the selected variables across the emulated arms, including the national test scores or grade point averages. Yet, we can see that the cutoffs chosen for time-zero and grace period generated a clear distinction of groups. The average estimated number of medication blocks—periods of treatment with no interruption longer than 30 days—was of 1.31 (SD, 0.64) for the ‘initiated’ condition and 0.41 (SD, 0.67) for the ‘control’ condition. This can also be seen in Fig. 3 , which shows the estimated percentage of medicated days between time-zero and the grade eight national test. In both the not-previously medicated sample and the no-washout sample, pupils in the ‘initiated’ group were medicated for about 85% of the days between their assignment and the posttest, whereas those in the ‘control’ group were medicated for about 12% of the days. In the ‘control’ group, 67.9% of pupils had zero estimated medicated days (72.1% in no-washout sample), while in the ‘initiated’ group, 6.1% of pupils had 100% estimated medicated days (5.8% in no-washout sample).

### Main analysis

Figure 4 shows the posterior distribution for the different causal effects estimated, both for the never-medicated-before sample (panel a in the top) and the no-washout sample (panel b in the bottom).

For the never-medicated-before sample, the SATE had a posterior mean (and compatibility interval) of 0.050 (CI 95 , 0.016; 0.084), 0.078 (CI 95 , 0.042; 0.117), 0.073 (CI 95 , 0.035; 0.108) standardized score points for the domains of English, numeracy, and reading, respectively (see Table 3 ).

Regarding heterogeneity, the estimated SATT posterior distributions show a small shift towards negative values for the numeracy domain. An ANOVA indicates that about 31.2% of the variability in effect estimates is accounted for by distinguishing the domain of the national test.

### Sensitivity analyses

Regarding results for the no-washout sample, the corresponding SATE and compatibility intervals were of 0.037 (CI 95 , −0.003; 0.076), 0.063 (CI 95 , 0.016; 0.111), 0.071 (CI 95 , 0.03; 0.111) standardized score points for the domains of English, numeracy, and reading, respectively (see Fig. 5 and Table 3 ).

Given the stark difference relative to Ref. [ 19 ], we performed an informal replication analysis to see whether the different effect sizes could be explained by the differing populations. We managed to estimate a similar point estimate after adjustment: −0.180 (standard error [SE], 0.07) and −0.176 (SE, 0.203), for Keilow et al. ’s population and ours, respectively. We did not manage to replicate their unadjusted effects, suggesting that the two populations are only somewhat comparable. Further details are available in the shared code.
discussion:
### Key results

Our main analysis suggests that, on average, initiating medication has a small positive effect on national test scores in the long-term in the population of children diagnosed with ADHD. Informally, the estimated compatibility intervals suggest that medication initiation bridges between 3.9% and 20.5% of the average gap between the grade eight scores of the ADHD sample relative to the general sample (see right panel of Supplementary Fig. S1 ). This is a slight overestimation as the achievement gap is calculated with the scores of medicated children. The estimated magnitude is consistent with long-term effect results from reviews [ 18 ] and from the MTA trial [ 11–13 ].

Effects vary minimally across test domains, with numeracy showing a slightly more positive effect. Detected heterogeneity of the effects via random slopes or interactions was negligible. Unobserved confounding was detected only for the reading domain (see Supplementary Material, Section E ), warranting cautious interpretation.

Regarding differences of effect sizes compared with some previous studies, we mostly attribute them to differences in estimand [ 40 ]. Under a comparable analytic and identifying strategy to Ref. [ 19 ] we are also able to estimate a larger order of magnitude effect in the Norwegian population. However, this effect is not a long-term intention-to-treat effect, but, rather, the effect of discontinuation among those who initiated medication (assuming random and sequentially exchangeable non-responsiveness to medication).

### Generalizability

Our studied population is restricted to children born in Norway, due to available registry data. Children born outside Norway face significant challenges throughout their education, which is reflected in lower levels of achievement and performance [ 41 ]. However, they are also less frequently diagnosed with ADHD [ 42 ], limiting their study participation so that their inclusion would not drastically alter our findings.

Moreover, the present study focused only on a long-term ‘as-started’ effect. This estimand informs about general policy effectiveness but does not address whether adhering to ADHD medication improves academic achievement, which may be more relevant to users themselves. However, discontinuation of treatment is not necessarily a treatment protocol violation [ 43 ], so ideally we would have data on the reason for discontinuation. Still, if in addition to satisfactory adjustment for baseline confounding we unrealistically assume perfect protocol adherence in the initiated arm, our intention-to-treat analysis would well approximate a per-protocol analysis. The estimated effect would be attenuated because 32.1% of control arm pupils had at least one medicated day.

### Limitations

Ideally, we would have intended daily dose, treatment duration, and prescription purpose (titration or stockpiling) data to inform about the actual treatment adherence of children. Instead, we used an algorithm [ 44 ] to estimate daily dosages and treatment duration, introducing an additional source of uncertainty in the process.

As with most observational studies, our causal interpretation rests on assuming no unobserved confounding. Any variable that would negatively affect academic achievement and increase the probability of treatment could partly explain why our estimated effect is so small. For example, disruptive behaviour in the classroom influences medication initiation independent of symptom severity [ 45 ]. However, this unobserved confounder should go beyond what was already adjusted for in our flexible model with a rich set of covariates, and should also have been undetected by the negative control exposure analysis.

### Implications

The main result of the present study suggests that initiating or continuing ADHD medication approximately one year after the grade five national test (and having an adherence pattern as naturally occurring in this subpopulation of children in this period) has a very small positive average effect on the later grade eight national test, for all three domains. This estimated magnitude was robust across a variety of model specifications, population subsets, and identifying strategies, although results for reading are more uncertain. This implies that ADHD pharmaceutical treatment initiation has a negligible average long-term effect on the acquisition of basic academic skills as measured by the national tests.

This does not rule out substantial positive (or negative) effects for specific children. However, individual treatment effects are harder to identify [ 46 ], and our model captured little to no heterogeneity of effects across measured covariates.

Our analysis is solely concerned with academic achievement, excluding other outcomes for which children might be medicated, like behavioural regulation.

### Future research

Besides replicating the analysis in other national registries with different contexts, we emphasize the need for studies that better quantify possible bias sources [ 47 ]. For example, studies on the causes of prescription and dispensation of ADHD pharmaceutical treatment, as well as the causes of exemption from national tests among children diagnosed with ADHD would inform on the extent of confounding and selection bias present, respectively. Likewise, quantitative validation studies into diagnosis practices among general practitioners and specialists in Norway would better inform inclusion criteria and the relevance of our analytic samples in generalizing to the broad population of children diagnosed with ADHD outside Norway.
A methodological conclusion is the importance of differentiating estimands [ 40 ] and triangulating identifying strategies for the estimation of causal effects [ 48 , 49 ]. Moreover, we highlight the use of negative controls in registry-based studies, where often a wide range of variables at different time points is available.

A clinical conclusion is that pharmaceutical treatment—as it was provided and implemented in the period and population of eligible children in this study—is insufficient to, on average, improve academic achievement to a relevant degree. Put differently, the achievement gap between the general population of children and those diagnosed with ADHD is far from being bridged by medication initiation.
target: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most commonly diagnosed mental disorders in children. The data were obtained through linkage of Norwegian registries (NorPD, Norwegian Prescription Database; NPR, Norwegian Patient Registry; KUHR, Database for Control and Payment of Health Reimbursement; SSB, Statistics Norway; MBRN, Medical Birth Registry of Norway).The resulting analytic sample size consisted of 8548 children diagnosed with ADHD, with about 9% missingness in their grade eight national test scores. The average age at pubertal onset has declined throughout the last century [ 1 , 2 ]. As earlier pubertal onset can have major health implications in adolescence and adult life, we need to identify potential modifiable factors in order to prevent further decline [ 3 ]. The Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) Puberty Cohort was established in 2012 with three distinct purposes: (i) to estimate the current age at puberty in a population-based sample, (ii) to identify the causes of earlier puberty based on the hypothesis that prenatal programming might affect pubertal development, and (iii) to identify the consequences of earlier puberty. The data collection ended in 2021 when all participants had turned 18 years of age.

The aim of this review is to gather and present the results obtained from the DNBC Puberty Cohort—the largest of its kind in the World to date—based on >10 years of research. The following aspects have been investigated as potential causes of earlier puberty: genetic predisposition and certain congenital malformations, maternal lifestyle and dietary factors in pregnancy, maternal diseases and medication use in pregnancy, prenatal exposure to potential endocrine disruptors, birth-related and postpartum factors, child health, and anthropometrics in addition to prenatal and early-life exposure to psychosocial factors.
This review is based on published studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort [ 4 ], nested within the DNBC [ 5 ]—an ongoing nationwide cohort of Danish women and their children. Recruitment into the DNBC took place from 1996 to 2002 at the women’s first antenatal visit at around gestational Week 8 at the general practitioner and ∼30% of all pregnant women in Denmark were included.

The women provided comprehensive information on health and health behavior at enrollment and in four computer-assisted telephone interviews scheduled during the pregnancy (gestational Weeks 16 and 32) and after the birth (6 and 18 months postpartum). In gestational Weeks 8 and 24, they provided blood samples for storage in the Danish National Biobank [ 5 ] and, in gestational Week 25, a subpopulation (72%) completed a validated, semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Seven- and 11-year questionnaires on maternal and child health and health behaviors have also been mailed to all participants for completion.

The DNBC Puberty Cohort includes a sample of children born to mothers participating in the DNBC, who answered the first interview in the DNBC and had not withdrawn from the DNBC by May 2012. Children were eligible for invitation if they were singletons who were born alive from 2000 to 2003. Of 56 641 eligible children, 22 439 were sampled [ 6 ] and invited to answer web-based questionnaires on current pubertal development. In total, 15 819 children (8123 girls and 7696 boys) participated ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ), corresponding to a participation rate of 70%. The questionnaires were sent out every 6 months from when the children were 11.5 years old until they reached 18 years or full maturity, defined as Tanner genital and pubic-hair development Stage 5 in boys and Tanner breast and pubic-hair development Stage 5 in girls [ 7 , 8 ]. Additionally, data on current pubertal development were obtained as part of the 11-year questionnaire. From 2012 to 2021, 98 195 questionnaires [average: 6.2 questionnaires (range 1–15)] were completed and returned ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

### Exposures

Information on exposures was obtained from gestational blood samples, from the DNBC enrollment form, DNBC Interviews 1–4, the mid-pregnancy FFQ, the 7-year and 11-year DNBC follow-ups, and by using ICD-10 diagnostic codes through linkage with the Danish National Patient Register (DNPR) and the Danish Medical Birth Registry (DMBR) ( Table 1 ).

### Outcomes

The pubertal milestones obtained from the DNBC Puberty Cohort included Tanner Stages 1–5 (breast and pubic-hair development [ 7 ] in girls and genital and pubic-hair development [ 8 ] in boys) with a short description and illustrations of each Tanner stage ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ); age at menarche (in years and months) in girls; the age at first ejaculation (in years and months) and voice break (yes, partly, no) in boys; and acne (yes, no) and axillary hair development (yes, no) in girls and boys.

Interpreting findings in our etiological studies, we looked at patterns of associations across the different pubertal milestones, but we also obtained a combined estimate according to the specific exposure of interest by using Huber White robust variance estimation. This technique reduces the risk of Type 1 errors by combining the estimates for the various individual milestones. These estimates are presented in the figures of this manuscript.

### Covariates

In all studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort, potential confounding factors were identified by using existing literature and directed acyclic graphs. Information on covariates was obtained from the DNBC or from the Danish registers ( Table 1 ).

### Statistical analysis

The duration, timing, tempo, and synchronicity of puberty have been described in two descriptive studies [ 1 , 9 ]. Risks of selection bias and information bias were assessed in two validation studies [ 10 , 11 ].

The statistical methods are described in detail in the Cohort Profile [ 4 ] and in the Supplementary text . As the children from the DNBC Puberty Cohort answered questions on current development every 6 months, the data on puberty were censored [ 4 ]. Therefore, all outcome data were analysed by using a regression model for normally distributed censored data fitted by maximum likelihood estimation, using the intreg package in Stata. Moreover, all analyses were fitted with inverse probability of sampling and selection weights [ 6 ].
### Descriptive studies

In girls, the onset of puberty (Tanner breast Stage 2) occurred at 10.5 years and age at menarche at 13.0 years. In boys, the onset of puberty (Tanner genital Stage 2) occurred at 11.1 years, voice break at 13.1 years, and first ejaculation at 13.4 years [ 1 ]. In girls, the mean duration of breast development (Tanner Stages 2–5) was 6.2 years and the mean tempo was 0.72 Tanner stages/year. In boys, the mean duration of genital development was 5.0 years and the mean tempo was 0.90 Tanner stages/year [ 9 ]. The mean age at menarche in girls was 3.6 (95% confidence interval 3.1, 4.2) months earlier than the mean age in their mothers [ 1 ], indicating that the age at menarche has significantly declined across one generation.

### Validation studies

Using information on an externally obtained marker of pubertal timing—the height difference in standard deviation (HD: SDS)—we found no association between pubertal timing and participation in the DNBC Puberty Cohort. This indicates that participation was at most only associated with the exposure of interest, indicating a minimal risk of selection bias [ 10 ].

By performing clinical examinations of 197 participants and comparing those to the self-reported information obtained from the puberty questionnaires, we found that the self-assessment of the pubertal milestones was fair to moderate with no tendency towards under- or overestimation except for genital development in boys. No difference in self-assessment was observed across levels of socioeconomic status [ 11 ].

### Etiological studies

The results are presented in Figs 1 and 2 .

Girls and boys of mothers who reported earlier age at menarche than their peers had earlier puberty by ∼4 and 2 months, respectively. Hence, this study provides epidemiologic support for shared genetic determinants of the timing of puberty in boys and girls [ 12 ]. Parental fecundity [ 13 ] and congenital heart disease were not associated with puberty [ 14 , 15 ]. Boys with hypospadias had later puberty by ∼2–3 months, whereas cryptorchidism was not associated with puberty ( Fig. 1a ) [ 15 ].

Maternal pre-pregnancy obesity was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls and ∼1.5 months in boys [ 16 ]. Maternal heavy smoking (>10 cigarettes daily) in the first trimester was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls and boys [ 6 ]. Alcohol intake was not strongly associated with puberty ( Fig. 1b ) [ 17 ].

Paternal age of >35 years at birth was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1 month in boys [ 18 ]. Prenatal exposure to father absence was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls [ 19 ] and prenatal exposure to maternal stress in pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ≤2–3 months in girls and boys ( Fig. 1c ) [ 20 ].

No consistent associations were observed for either dietary intake of nitrate or nitrate from drinking water [ 21 ], intake of folate or vitamin D supplementations [ 22 , 23 ], whereas lower vitamin D levels predicted by using the season as an instrumental variable was associated with slightly earlier puberty in girls and boys ( Fig. 1d ) [ 24 ].

Gestational diabetes mellitus was associated with earlier puberty by 2.5 months in girls [ 25 ]. Girls of mothers with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) experienced earlier puberty by ∼3.5 months. When only adrenarche (pubarche, axillary hair and acne) was looked at, girls of mothers with PCOS experienced earlier puberty by on average 5.4 months [ 26 ]. Preeclampsia, eclampsia or Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzyme, and Low Platelet syndrome were associated with earlier puberty by ∼2 months in girls [ 27 ]. Maternal hyperthyroidism was associated with earlier puberty by ≤3 months in boys [ 28 ]. Maternal nausea in the first trimester was not associated with puberty [ 29 ], whereas maternal asthma in pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1 month in boys ( Fig. 1e ) [ 30 ].

Maternal unintended intake of oral contraceptives in early pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1–1.5 months in girls and boys [ 31 ]. Neither prenatal exposure to antibiotics [ 32 ], glucocorticoid treatment [ 33 ], nor nitrosatable drugs [ 34 ] were strongly associated with puberty. Intake of acetaminophen in pregnancy showed a tendency towards earlier puberty in girls by 1.5 months ( Fig. 1f ) [ 35 ]. Prenatal exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was associated with altered puberty, although the magnitude (range: –7 to +5 months) and pattern of association varied by sex, type of pubertal indicator, and specific PFAS. Moreover, only a small sample ( n = 1167) had PFAS measured in maternal blood samples, thus the confidence intervals were broad ( Fig. 1g ) [ 36 ].

Girls and boys of mothers being in the first pregnancy trimester during the winter half-year had earlier puberty by ≤1 month [ 24 ]. Delivery mode was not associated with puberty [ 37 ]. Girls experienced slightly earlier puberty per standard deviation lower placental Z-score [ 38 ]. Being born large for gestational age (birth weight >90th percentile for age and sex) was associated with later puberty by ∼2 months in girls but by ∼1 month in boys, whereas being small for gestational age (birth weight <10th percentile for age and sex) was associated with later puberty by ∼1 month in both sexes [ 39 ]. Absence of breast feeding was associated with later puberty by 4 months in boys ( Fig. 1h ) [ 40 ].

Having atopic dermatitis was not associated with puberty [ 41 ]. Childhood obesity was associated with later puberty by ∼5 months in girls and ∼3.5 months in boys [ 42 ]. Father absence in childhood was associated with later puberty by ≤2–3 months in girls and boys [ 19 ]. Girls and boys with no siblings had earlier puberty by ≤5–6 months, and girls and boys with half and/or stepsiblings had earlier puberty by ≤2 months [ 43 ]. Gender incongruence (i.e. a mismatch between one’s gender and the birth-assigned sex) was associated with later puberty by 2–3 months ( Fig. 1i ) [ 44 ].

Overall, some of the studied exposures were associated with later puberty, some exposures showed weak or no associations with puberty, while some of the studied exposures were associated with earlier puberty of a magnitude that is likely to have a clinical impact at the societal level. Most pronounced were the associations for child obesity, maternal smoking in pregnancy, most psychosocial exposures, absence of breastfeeding (in boys), and most maternal gestational diseases ( Fig. 2 ).
discussion:
### Key results

The DNBC Puberty Cohort was established and the data collection successfully completed with a high participation rate and several consecutive questionnaires per participant. Data were analysed by using state-of-the-art statistical methods. The estimated age at puberty in this large population-based sample indicated a further decline and characteristics such as pubertal tempo, duration, and synchronicity were described for both sexes. The validity of the collected information on pubertal milestones was deemed sufficient in terms of potential information bias [ 11 ] and the risk of selection bias was investigated and found to be minimal [ 10 ]. Moreover, several etiological studies identified associations with earlier puberty and, for some factors, also later puberty.

### Strengths and limitations

Children participating in the DNBC Puberty Cohort had parents of higher socioeconomic status and their mothers were more likely to be of normal weight, nonsmoking in the first trimester, and older at delivery compared with mothers of nonparticipating children [ 10 ]. Reassuringly, we found no association between puberty (by using a register-based marker of puberty) and participation in the DNBC Puberty Cohort, indicating a minimal risk of selection bias, even if the studied exposures were associated with participation [ 10 ].

Information on puberty was obtained by self-report. This approach was chosen following the recommendations of an expert panel urging the need for large-scale studies on pubertal timing [ 2 ]. In comparison, inviting children for a clinical examination is costly and induces a larger risk of selection bias due to lower participation rates and risk of selective participation by specific subgroups. Though we risk misclassifications, the self-assessment was found to be fair to moderate and independent of levels of socioeconomic status [ 11 ]. Moreover, the longitudinal data collection of all pubertal milestones constitutes a major strength of the DNBC Puberty Cohort, limiting the risk of misclassifications due to recall. Altogether, the study demonstrated that the self-assessment of pubertal development serves as a reasonable and time-saving tool to obtain pubertal information in a large prospective setting.

Enriched by the unique and detailed information from multiple follow-up waves in the DNBC, we had excellent opportunities to investigate numerous exposures by using the high-quality longitudinal data and to sufficiently control for confounding to an unmatched extent in cohort studies of this size.

### Interpretation

A secular trend of earlier age at menarche during the last century is evident [ 45 ]. The primary driver of the early part of this decline has been attributed to better nutrition and living conditions [ 45 ]. We found that girls had menarche at a mean age of 13 years—almost 4 months earlier than their mothers [ 12 ], indicating that the age at menarche is continuing to decline. We also found that childhood obesity was associated with significantly earlier puberty, suggesting that the obesity epidemic may be a major driver of this continuing decline [ 42 ]. Further, maternal age at menarche was strongly associated with puberty in both girls and boys, indicating a strong genetic component of pubertal timing overlapping between genders [ 12 ].

We found that both prenatal and childhood biological and psychosocial exposures might affect puberty. Our findings thus support the hypothesis that prenatal programming might affect pubertal development [ 46 ]. Most of the studied factors were associated with earlier puberty and the different exposures in combination may potentially drive some of the observed secular trend towards earlier puberty. The strongest risk factors for early puberty were child obesity [ 42 ], maternal smoking in pregnancy [ 6 ], most psychosocial exposures [ 19 , 43 ], absence of breastfeeding (in boys) [ 40 ], and most maternal gestational diseases [ 25–28 ]. This highlights the potential of intervening in e.g. maternal smoking in pregnancy to prevent earlier puberty. On the other hand, psychosocial factors do not offer obvious opportunities for intervention. Still, society and healthcare workers should know and understand these associations with the potential to identify vulnerable adolescents at an increased risk of earlier puberty.

Besides having no siblings, an absence of breastfeeding was the strongest risk factor for earlier puberty in boys, whereas breastfeeding was not associated with puberty in girls. On the contrary, most maternal diseases during pregnancy were associated with earlier puberty in girls, whereas boys appeared largely unaffected. Overall, maternal health and different exposures might influence puberty in a sex- and condition-specific manner. In addition to the well-established potential consequences of maternal diseases during pregnancy, prevention and treatment are likewise important in relation to the future reproductive health of children.

Environmental endocrine disrupters (EDCs) have been suggested to play an important role in the declining pubertal age [ 47 ]. Studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort did not support consistent effects of EDCs, although we cannot exclude moderate effects of some of the examined factors [ 36 ]. Future steps would be to examine the potential cocktail effect of constantly being exposed to multiple factors in our environment and, in recent years, several analytic approaches have been developed for this purpose [ 48 ]. Further, capturing the true exposure levels by combining self-reported information with biological measurement in addition to details on the specific timing of exposure, duration, and dosage are important for improvements in future studies.

The DNBC Puberty Cohort has been extended to identify potential causes of later puberty too, as later puberty may also be associated with mental health consequences and fecundity [ 3 ]. We found that boys with hypospadias [ 15 ] and boys of mothers with asthma [ 30 ] had later puberty by ∼1–3 months. Also, most maternal dietary factors (folate, vitamin D) in pregnancy were associated with slightly later puberty in boys [ 22 , 23 ]. Hence, most associations with earlier puberty were strongest in girls and later puberty was primarily found in boys. This is concerning, as earlier puberty in girls and later puberty in boys may have psychosocial and mental consequences in adolescence [ 49 ].

Leveraging the unique longitudinal design of the unique DNBC Puberty Cohort, key risk factors associated with earlier puberty have been identified, thereby significantly advancing the scientific understanding within this critical area of research. A subset of the DNBC Puberty Cohort has already been genotyped and ongoing efforts to genotype even more participants aim to enable the integration of genetic, environmental, and social data, providing deeper insights into the interplay between these aspects and puberty.

### Perspectives

The data collection in the DNBC Puberty Cohort is complete and the children who were followed through adolescence are now young adults. Therefore, the consequences of earlier puberty can be assessed. By using the rich data in the Danish registries, all participants from the DNBC Puberty Cohort can be followed regarding the development of health conditions, morbidities, and medicine use. Further, in an 18-year DNBC follow-up, adolescents answered questions on mental health in a web-based questionnaire, enabling us to investigate associations between earlier puberty and self-reported mental health. During their twenties, they are invited to answer questions on health and health behavior, mental health and well-being, fertility intentions, and fecundity. This gives the opportunity to investigate whether earlier puberty is an early marker on the path towards poor reproductive health and health in general.

Accelerated biological aging, defined as a greater biologic than chronological age, is a major risk factor for the occurrence and aggravation of cardiometabolic diseases (e.g. stroke, diabetes), cognitive decline, dementia, as well as multimorbidity and increased mortality [ 1–3 ]. Accelerated biological aging acts as a key and shared pathogenic process underlying the development and progression of a wide variety of diseases, reflecting integrated molecular and cellular damage, as well as systemic dysregulation [ 2 , 4 , 5 ]. To effectively mitigate biological age acceleration, there is an urgent need to better understand the determinants of the biological aging process.

Except for genetics, ambient environmental factors are a major contributor to biological aging [ 6 ]. Exposure to climate-related disasters has been found to be associated with persistent elevated risks of morbidity [ 7 ] and mortality [ 8 , 9 ] in the population. At the cellular and molecular levels, these long-term adverse health effects may be partially attributed to epigenetic aging acceleration after exposures, as severe hardship could induce acute and chronic stress responses such as chronic low-grade inflammation and immune-cell expression changes (e.g. the abundance and functional state of leucocyte subtypes), thereby advancing canonical hallmarks of aging [ 10–12 ]. However, to our knowledge, no population-based studies have yet been conducted to assess the association of extreme weather event exposures and biological aging acceleration. This would help elucidate the potential mechanisms by which climate-related disasters affect human health, which is particularly important given the aging population and the increasing severity of climate-related disasters in a changing climate [ 13 ].

To address this research gap, using blood data from participants across Australia, we calculated the DNA methylation age (DNAmAge)—a very robust biomarker of biological aging in predicting the physical and physiological functional capability of a person (e.g. musculoskeletal strength and mobility) compared with other biological aging indicators [ 14 , 15 ]. Furthermore, DNA methylation is modifiable by environmental factors and interventions, making it a more sensitive indicator of environmental stresses and a validated tool for identifying healthy aging determinants [ 16 ]. Although there are stressor-specific patterns observed in chronic (e.g. socioeconomic stress) versus acute (e.g. trauma) exposures [ 17 , 18 ], DNAmAge integrates these diverse impacts into a composite measure of biological aging. Tropical cyclones (TCs) and floods are the two most common and destructive climate-related disasters [ 19 ] and share similar pathways in affecting public health (e.g. interrupting health services, increasing psychosocial stress) [ 7 ]. Therefore, we aimed to investigate whether these exposures were associated with higher DNAmAge acceleration (DNAmAgeAC, i.e. the difference between DNAmAge and chronological age) in the population and to evaluate various leucocyte subtypes as potential mediators reflecting immune states or responses following these exposures.
### Study settings, design, and participants

We leveraged the existing data and study design from the Australian Mammographic Density Twins and Sisters Study (AMDTSS), described in detail previously [ 20 , 21 ]. This study employed a twin and family design, focusing on female twins aged 40–70 years who had no historical records of breast cancer and were not pregnant or nursing mothers. Eligible participants residing in three distinct Australian urban centers (Melbourne, Sydney, and Perth) were recruited through the Australian Twin Registry between 1995 and 1999. An extended recruitment was subsequently conducted between 2004 and 2009 to include additional eligible participants [ 20 ].

All AMDTSS participants with DNA methylation measurements were eligible for the present study, which comprised 479 women from 130 families. Written informed consent was obtained from all individuals prior to participation. Ethical approval for the AMDTSS was obtained from the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Melbourne. This specific analysis received approval from the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee (reference number 17813).

### DNA methylation data and DNAmAge

Between 2005 and 2008, the participants provided a 27-ml peripheral blood sample via a visit to a designated pathology laboratory. Trained phlebotomists conducted blood collection at their homes in cases in which participants were unable to access the designated laboratory. All blood samples were dispatched to the biobank for processing within 48 hours of collection. Blood processing included the preparation of a Guthrie card for each participant. DNA was extracted from the Guthrie cards for DNA methylation measurement. The methylation of blood-derived DNA samples was measured by using the Illumina Infinium HumanMethylation450 BeadChip arrays [ 22 ] and processed by utilizing the Bioconductor minfi package [ 23 ], with detailed methodology elucidated in our previous work [ 21 , 24 ].

Based on the cleaned DNA methylation data and an online calculator ( https://dnamage.clockfoundation.org/ ), we calculated six metrics of DNAmAge, including Horvath’s age (derived from 353 cytosine-phosphate-guanine sites [CpGs]) [ 25 ], Hannum’s age (71 CpGs) [ 26 ], PhenoAge (513 CpGs) [ 27 ], Zhang’s age (514 CpGs) [ 28 ], and GrimAge versions 1 (GrimAge1) and 2 (GrimAge2) (both derived from 1030 CpGs) [ 29 ]. A summary of the relevancy of these markers is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . This calculator, which uses well-established and widely validated DNA methylation-based epigenetic clock algorithms, has been widely applied in previous studies to estimate biological age [ 21 , 30 , 31 ].

### TC and flood exposures

We obtained the global TC and flood events data for between 1993 and 2009 from the International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship [ 32 ] and Dartmouth Flood Observatory [ 33 ], respectively, to estimate the TC and flood exposure of each individual based on their residential address. A participant was considered exposed to a flood or TC if their home was located within the affected areas. A detailed methodology of the exposure assessment is provided in Supplementary Text S1 . Our primary exposure was defined for each subject based on whether they had been exposed to TCs or floods.

### Covariates and candidate mediators

We collected demographic information and self-reported lifestyles from each participant through a telephone-administered questionnaire. Detailed questions were reported in our previous work [ 21 ].

We defined potential confounding variables as factors that could affect both the TC and flood exposures and DNAmAge, but were not on the pathways between them [ 34 ]. We used a directed acyclic graph, constructed by using DAGitty v3.1 software [ 35 ], to identify potential covariates to adjust for confounding and candidate mediators between the exposure and outcome based on the literature ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The covariates included were chronological age, educational level, marital status, smoking and drinking status, area-level socioeconomic status (SES), and annual mean temperature and relative humidity (RH). We incorporated various types of leucocyte cells as candidate mediators, based on the assumptions that (i) TC and flood exposures could influence DNAmAge by changing their levels [ 36 , 37 ] and (ii) these blood cell types were unlikely to affect the probability of TC and flood exposure (i.e. not a confounder) ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). A detailed definition of these covariates and mediators is given in Supplementary Text S2 .

### Statistical analysis

To account for the clustering within families in our data, we used a linear mixed-effect and distributed lag nonlinear model to assess the DNAmAgeAC associated with TC or flood exposures. A distributed lag term of ≤12 months after exposures was included in the model to account for the potential delayed effects [ 38 ]. Detailed model descriptions and specifications are provided in Supplementary Text S3 . The results are presented as the change (i.e. the regression coefficient of β ), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), in DNAmAgeAC among the participants exposed to TC or flood compared with those unexposed. A series of sensitivity analyses (e.g. different model specifications) was conducted to test the robustness of our results, as detailed in Supplementary Text S4 .

To identify potential effect modifiers and vulnerable populations, we further conducted a pre-specified subgroup analysis by using the same modeling strategy as in the main model analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed by using area-level SES (lowest 50% vs highest 50%), educational level (secondary or below vs higher than secondary), age group (<60 vs ≥60 years), smoking behavior (never smoked vs current/former smoker), DNA methylation-based smoking index (≤ median vs > median), alcohol use (never drank vs current/former drinker), marital status (married or living as married vs never married/widowed/separated/divorced), and suburban residence (rural vs urban). Between-subgroup statistical difference in effect estimates was tested by using a Wald-type test [ 39 ]. A causal and parallel mediation analysis was performed to assess the potential mediation effects of the candidate mediators [i.e. the seven types of leucocytes, including naive CD8 + T cells, exhausted cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, plasma blasts, CD4 + T cells, granulocytes, monocytes, natural killer (NK) cells] [ 40 ], as detailed in Supplementary Text S5 .

All analyses were performed via R software (version 4.1.3), using the R packages of ‘mice’ [five multiple imputations by chained equations to impute missing values for educational level (two participants) and area-level SES (one participant)], ‘lme4’ (linear mixed-effect model), ‘splines’ (nature cubic splines), and ‘dlnm’ (cross-basis function).
A total of 479 participants from various regions across Australia were included in this study ( Fig. 1 ). All participants were female, with an average chronological age of 56.4 years (SD: 7.9) ( Tables 1 and 2 ). The distribution of participants across different area-level SESs and educational levels was similar. Approximately 28.4% (136/479) were exposed to TCs or floods during the 12 months before their blood draw and the remaining 71.6% (343/479) were not exposed during this period ( Table 1 ). Among the six metrics of DNAmAgeAC, Zhang’s age acceleration exhibited the smallest variation [SD: 1.34, interquartile range (IQR): 1.47], whereas PhenoAge acceleration showed the largest variation (SD: 5.78, IQR: 8.17) ( Table 2 ). The distributions of these metrics by exposure status and subgroup variables are presented in Supplementary Tables S2–S6 .

Figure 2 shows the temporal pattern of DNAmAgeAC related to TC or flood during the 0- to 12-month post-exposure period. The magnitude of the DNAmAgeAC associated with TCs or floods generally decreased over time after exposures ( P for trend was consistently < .001 for the six DNAmAgeAC metrics). The effects of a TC or flood on DNAmAgeAC tended to be minimal 6 months after exposure. We thus focused on the effect estimates of DNAmAgeAC in the first 6 months after exposure. The cumulative effects of a TC or flood on DNAmAgeAC over the 6 months after exposures are shown in Fig. 3 . Overall, participants exposed to TCs or floods had higher DNAmAgeAC based on Horvath’s age (2.66 years, 95% CI: –2.94 to 8.27; P = .357), Hannum’s age (6.81 years, 95% CI: 1.75–11.88; P = .008), PhenoAge (8.96 years, 95% CI: 2.35–15.57; P = .008), Zhang’s age (0.93 years, 95% CI: –0.56 to 2.42; P = .224), GrimAge1 (2.60 years, 95% CI: –0.64 to 5.83; P = .115), and GrimAge2 (4.31 years, 95% CI: 0.52–8.09; P = .026), and compared with those unexposed. Similar results were observed in the sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Figs S2–S6 ).

When the effects across population subgroups were assessed ( Fig. 3 ), the age acceleration of GrimAge2 related to TC or flood exposures was higher among the participants whose area-level SES was below the median of Australia compared with those with a higher area-level SES (8.99 years, 95% CI: 1.07–16.90, P = .026 vs 0.98 years, 95% CI: –3.85 to 5.80; P = .704). The effect estimates also varied between age groups, with greater TC- or flood-associated age acceleration in PhenoAge and Hannum’s age for participants <60 years old compared with their counterparts. However, there was not sufficient evidence to detect the between-group difference for other DNAmAgeAC metrics.

For participants in different smoking categories, no difference in the DNAmAgeAC level was found between current/former smokers and never smokers after TC or flood exposures ( Fig. 3 ). However, when a DNA methylation-based continuous smoking index was used to indicate the smoking levels, participants with a higher smoking index (> median) had greater age acceleration in PhenoAge and Zhang’s age compared with those with a lower smoking index (≤ median). By comparison, current/former drinkers exhibited higher age acceleration in more DNAmAgeAC metrics, including PhenoAge, Horvath’s age, Hannum’s age, and Zhang’s age, compared with the nondrinkers. There was insufficient evidence to detect the differences in DNAmAgeAC metrics between subgroups based on educational level, suburban residence, or marital status.

In the mediation analyses ( Table 3 ), we found that the seven subsets of leucocytes mediated a major part of the effects TC or flood exposures on DNAmAgeAC based on PhenoAge (48.3%, 95% CI: 28.0%–76.9%), GrimAge2 (74.3%, 95% CI: 46.3%–124.9%), and Hannum’s age (58.4%, 95% CI: 36.9%–92.4%). In general, naive CD8 + T cells, exhausted cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, and granulocytes were the leading types of cells that contributed most to the mediation effects. The mediated proportions of naive CD8 + T cells, exhausted cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, and granulocytes ranged from 23.0%–29.4%, 9.1%–28.3%, and 10.3%–20.5%, respectively, across various DNAmAgeAC metrics. In contrast, consistently weaker and nonsignificant mediation effects were observed for plasma blasts and CD4 + T cells.
